ghe first 'marriage of Oolin, Earl of Lindsay and 13i'im'rres, to Manrizia it Ni:ssau, took place in extreme youth, at I.tle Court of James LI., under the circunistances narrated.] In blithe London Town Ne'er such bridal was known this of Earl Colin, the Lindsay so gay:; O'er the Border, in soiiith, Never came bonnier youth, Aud the King's self shall give the fair hdy away. The bridesmaids and bride Are here in their pride it why ere the rite this long pause and delay? 'Tis for Colin they wait— The 'Light Lindsay.' is late; The bridegroom forgetteth his own marriage-day

The envoy was meet, And the bridegrcom is fleet, ' Ile.stands at the altar in bridal array; But what lacks he now? Why this cloud on his brow ? The ring that should make her his countess for aye! Oh, a ring's easy found 'Mid the guests standing round! .T :And a borrowed ring served on that strange marriage day; But when spoke was the oath That united them both, She looked on the ring, and she fainted away. 'Twas a ring with a tomb And a lend of grloom, And she wist that to death she was wedded that day. They cheered her amain; But, alas, 'twas in vain! And she drooped and she died ere a year was away. —Jetty Vogel in Clutinhers's Journal.

ON YARROW BRAES. The wind, the summer wind of June, Was on our cheeks as, in the heather, We lay that happy afternoon On Yarrow braes together. Far down below was Yarrow Manse, Within its little woOdland hiding, And by it, like ri silver glance, The stream itself was gliding. And farther up in greyer light, The "dowie dens' lay in their shadow, And only half made out to sight By spots of corn and meadow. And Tinnis hill rose huge and steep, Its ridge against the sky receding; And white upon its breast the sheep By twos and threes were feeding. Westward from Yarrow Kirk, within A field that speaks of love and loving, - A single stone was seen to win The eye from all its roving. Atil well it might, for round that stone Such tender consecration hovers, That love might. rest his cheek thereon And weep for hapless lovers. And in the wind that came and went, We heard a music weird and lonely; The past was in its tones and blent With human sorrow only. And pity for all things that love Has set in legendary story, 'To haunt grey crag and hill, and move Round ruins bleak and hoary. The dim old world of song that sings Of tender love in old romances, `Was with us, touching all the strings . That, woke our saddest fancies. 'We heard the sounds of wail and pain, Faint from that far-off time of sorrow; The misty years came back again, 4.. And look-'d with us on Yarrow. All this, and more, that summer day, Was with us, as among the heather, A ballad on our lips, we lay Ott Yarrow braes together. Goa 'Words. ALEXANDER ANDERFON.

esTeaeiltal Exercise—Turning over money. As Teasoriably expect oaks train a mushroom bed as great and durable profits from small and hasty alerts. He who loves his kind and does not live for himself has true happiness, and of p, kind which poverty does not rasp nor the direst misfortures kill. When the forenoons of life are wasted there is not much hope of a peaceful and fruitful evening. Sun- risings and sun-settings are closely connected in every experience. All ignorance and all ill-doing redound to the injury -elf the entire community; therefore each one is vitally and personally interested in the character and 'welfare ' of every other one. Remember that you are never justified in aiding or abetting on the wide theatre of national responsibility what in the narrowest sphere of private life, as a con- scientious man, you would disown. Pride emanates from a weak mind. You never see a man of strong intellect proud and haughty. Just look about you. Who are the most given to this folly? Not the intelligent and talented, but the weak-minded and the silly. There is no such certain badge and ensign of a sovereign mind, as that tenacity of purpose, which through all change of companions, of parties, of .fortune, changes never, bates no jot of heart or hope, but wearies out opposition, and arrives at its port. WORRIED ABOUT Hies—He had been out fora day's fishing. and as he proudly displayed the contents- of his basket to his wife, she exclaimed: "Oh, John, aren't they beauties! But I've been so anxious for the past hour, dear'!" "Foolish 'little one!" said John caressingly, "Why, what could have happened to me?" -" Oh, I didn't worry about you, love, but it grew so late I was afraid that before you got back to town the fish markets would all be closed." The one primary necessity of all fine language is sin- cerity. Let a man utter what he honestly thinks or earnestly feels, and at once his diction becomes; clear, and even pure. The very tlffort to say exactly whathe means educates and refines his speech. On the other hand, if he•be not sure of what he means or feels, if he tries to accommodate himself to what he supposes is expected of him, or if he more deliberately aims to convey a false impression, his language will be contused and obscure. We are touching our fellow beings on all sides. They are affected by what we are, by what we say and do, even by what we think and feel. May flowers in the parlour breathe their fragrance through the atmosphere. We are each of us silently saturating the atmosphere about us with the subtle aroma of our characters. In the family circle, besides and beyond all the teaching, the daily life of each parent and child mysteriously modifies the life of every person in the household_ The same process on a wider scale is going on through the community. No man liveth to himself, and no man dieth to himself. Other are built up and strengthened by our unconscious deeds; and others may be wrenched nut of their places and thrown down by our unconscious influence. A PAIR OF THE-AL—I must tell you of something I heard about a lady from the South (I can't believe from Georgia), who, the other day, was chaperoning a young female friend from her seCtion in Washington. In the Corcoran Gallery the lady, after other siehts, led her • ileve to the statues of Apollo and Diana. "Now here, my dear Bessie," she said, with as much spirit as was possible to a rather languid person who had so much of that sort of work on hand—" here is one of the ver' , splen,diJest things in this whole town. That is the ' cele- brated Apollo, and that," she said, pointing to his no less famous sister,'" is—Appolinaris." This reminded me of a scene I witnessed at the Centennial. I was standing before the statue of " The Young Achilles" in the Anneii, when d portly lady, accompanied by a couple of grown- up girls (I hope they were not Vermonters), came Up. After reading the card she said, " Ah, now! Yes, that's the young Are,hilus! Now don't he look sweet ?"_._ Harper's Magazine. WHAT TH,E IcIITHYOSAURUS SAW.—MiIIiOTIS. of years . ago a creature existed which the astronomer can hardly • regard without feelings al:in to envy. The iclithyosaurus ,cannot be coneidered strictly beautiful, according to 'modern ideas. A gigantic lizard, with monstrous flap- leers, and a particularly objectionable "smile" (to use -11 r. Venus's expression), would compare unfavourably even with the most flatfooted of the platpieds of science, Ilandly explaining to an exhausted audience the pecu- liar advantages of quadri-dimensional space. But the ichthyosaurus had an eye which even a Herschel might .envy. This eye (of course he had a pair, though they new have been to our ideas singular) was about a foot in diameter. rnfortunately, in regard to astronomical research, the ichthyosaurus would appear to have passed the greater portion of its time under water, and in a dim, stliough scarcely religious light. Still the creature must occasionally have raised its head above the water, espe- cially when the mantle of night was spread over the earth. At such times, what a glorious scene must the licav6ns have displayed to this large-eyed reptile! For each star ehe modern astronomer can see, the ancient ichthyosaarus must have seen hundreds if not thou- sands. Instead of some three thousand stars, it must have seen hundreds of thousands if not millions of suns all at one grand view. Perhaps it did not care much for all those glorious suns. As it paddled along, snorting on its way for want, or thought, it probably paid much more attention to conveniently juicy objects of prey than to the "Celestial objects for common telescopes" -which must have been easily within therange of its un- common vision. Its cranium corresponded by no means in capacity with the light-gathering power of its gog- gling eyes and three millions of sus would be less in- teresting than a couple of succulent mouthfuls to a crea- ture which probably could not count up to 'three. But -•we do not lose interest in the Reese telescope because it thinks nothing a all the Wonders it reveals.—" 2V3w Eyes . for Science," in Cornhill 2.fagazine. .As COOL AS A CUCUMBEIs."—Ladies will find " Beetham's Glycerine and cut umber delightfully cooling and refreahlm: if applied to the hands .or face after being out in the hot Puri, tennis playing, yachting., de. The Train was only Half-loaded.--Scene—American restaurant. Guest: "Why don't you beat your steak be- fore cooking it? This seems to be rather tough." Waiter: "Beating doesn't help our steak. We do better than that. We put it on the railroad track and let a freight-train run over it; but this morning the train was only half-loaded, and consequently the Steak is not quite as tender as it ought to be." Of the countless good stories attributed to Artemus Ward, the best one, perhaps, is one which tells of the advice which he gave to a Southern railroad contractor soon after the war. The road was in a wretched condi- tion, and the trains, consequently, were run at -a phenomenally low rate of speed. When the conductor was punching his ticket, Artemus remarked, "Does this raiiroad company allow passengers to give it advice, - if they do so in a respectful manner ?" The conductor 'replied in gruff 'tones that he supposed. so. "Well," Artemus went on, "it occured to me that it wculd be ovell to detach the cow-catcher from the front of the 1-engine, and hitch it to the rear of the train; for, you see, 1 we are not liable to overtake a cow, but what's to pre- 'vent a cow strolling into this car and biting a passenger. 1 A CHEERFIIL ITINERANT.—The following is sent as an indication of the cheerful resignation of some of the 1 itinerants, by the pastor of the Methodist Episcopal ' Church in an inland town, who says :—" Not long since 'one of the preachers in this district of the Illinois Con- ference sent the following quaint epistle to his Presiding I Elder. The writer of the poem is a genius in his way. • He himself built the waggon in which he travels his cit.- : cult, and has invented :fly brush which works with a 1 treadle for the table, and the table itself is made with ' two circular tops, the lower one Stationary, and the upper one revolving, whenever one of his children de- sires anything opposite him, by simply giving it a whirl. • I think this ought to be interesting, as I have found nothing so quaint for a long time :" B—.' Illinois, March —. Rev. —. Dear Brother,—l have . received since Conference from Bath Society, $1 ; from Union, I 81. .No one makes any effort in that directioa. I can only ! trust and wait. I have added the following to my prayers : Since all my money now is gone, And I have naught to live upon, Grant me, 0 Lord, the special grace For meat and bread to run my race. As I have followed, at Thy call, To preach the Gospel unto all, Give me. 0 Lord, for every day My bread, for which I can not pay. I must depend, 0 Lord, on Thee; I The stewards can't collect for me, For people have to pay their tax, I No matter what Thy kingdom lacks.
I am trying to raise the deficit on youi: claim, but don't have much encouragement. Will do my best.—Your brother in Christ,

—Harper's Magazine. Noss.—A popular lecturer in one of his discourses had occasion' to speak on noses, and he himself," defec- tive only in his Roman nose," declared, had he the choice of noses, his face should be ornamented by a "regular weather-cutter." The desire was commend- able and worthy attention' for strangers are instinctively judged by their noses. The nose indeed proclaims the man, and is the outward and visible symbol of inward mental calibre and intellectual character. 'Men of note almost invariably possess decided and prominent" lead- ing articles ;" whilst an insufficient nasal accompaniment not unfrequently denotes inanity, lack of moral -vigour, and at once negatives qualities which would otherwise give respect and credit. Of course there are extremes and exceptions; but generally it is that the more pro- longed the proboscis the more striking is the counten- ance and the more original the force of character. An extreme case is recorded of a Lancashire man, whose prodigious feature became a centre of attraction in the busiest thoroughfares of Manchester, whilst:he:was on a visit there. Becoming at length either tired or con- fused by the inquisitive attention and wonderment of a ! crowd of admirers, he seized his nose with both hands and gave it a sudden impatient twist, as though remov- ing an obstruction from the footway; andOid sharply: "There—be quick, and get past as soon as you can." A 1 Yorkshire manufacturer whose good living had given ' him "a nose as red as a comet," was told by a wealthy friend very bluntly, "1 couldn't afford to keep that nose of thine." Amongst the South Sea .Islanders the nose is made to be a •medium of expression of affectioni and I amity. Tribes swearing everlasting peace seal the com- pact with -a promiscuous rubbing of noses against noses; by the same frictional process maidens declaim their woes at parting and joys on reunion with other maidens, I the action being attended by—so said an eye-witness— "the shedding of a power of tears." Lovers make their amatory declarations through their noses, their court- ship being a protracted series or rub-rub-rubbing of I nose to nose. We recall an interruption Dr. Binney had whilst he was preaching on one occasion:all° saw oppo- site to him in the gallery a countrymatt making .elabo- rate preparations for putting his handkerchief to the common usage appointed to it. The doctor became in- terested, and stayed expectant in his discours:e just , before the crisis. The countryman blew a terrible blast, awakening the echoes, and almost perceptibly:shaking ! the building to its foundations. The doctor, haying Met with many a breeze before. . But never such a blow, waited for the fainting echoes to die, and then said with impressive gravity: "Let us now resume."—Chambers's Journal. WONDERS OF MEMORY.—Many an instance might be cited to show that men of very moderate intellectual capacity may be endowed with a power of memory which lis truly prodigious. In addition to this, there are plenty of well-authenticated examples of the extraordinary power of memory displayed even by idiots. In the me- Imoirs of Mrs. Somerville there is a curious account of a most extraordinary verbal memory. "There was an idiot in Edinburgh," she tells us, "of a respectable family who had a remarkable memory. He never failed to go to the kirk on Sunday; and on returning home, could repeat the sermon, saving: Here thelminister coughed; here he stopped tallow his nose.' "During the tour we made in the Highlands," she adds, "we met with anothe- idiot who knew the Bible so perfectly, that • if you asked•him where such a verse was to be found, he could tell without hesitation and repeat the chapter." ! These examples are sufficiently remarkable ; but what shall be said of the case cited by Archdeaconrearon in his valuable pamphlet on Mental Vigour? "There was in my father's parish," says the archdeacon, "a man who could remember the day when every person had , been buried in the parish for thirty-five years, and could repeat with unvarying accuracy the name and age of the deceased, with the mourners at the funeral. But he was a complete fool. Out of the line of burials, he had but one idea, and could not give an intelligible reply to a single question, nor be trusted to feed himself." These phenomenal instances may be matched by the Sussex • farm labourer George Watson, as we find recorded in Hone's Table Book. Watson could neither read nor write, I yet he was wont to perform wondrous feats of mental ! calculation, and his memory for events seemed to be I almost faultless. "'But the more extraordinary circum- stance," says Hone, -"is the power he possesses of recol- lecting the events of every day from an early period of 11iis life. Upon being asked what day of the week a given day of the month occurred, he immediately names it, and at's° mentions where he was and what was the state of the weather. A gentleman who had kept a 1 diary put many questions to him, and his answers I were invariably correct:" Of a similar kind is j the memory for which Daniel M'Cartney has be- come famous in the United States. The strange story , of this man's achievements is told by Mr. Henkle in the .1 Journal of Speculative Philosophy. M'Cartney, in 18R9, wdeclaredile nh de m aet hattw af from nineli e couldjayneua arsr January, emember the day of week for any years-and thatrm ontihs,s forloam—ftohretyt-timwoe and a half years. He has often been tested, and, so far as Mr. Henkle's account goes, has not failed to tell his questioner " what day it was," and to give some information about the weather, and about his own whereabouts and doings on any one of the fifteen thousand or more dates that might be named. When Mr. 'Reticle fast met this man of marvellous memory, he was employed in the offiee of the Honourable T. K. Rukenbrod, editor of the Salem Republican, where nothing better,could be found for M'Cartnev to do than "turn the wheel of the printing-press on two days of each week." On the first formal examination this man underwent, 11:s answers were tested by reference to the file of a newspaper which gave the day of the week along with the date. In one case his statement was disputed, for the day he named was not the same as that given by the paper; but on further inquiry, it was i found that the newspaper was wrong, for the printer I had made a mistake. Shorthand notes of the conversa- tion were taken at subsequent interviews. The report of these is very curious reading. Take the following as a sample :—" Questiox. October 6, 1826? .An.9teer (in two seconds), Wednesday. It was cloudy and drizzled rain. I carried dinner to my father where he was getting out coal.—Question. February 21, 1829? Answer (in two seconds), Saturday. It was cloudy in the morning, and clear in the afternoon; there was a little snow on the ground. An uncle who lived near sold a horse-bet that day for thirty-five dollars." And so the conversation ran on for hours, ranging over forty years of M'Cartney's personal history, Mr. Henkle tells us that if he went over some of the dates again, after a few days' interval the answers, although given in different terms, were essentially the same, "showing distinctly that he remembered the facts, and not the words previously used."—Chambers's Journal. cuaAPesT House In the city for Glass, China, Oriental w area, and Fancy Goodg.-175, Oxford-street, Manchester.- 4Wet.

One discovery at least has resulted from the "Colo- nies." Messrs. Joynson have discovered the possibility of making excellent paper out of the " mullett" fibre which Sir Samuel Davenport has brought from his estate in South Australia, and the daily programme is to be printed on it some day during the present week. AN ARCIIXOLOGICAL DISCOVERY.—The foundations of an old Norman castle have just been discovered at Duf- field, near Derby, having a moat and a ground plan only 21t. smaller than the Tower of London. The thickness of the walls ranges from 10ft. to 15ft. The Rev. J. C. Cox, LL.D, author of "Derbyshire Churches," has pro- nounced the castle to have been one ,of the finest in Eng- land after the Tower of London. The Derbyshire Archeological Society and a committee are obtaining, funds to thoroughly carry out the excavations. Con- siderable historical importance is attached to the dis- covery.

A Cuttious OPTICAL ILLUSION.—M. de Parvelle has called the attention of the French Academy of Sciences to a curious illusion of the vision which may account for the apparent oscillation or swinging of sears some- times observed, and called by the Germans Sternschwanken. When the eye looks for some time at a small feebly- lighted body, itself being in complete darkness, the body appears to oscillate or describe certain curves. It is a phenomenon of the subjective order; and appears to be of the same nature as the movement of a star observed when a person leans the head against a wall and fixes his eye upon the star. The star appears to be agitated in its place, and to oscillate rapidly. In order that the motion may be noticed there should be no moon, and the sky should be clear. A lunette takes away the apparent motion.—Engineering. THE LAST OF THE GHETTO AT ROME.—Another pictur- esque piece of antiquity is doomed; and the Jews' quar- ter at Rome will in a week or two's time be a thing of the past. From the sanitary point of view the demoli- tion of the Ghetto is no doubt highly desirable; but the traveller seldom troubles himself about the health of the people whose streets he visits, and he will regret that he will see no more those picturesque ruins creeping up beside the ancient monuments, leaning against the gate of Octavius, swarming with an active and industrious folk who lived, so to speak, on their doorsteps. All this is disappearing. The Jews have made themselves there a sort of second fatherland; their habits, their traditions had followed them there, and they were a little town to themselves. The present Government dispossesses them, and gives them wide streets, and Israel is again dispersed,

REDISCOVERED FRESCOES AT AMSTERDAM. - Lovers of art have long been puzzled to account for the disappear- ance of several frescoes and other decorative paintings described by Jacob Vos in his account of the Museum at Amsterdam. They were not to be found any longer, and there was no record of their fate. Some years ago M. Greeve, the curator of the Academy of Sciences, disco- vered a fresco on a ceiling in the museum which had been painted over. This fresco was by Niklass Held Stokade, according to Vos. He has again lately, in the hall in which Rembrandt's "Night Watch" is placed, discovered a series of frescoes, which seem to be nearly as old as the building. They were all, covered over with a thick paper, which had been painted and grained to imitate walnut wood. It is conjectured that this was done about the time of the French invasion, 90 years ago, to protect the pictures from appropriation by the French Generals. On the whole they are in a fair state of preservation.

A PROJECTED SUBMARINE RAILWAY TUNNEL BETWEEN DENMARK AND SWEDEM.—A Copenhagen correspondent writes :—" Mr. Alexandre de Rothe, an engineer, who has been working at Panama under M. de Lessens, has pre- sented to the Governments of Denmark and Sweden a project for a submarine railway tunnel under the Sound between Copenhagen and Malmo. The tunnel is to have a total length of twelve kilometres, three between Ameger and the small island Saltholmen under the strait Drogden, and nine between Saltholmen and! Sweden. The ground to be worked much resembles that in the Channel between England and France, and is said to offer no difficulty to the execution of the work. The cost of construction is calculated ti amount to thirty millions of francs, or £1,200,000. The Swedish Govern- ment takes a great interest in the plan, while the Danish at present is keeping somewhat back. Mr. de Rothe entertains sanguine hopes of a successful result of the negotiations. The tunnel would be of the greatest im- portance for the future commercial connection between Sweden-Norway, and later on of Russia and the whole continent, as laden railway waggons could then run from the north of Norway, Sweden, or. Finland, down to the south of Italy." THE USEFULNESS or A PLAGUE.—Dr. Brandes, a physi- cian at Ilitzackes, Hanover, has written an article in a German medical paper, in which lie demonstrates the valuable properties of the anacharis alsinastrum, a water plant which has hitherto been considered as an unmiti- gated plague, choking up rivers, and altogether useless. Dr. Brandes has remarked that in the district where he lives, and whdre malaria and diarrhcea yearly appeared in a sporadic or epidemic form, these diseases have gra- dually decreased since the anacharis alsinastrum began to infest the neighbouring rivers and marshes, and, since four years, have totally disappeared. The above-named water plant nourishes itself on decayed vegetable matter, and grows with incredible rapidity. It thus destroys the germs which produce malaria and diarrhcea ; and, be- sides, its presence obliges the frequent cleansing of stand- ing waters, a measure beneficial to health. Dr. Brandes therefore proposes that the experiment should be tried of planting the anacharis alsinastrum in marshy districts. It is also useful in protecting the young of fish, and affords an excellent dung. The plant came originally from Canada, whence it was brought to England, and thence to Germany about 1840. In North Germany it rapidly spread far and wide, and this year appears in all parts in unusual luxuriance. A PROPOSED AMERICAN BALLOON VOYAGE.—What is stated to be the largest balloon ever constructed has re- cently been built at San Francisco by M. A. P. Van Tassel. It has a capacity of 150,000 cubic feet of gas, and has been constructed for the special purpose of enabling that aeronaut to undertake a journey across the North Ameri- can continent from ocean to ocean. The height from the floor of the wicker car to the top of the gas reservoir is 119 ft., and of the dilated reservoir alone 68ft. The en- velope of the balloon is made of finely-woven cloth, manufactured expressly for the purpose, and is varnished, as usual, in order to make it gas-tight. The car has ac- commodation for 15 persohs. It is 21ft. in circumference, and its sides are 34in. high. The supporting ropes are kept in place by the usual concentrics. Hydrogen gas will be used in inflating the balloon. The cost of the structure is stated to be $6,000. M. Van Tassel has had considerable experience in aerial travelling, having crossed the Wichita Mountains, 15,000 feet above sea level. His present attempt is more ambitious than , any he has yet made. A careful study of the aerial cur- rents leads him to believe that, by seeking the proper stratum of air, he can be carried eastward at a high speed—possibly 100 miles an hour. THE MANAGEITENT OF POULTRY. THE PRESERVATION OF EGGS. The fact that eggs are more plentiful at one season of the year than at another has led to the trial of many ways for their preservation. It seems to promise a large profit if eggs can be kept at the time when they are plentiful and cheap, and sold when they are dear; and it Is small wonder that the means of making this aug- mented profit has been dilic,rently sought for. We do not 'think that the result has been as satisfactory as could have been wished, but it is a fact that enormous numbers of the eggs imported from the Continent dur- ing the winter season have been preserved, or pickled, as it is called. These too often are far from being what 'we should like to eat, but there are vast numbers who .are by no means fastidious in this matter. Perhaps they have something of the Chinese taste, for the denizens of the Celestial Empire regard eggs as the more dainty when they are rotten. That, happily, is not the case with Western nations, who as a rule prefer to have them as fresh as possible. Though we think that the methods adopted for the preservation of eggs are by no means so successful as could have been wished, yet there are ways in which they can be kept for a considerable period, and be good for culinary purposes, and not objectionable to many palates for eating in the ordinary way. Some time ago we were asked to describe the German method of preserving eggs, and the promise we then made had better at first be redeemed. There are several ways, but that most commonly used is as follows :—The eggs are placed in tubs or large vats as soon after they are ob- tained from the poultry keepers as possible. Some of the vats hold hundreds of dozens, and are kept by the dealers who buy them in from the poultry owners. A preparation of lime and water is made by mixing about twenty gallons of water with four gallons of fine 'slaked lime, into which a gallon of salt is also put. When the water appears to have taken into solution as much of the lime as it is capable .of holding, it is then put over the eggs so as to completely cover them, and it is usual not to pack the eggs quite to the top of the vat, so that there may be two or three inches of water above the top layer of eggs. It is, however, found necessary to add from time to time a little more lime, or by keeping a cloth of lime on the top touching the water, in order that as the lime in the water is absorbed or loses its effect more can be taken up. Without this is done, the preservation will not be successful, for water alone will not be sufficient to keep the eggs in a fresh state. The same end can be secured by throwing a handful of the fine lime into the vat every few days, but this is a rougher method which may lead to trouble if not very carefully done. We once knew a test made of this lime water process, but instead of putting the lime water only into the barrel, a thick sediment was allowed to remain at the bottom. When the time came to take out the eggs the whole was a solid mass, and the eggs would have had to be got out with an ice hammer, if they had to be got out at all. The great object, therefore, in preserving eggs by this method is to supply enough lime for the preservation, but no more. When the eggs are to be taken out of the pickle, they are carefully wiped and packed in straw. Properly preserved, it is difficult for anyone not accustomed to the buying and selling of eggs to know them from freshly laid ones. They have not, of course, that bloom by which a fresh egg can always be known, but then there are not ten persons in every thousand who know anvthing about the bloom. • Eggs can be preserved in dry salt, and so preserved keep good for a very long time. Salt effectually keeps laway the air, which is a most desirable thing with all eggs to be kept long, and it prevents mildew or the growth of fungi. There is a slight taste given to the egg when salt is used, but this is not at all objectionable. Mr. Tegetmeier some time ago recommended a plan of keeping eggs in salt which deserves to be repeated here. He suggested that a wooden box should be used, with the bottom in one piece, fastened on with well-greased screws. A layer of salt, one inch deep, should be first placed in it, on which the eggs should be put on end, close, but not touching. More salt should then be put in until the eggs are well covered. This must be well shaken down and a second layer of eggs treated with the salt as before, and so on until the box is filled. The box, when filled, must be closely packedaip to the top with dry salt and fastened down. If put in a cool place, the eggs will keep for weeks, and it is an advantage to be able to continue the filling of the box as long as is necessary, for the salt prevents the air getting to the eggs. When they are to be used, the bottom is un- screwed, and the oldest eggs can thus be used first. The only disadvantage which we know of from the use of salt as a peservative is that it absorbs some of the moisture in the egg. Thus it is that eggs so preserved are found to have the contents loose. For table use this would at once raise a prejudice, and it would be impos- sible to market such eggs, as it is generally supposed all that rattle inside are stale. But there can be no objec- tion of this kind when they are only to be used for cook- ing purposes. Some time ago we came across the following method, which the writer stated had been a perfect success with him. A mixture of sulphur and lamp black was made. A lot of eggs were placed within a common Aim, one with a single hole in the side. On the top of the eggs was placed a saucer full of the sulphur and lamp black compound. This was set fire to by a match, the churn cover put on, and a sheet wrapped over the whole to keep in the fumes. Next morning, when opened out, the eggs were found -to be entirely coated with black, but so effectually had they been preserved that six months afterwards they were quite fresh. Whether the fact of the shell being blackened would not be objectionable to many need not be here discussed, for it is not likely any one would prepare eggs in this manner for marketing. Experiments made during recent years have shown that there are several other ways of preserving eggs. At one of the competitions in connection with the Birmingham show a lot of eggs won that had been pre- served in the following manner :—Each egg was first wrapped in fine tissue paper, leaving a screw of the paper to hold by. A mixture is made of sperm and wax, or suet and wax, heated to 100 degs. Each egg is dipped in this and then left to cool. When the first coat is dry the process is repeated. The eggs are kept in fine flour, and the result showed that they can be kept for two or three months in this way, though it is only right to say that in a competition at the dairy show of 1885 eggs kept by this process were found to be unfit for eating. This must have been due either to some fault in the eggs, or the method of preserving had not been properly carried out. This process, however, like many others, may be adopted by those who have plenty of time at their disposal and do not mind the trouble, or who perhaps like it all the better because it is uncom- mon and involves trouble, but for the majority of poultry-keepers it would be of no use whatever. There are other ways of the kind, such as coating the eggs in wax, or paraffin, but they are open to the same objec- tion as that just named. For the great majority of our readers any proce s which involves a great amount of trouble is simply out of the question. There are some other ways of preserving eggs for which we have not room this week and must therefore leave over, and also some facts as to the general principles and the best methods. SEASONABLE HINTS. Farmers should now take the advantage offered them of getting their birds out on to the fields, when the crops are taken off. If there are no movable poultry-houses at hand, there will be some timber that can be utilisea in the making of a few, and a day spent in this way by a handy man will be enough to supply a reasonable sized farm. The birds in this way will be fed for nothing, as they will eat the grain that would otherwise4se wasted; they will clean the land, manuring it at the Aame time ; ' so that the advantage will be a treble one. Whilst the birds are thus out for their autumn holiday, the perma- nent houses cap be limewashed inside, and Painted or tarred outside, and the runs will obtain a much needed rest.

If the key-note of all your conduct tn others had its spring in a fine self-reverence, there would be no dis- courtesies. A bankrupt Irish gentleman ilectred before a Com- missioner that his available assets included a great num- ber of debts.

He who would command must first learn to obey, and the boy who would learn to paddle his own canoe must first be paddled, and very frequently. "Benevolence is not a thing to be taken up.by chance, and put by at once to make way for every employment which savours of self-interest. It is the largest part of our business, beginning with our home duties, and ex- tending itself to the utmost verge of suffering humanity. A vague feeling of kindness towards our fellow-creatures is no state of mind to rest in. It is not enough for us to be able to say that nothing of human interest is alien to us, and that we give our acquiescence, .or, indeed, out transient assistance, to any scheme of benevolence that may come in our way. No ; in promoting the welfare of others, we must toil; we must devote to it earnest thought, constant care, and zealous endeavour. THE CARDIFF ELECTION RIOTS.—Mr. Bridge conelud,cl, on Saturday, the inquiry into the Cardiff election distur- bances, and the allegations against the borough and county polici.—On behalf of the borough police Mr. Clifton, of Bristol, urged that the action which they took was justified owing to the attitude of the mob—ln reply for the rate- Payers, Mr. David, of the Oxford Circuit, said that even if there had been justification for the order to draw staves, there was no justification for their :Ise unless the people resisted, while even if there had been resistance, nothing would justify the police in striking mon and women as they lay upon the ground, as had been done at Cardiff.—The Commissioner will report to the Home Office towards the end of the week.

The Buenos Ayres Standard says :—" Cattle-breeding for the purpose of meat exportation is making much progress, the Hereford and Shorthorn breeds being pre- ferred. This business must in time surpass even that of wool, and promises the most brilliant results to Buenos Ayres." The annual sheep returns for New Zealand show that the total number in the colony is 14,546,001, as compared with 13,978,520 in 1885, an increase of 567,481. The in- crease is spread over all the districts except Wanganui and Marlborough, in which there are decreases of 3,712 and 14,179. In Canterbury the increase is 331,213, and in Otago 97,540. The proposed removal of the duty on Mexican cattle is not received favourably by American breeders, except by the few who expect to derive advantage from sending bulls Of superior breed to Mexico, and they believe that free trading would increase the demand for their cattle. The Texas s:ockovrners especially object to open com- petition with the owners of great herds fed on the 'free pastures of Mexico. _ .

BUTTER FRAUDS.—The trustees of the Cork butter market are vigorously prosecuting any who attempt to pass off fraudulently made-up firkins that bring dis- credit on the market, and the local magistrates seem quite disposed to second their efforts. Last week, at the Cork Police Office, two farmers were fined £4leach and costs, one for having added water to his butter, and the other for having plastered some inferior stuff round the sides of his firkin, so that it might escape the borer used by the inspector. According to the theories of Darwin, the tendency of all animals is towards improvement. The man who in- vented the Spanish breeds of non-sittinc, fowls, may have thought that he had " improved " them by getting rid of the propensity to sit, and as there are several strains of these non-sitters, according to Darwin, if you cross those strains the progeny would naturally have a double non- sitting propensity, but the result of such a cross is just the reverse, for it is a fact that if you cross two non- sitting strains, the progeny will all sit. In other words, the tendency is always away from the improved animal.

div.head: NORTH LANCASHIRE FARM NOTES.
div.p: NORTH LANCASHIRE FARM NOTES.
trIZVel%

In a walk through the district recently, several things adverse to agriculture were painfully evident. Formerly, it used to be said that our district was second to none in fertility, cleanliness, and the excellence and stocking of our farms as affecting live stocks—all were pretty much of the best. This cannot now be said, and several reasons may be aduced for the change. At a time when grain was grown to good profit, there was a large area under the plough, straw was little thought of as a feeder, but was used for bedding and conversion into manure. Thus if we cropped hard, we manured plenti- fully, and the soils were kept in the cleanest possible state. To farmyard manure was added the contents of privies and ashpits ; these were supplemented by lime, soot, &c., sweetening the land, liberating fertility, and keeping down insect pests, for lime-kilns existed on nearly every farm. Then came the Sanitary Acts on sewerage, sending the manure of towns and Tillages to the sea in place of to the land. This loss ot manure was met in turn by the introduction of artificials ; but from lack of knowledge of the latter, farmers bought not wisely, but too well, impoverishing both their pockets and the land ; for with the use of artificials, they neglected other manures. These latter results were gradual, but none the less sure, for when the process was begun profits were still to be made in agriculture. Then set in the depression, from which we are yet suffering. Year by year prices for all agricultural produce de- clined, and year by year something had to be done to meet the decreased profits. The area of plough land was lessened, and laid to grass in order to lessen expenses of labour. Artificial manures were dubbed worthless and a snare, and only a minimum has been used of recent years. Then the number of hands on the farm was re- duced, and the effect of this is now seen in the dirty state of many farms. Where the land is both im- poverished for lack of manure, and has in addition to support a full crop of weeds, it bodes ill for the crops, ill for the tenant, ill for the landlord. On many farms, too, the scarcity of live stock is painfully agyarent. Formerly, it was usually matter of difficulty to arrange change of pasture for the stock; now, on but too many farms, there are not animals to eat the grass, and many of the pasture fields are :more like hay meadows. There are yet farms that are well and cleanly cultivated, well stocked with the animals of the farm, and these but show the others in stronger relief. Where the balance at the bank is not yet ex- hausted the crops on the farm of all kinds arc looking well, although late, in sympathy with a late season. Swedes are just about rubbina- shoulders, cabbages look like making heavy weights, and cereals may be yet any way, as subsequent weather may decide. Mangolds have been attacked by maggot, but the rains came oppor- tunely to their relief. The maggots have eaten through their lodgings and disappeared. But where have they gone? is the puzzle. In what state have they gone? I have examined the soil about the roots and can find no trace. Yet in several previous yeas, with favouring weather, 1 have known the attack to be several times re- peated. Do these subsequent attacks result from the original fly or from the descendants, which, when wet weather sets in, fall to the earth, burrow into it, and there pass through the various stages? Or does the rain kill the young maggot? These are matters which I ven- ture to think are well worthy the attention of our fair "Royal" entomologist. To return to the state of our farms. What is the remedy? Where are we to look for re- lief? They remind me of a personal experience of a few years ago. I was the co-trustee of a small estate in the neighbourhood of a town, my fellow trustee assuming the management. He let it in parcels to the highest bidders, the lettings, at an inn, costing no little in liquor. Of four tenants in four years two failed to pay the rent, so that we just got half the rentals, and had all the ex- penses of lettings in addition. The land became so poor that it was scarcely worth a rent. Since then I have selected my tenants at a reasonable rental. For the past few years the rents have been promptly paid, and the land is in good heart, but each tenant has a guarantee that so long as ho farms in conformity with good hus- bandry he will not be disturbed nor his rent increased. It Seems to me that there are many cases in Lonsdale North where a like course would result to the benefit of both landlord and tenant, for if I, as a native, read the present signs aright, the day is not far distant when some of the landlords will find a difficulty in drawing their rentals.—R.

A new scale of solicitors' costs in tankruptcy cases will come into op,ration immediately after the long vacation. The revised legal charges will be on a more liberal scale than those which they replace.

SHOCKING ACCIDENT.--A fearful accident happened on Monday evening on Werneth Cricket Ground, Oldham. The groundsman was engaged in rolling the ground with a horse roller, and put James H. Musgrove, ten years, and his brother Walter. 15 months, sons of W. Musgrove, Coppice, Oldham, upon the carriage of the roller. Sometime after he lifted the elder lad off, and was putting the child Walter in his arms, whf.7) he let the child slip, and he fell in front of the roller, which passed over him, crushing him in a fearful manner. Death was almcst instantaneous.

div.head: COMEDY OF ERRORS.
div.p: A COMEDY OF ERRORS.

"One woe doth tread upon another's heel, So fast they foIIow."—SHAKESPEARF:. There are perhaps no transactions in life which we try to discharge with so much precision and solemnity , as•those last sad rites which pertain to the burial of our dead relatives and friends;. yet most of us can call to mind some idgtance where one, or a series of blunders or accidents transformed the whole affair into a painful comedy or a capital farce, as illustrated by the two fol- lowing stories, which, names excepted, are literally true, and of recent occurrence. Billy Badger is a " call " weaver, which means, in these latter days at least, that Billy Badger is poor. A few months ago he took a house he couldn't furnish,and a wife he couldn't keep, and in a wonderfully short time after a young Badger entered on the scene; but, for- tunately or unfortunately, the same convulsion of nature which brought on. Badger fits took off Badger mere.

Badger's castle was, speaking now in the past tense, located in a small village about 'a mile from Mudborough on the one hand, and six miles from Flanneril on the other, and after collecting the money due to him on the demise of his wife from two or three clubs, Badger had next to arrange about the funeral cortege, and some lvnatic persuaded him that it would be cheaper to have a hearse and coach from Flanueril to take the party from the house to Mudborough than it would to have the same from Mudbarough—in other words, that it would cost less to travel fourteen miles than two. Arrangements were accordingly made with an under- taker at Flanneril that a hearse with two, and a coach with three horses, should be at Badger's domicile on a certain day, at two o'clock in the afternoon, to convey the funeral party to Mudborough cemetery, from there to a certain place mentioned, in Mudborough aforesaid, to tea, and then back to the house. This arrangement appeared to cover everything, and left nothing to be desired; but, alas! we all know what Bobby Burns says of—" The best laid schemes o' mice an' men," &c. and it happened so in this case. The day appointed 'for the funeral was preceded by a night of setere frost, which, following several rainy days, converted the roads into a paradise for schoolboys and other juveniles, and a state of purgatory for horse-drivers and pedestrians generally. The mourners all assembled, as in duty bound, and were accommodated in several draughty houses, where there was nothing strong only the cold wind, and nothing weak only the British wine, and the foundations were laid for many a cold, if nothing worse. Two o'clock came, and all were in hopes that the end of their sufferings was near, but not yet. Then after what appeared at least six hours of martyrdom, three o'clock came, but the carriages didn't, and as by this time all the local scandals, the British wino and the tobacco, were exhausted, most of the company ad- journed into the street, just to have the wind the other way for a time. And now here and there dark hints began to be thrown out that the carriages had never been ordered, or that a wrong date had been given; but Badger stoutly averred that he had made no mistake, and in proof he called " Deeaf Harry," his father-in- law, as a witness, but it was utterly impossible to make him hear a question, his answers were altogether unreliable. To settle the point, an exploring party was sent out, which after proceeding two miles, found the hearse and coach engaged in pushing five wretched, unsharpened, sexagenarian horses along the slippery, road, and the chances were that the procession would never reach its destination until the next thaw, but fortunately, one or other of the horses fell down about every minute, and aS they always fell forward, it was so much gained. When they did reach the house it was four o'clock, (and they were due at the cemetery at three), then the question arose, if the horses could not draw the vehicles when empty, what would they do when they were loaded? and this question assumed greater gravity from the fact that the first quarter of a mile of the route was all on the collar. However, to minimise the dangers% and makes things look cheerful, the horses were changed ; those which had knelt down the oftenest being placed with others of more atheistic principles, while the company walked up the hill, except those required to hold the horses up and prevent them coming unglued by the way. With many misgivings the company now entered the coach, with the exception of the parson, who, looking again at the turnout, and not wishing to expose his body to injury, and his soul to sin, shook his head, and saying he would wait for them at the cemetery—perhaps there was a double meaning in this expression—he walked on. The route from this point to the cemetery, except the last hundred yards, was all downhill, and by alternately sliding and sitting down, the horses covered the next, quarter of a mile in good time; but now they reached a rather sharp curve in the road, and suddenly came to grief. In taking the turn the coach began to slide side- ways, and the horses, not being able to hold on to the ground, began to do likewise, ending in the "off" horse going down, and getting mixed up with his companion's legs, he caused considerable gynastic,s, until they t2o threw up the sponge, and lay down beside him. Still the coach continued to slide, and nothing but the dead weight of the fallen horses, and the assistance of the male portion of the company prevented it from going over the low fence into the railway below, which would have meant a fearful loss of life, and all that a rascally undertaker might save a few shillings. All this time the hearse could be seen, now near, now far ahead, tacking about like a ship in a head wind; but when the driver saw the coach hopelessly stranded on the roadside, he went on as best he could, trusting to the company to follow on foot. It was fully a half mile from the wreck to the ceme- tery, and getting quite dark; but as soon as they could get out of the coach, the mourners started off in twos and threes, some on the footpath and others in the middle of the road. Arriving at the foot of the incline, leading into the cemetery, the hearse stopped, ostensibly to wait for the mourners, in reality because it could not go any farther, and when a sufficient number of the men came up, the coffin was taken out of the hearse and carried, without bier or pall, to the cemetery gates. Passing over the next proceedings, let us join the company as they i emerge from the cemetery, nearly frozen, with a good mile walk between them and their tea. Wearily they-plod up the slippery road, and when they reach their destination, cold, tired, and hungry, it is only to find that yet another drop of gall has to be added to their cup of misery, for the purveyor of the tea having become convinced that he had either been fooled or some mistake had been made, had long since removed the provisions and closed the tea room. To refurnish the table and make fresh tea took up time, and we should not be believed if we stated the time when the company started for their respective homes. Some time that evening they did start, and as they did the journey , on foot, we may fairly presume that they reached home safely before they went to bedl

Bobby Wobbles is a good specimen of a class of' per- sons now rapidly becoming extinct. He has vegetated for sixty years at Stonefield iithout a wish—except at rare intervals—to go outside rlis own little world, con- sequently his knowledge of men and things beyond those limits is very slight indeed. Seeking no change himself, he cannot understand it in others, and he has a morbid dislike to anything which disturbs the dull routine of his everyday life. The other day, however, Bobby received a letter inti- mating that his old neighbour and crony, Harry o' Tatts, who had removed to Accrington some four years before, was dead, and the funeral, to which he, Bobby, was invited, would take place on the Thursday fol- lowing. Bobby didn't want to go; but still he could not think of his old companion being consigned to his mother earth, and be not there to show his respect for him on the last possible occasion. Bobby's wife thought so too, and that ended the matter. • This important event called for much discussion and preparation. Bobby's best suit, which he only wore on red-letter days, had to be overhauled to see that it was in a perfect state of preservation, and then well aired. His shoes were soled, and his best " haliday shirt" care- fully starched, and as as carefully ironed—in fact, every- thing was done that a good wife could think necessary. But how fallible is man, and also woman! Things neces- sary and unnecessary had been so seriously discussed by Bobby and his wife that it scarcely appeared possible that a most important item could have been overlooked, yet it was so. Bobby and his better-half had several times gone over the letter which was causing all this commotion, and never once noticed the superscription or address from which it was sent. This strange oversight is, no doubt, to be ascribed to the fact that about two years before, Bobby went to Accrington to see his friend, who, meeting him at the station, saved him the trouble of remembering either the name of the street or the number of the house, and Bobby, never dreaming that his friend might have changed his residence in the interval, was quite sure he could find the place again. The eventful Thursday morning saw Bobby safely on his way to Accrington and also his safe arrival there, when he at once proceeded to look for Harry o' Tatts' house. Looking for it was one thing, but finding it was another. However, after carefully examining several streets, and refreshing himself with " three-pen'oth o' porrita pie," he found the place he was looking for; but not so fortunate in the house. He had an impression that Harry lived a few doors from arbeerhouse, but in no such house could he see any indication of a funeral; but he found such indications a few doors from a "pop-shop," so he was not so far wrong after all. Going tip to the door of this house he was about to make inquiries, but the old lady who opened the door cut hiei short with—" 0, yo're reet, maister, come in an' sit yo' daaon." Bobby entered, and took the chair indicated; and then began to look around on the company for some familiar face, and he thought it strange that he saw none, but consoled himself with the thought that he would do by and by. Meanwhile, he made himself comfortable with the mulled ale and tobacco; but when the undertaker was going to make up the coffin, Bobby left his seat to have, as he said, "0 last look ut th' owd mon," when he found, to his horror, that the deceased was a young man. Without a word to the surprised company, Bobby picked up his hat, and very soon disappeared round the

first street corner, and when he found himself out of the sight of the house, he found nimself in a cold sweat, and for want of other refuge, he entered the nearest public- house, and called for a glass of ale. When the landlord entered the room and saw our firtgq In a suit of sables, he said, "Fine day, mester ; fi gooin' to a funeral ?" "Aye," replied Bobby, "I should be. Harry c? is buried to-day, but I miss't th' funeral some way." , "Well, I'll bet that's id ud's just gooan daaon th street," said the landlord. "If yo' look sharp yo'll catch. I it."

Bobby jumped up, and nothing doubting that the landlord was right, he hurried down the street, and WaS' soon up with the last conveyance, when the occupants/ noticing his woebegone appearance, at once motioned l 0 to get in. Nothing loth Bobby did so, and thus travelled to the cemetery. Here he joined the mourners, and after the service, he went to the grave side to have a look at the coffin, when, shock No. 2 ! he learnt from the coffin" plate that this deceased was "Peggy Wagg, aged 40, U., &c." At this discovery, Bobby was completely flabber- gasted," and didn't know what to do, but had just sufficient sense not to expose his mistake, and also 18° get into one of the conveyances and ride back to Ae- crington. When the coach reached the public-house from wbiell he had started on his bootless errand, Bobby got out, and, finding the landlord, he made some oriOnal remarks that were very near getting that worthy In a passion, when, fortunately, a hearse stopped at the door, and the driver, calling for a glass of ale, told the landlord to look lively, as he had had two funerals that afternoon, and was now going to a third, and it Was getting late. "Whoa arta gooin' for naaow ?" asked the landlord- " Owd Harry o' Tatts," replied the man; "un if ovYcl Harry isn'd gradely deeod, he'll be nooan suited od 'l5 beM' so late. Gee up." When Bobby heard this, he called out to the driver te, wHowd on, mon, I've bin twice to owd Harry's buryila to-day, un thir booath th' wrong uns ; let's see if this i 5 him hissell."

The hearse was soon at Harry o' Tatts' late residence.; when it dawned on Bobby's mind, on looking up an down the street, that his friend had "flitted" since he' he saw him last, and then he wondered if "that letter said anything about the change, and he had just cont ' eluded hat he was a fool who never ought to have lef home, when the mourners began to file into the stree,! preparatory to entering the coaches. Bobby, a Haw suspicious that he might be wrong again, stood back; but when the coffin was brought out of the house, fel' lowed by the family of the deceased, he at once reco_ nised the widow and some of the children. Satisfleu there was no mistake this time, Bobby took his second ride to the cemetery. At the subsequent tea Bobby detailed his adventureg to owd Harry's family, when he was both laughed at and commiserated. The mistake is not likely to occur again, for Bobbi - says, " He'll read his letter all through th' next til3e, afoor he gooas to oather funeral or aught else," anu perhaps other persons may find that determination a wise one in their own affairs.---JOHN SILA.CKLETON, in .Befl Brierley's Journal.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.
I

Suckering and earthing up Celery has occupied much of our time during the past week, as we were anxious to confine the wet, in order to save further watering for this season. Plants that were earthed for the first time had an inch or two of the most mellow soil drawn to them with one hand whilst the other grasped the plant. The sides of the trenches were afterwards chopPed down, and this soil in time crumbles and becomes fit for, the next earthing. Turnips were sown on land occupied by early potatoes, and it will be the last this year frore which we expect any useable roots, but another will be made to supply tops in spring, which many think much of cooked as a vegetable. Onions of the Tripoli clasS should be sown at once, either in drills or broadcast on piece of ground that is in good heart and in a warra sheltered position. THE Fnomr GARDEN.—Standard Roses are not grow° so generally as they once were, as it has been found by experience that those in their own roots are more satis- factory to the general growers. Indeed, in the neigh- bourhood of towns or smoky districts Standard Roses are extremely short-lived. Many growers for exhibition, however, maintain that they secure their best flowers from budded plants or standards in their first or second year. Those of our readers who have acted on previous instructions and secured their briars will find the pre" sent an excellent time for budding. It is as well te select two or three shoots on each to operate upon in case of failure, though experienced budders rarely insert more than two and often only one. Just now the bark of the bud and stock part so freely from the wood that the veriest tyro could not fail to succeed. the rose season is practically over even in the North, and as far as we have observed it has turned out the best for yearS, and some remarkable instances of floriferousness have been related to us. We saw a Victor Verdier planted tWe years ago in the garden of the Head Master of the Boys' National School, Lancaster, with 39 flowers and buds on one shoot, pegged down as advocated in this column; and a Countess of Oxford with nearly as many more on the whole plant. Other varieties were correspondinglY good. Not far behind these, in the same town, was a plant in Mr. Willie's front garden. The other day vire had a great treat afforded us in inspecting the collection that has been formed during the past three or four yearS by Mr. Carne, gardener to G. Dewhurst, Esq., Clayton Green. There are 200 varieties, and it is estimated that there are more than 500 flowering plants and about 200 yearlings distributed all over the flower and kitchett garden, some in beds on the lawn, others in groups or broken lines in the borders. Odd plants of the ScZteh briar occupying the centre of sundry groups as we ap- proached them forced their fragrance perceptibly on our olfactory organ, overpowering the rose odour for the time, a little too much. Some varieties succeed better ill certain gardens than in others, and though none looked unhappy in the Clayton Green collection the following arrested attention as we strolled amongst them :--Fisher Holmes, an imbricated bright scarlet flower; Earl of Beaconsfield, light cherry carmine, a well-shaped flower; Dupay Jamain, very bright cerise, large, full, and fine form; Madame Marie Finger, a most beautiful fresh. coloured flower, large and globular; Victor Verdier, light cherry-rose shaded with carmine, a very fine, free grow- ing hardy rose; White Baroness, white flowers, large and full; Madame Eugene Verdier, light silvery rose, large fine petals, globular shape; La France, rosy lilac, a very distinct large and full flower; Duke of Edinburgh, rich velvety vermilion, a very hardy and vigorous growing rose; Pierre Notting. blackish red with light violet tint; Alfred Colomb, bright fiery red; and Duke of Teck, bright crimson scarlet, clear and distinct, good form and free bloomer. We were assured that others had been equally good, but the best blooms had gone a few dayS previous to our visit, and we were continually being buttonholed to closely inspeect the successionals and express our impression as to what they would be ins few days. THE GREMITOUSE.—As Cinerarias fill the pots with roots they should be moved into larger ones, using a compost of fresh turfy loam, three parts, and one of leaf mould, with one-eighth of the whole of decayed maniple. As soon as the potting is completed, place the plants in a frame, if there is one available; if not, stand them in some shady situation at present in preference to the greenhouse, which is generally hot and dry—con- ditions most inimical to the growth of the Cineraria, and they very soon become a prey to green-fly. We like to see the plants with bedewed foliage every morning, and this cannot be secured in an airy house even by night spripkling, unless the outside atmosphere is loaded with moisture. If the plants are at all infected with green- fly, move them into the greenhouse to fumigate them before they are potted, which is always best crone in the evening, and, instead of applying one strong dose, we would give two weaker ones, the second the following morning or evening, and before the plants are taken out they should be thoroughly examined to see if the insects are dead. Chinese Primulas will do under similar condi- tions to the Cineraria, except that they require about one-sixth sand in the potting compost as well, being un- able to stand so much moisture.

GREAT NORTHERN RAILWAY.—The half-yearly meeting of the Great Northern Railway Company was held on Mon- day, at King's Cross Terminus, London, Lord Colville of Calross (the Chairman) presiding. 11,3 stated that, not- withstanding the depression in trade, the gross receipts were satisfactory, showing a considerable increase. There were signs of improvement in trade in some of the great indus- trial centres of Yorkshire, although they were not observ- able in other portions of the Gn-at Northern district.

ALLEGED MURDER BY A BRITISH CONSUL'S SERVANT.— The steamer Lualaha, belonging to the British and African Steam Navigation Company, has arrived in the Mersey' from the West and onth-West Coasts of Africa, including the river Congo. H.M.S. Alecto left the Island of Mondole on June 26th, a few days before the Lualaba's arrival. The object of the Alecto's visit was to bring up Consul Hewitt to investigate a charge of murder against Veripan David, the servant of Mr. H. H. Johnstone, the Btitish Vice-Con- sul of that part of the coast. The allegation is that David bad stabbed two Krootnen, one of whom died. He was also said to bo the cause of the disappearance in a mvsteri- ous manner of another Krooman. Mr. Johnstone had been to Old Cllab Ir. le tying D,vid in charge of his place and his black servants. It is aft ged that the latter were harshly' treated during Mr. Johnstone's absence, and on his return some altercation took place between David and the two men, when the former is said to have attacked them with a large butcher's knife, killing rho headman instantly and Wounding the other. The latter escaped to the house of a trader and informed him of the circumstance. The trader went down with his own no t. aid arreted the accused. Mr. Johnstone himself was very Pl, and his condition when the Lualaba left was very serious David was placed in the cus- tody of Chief Brue, who is held responsible for his delivery' up to justice when the Alecto returns. One of the Kroomen disappeared in a mysterious manner a short time More, and on Pavid being accused if being the Cause of the man's disappearance. he could not, it is stated, give any satisfac- tory reply. Veripan Day:d is a young man of rather pre- possessing appearance. hle is a niti\ve of Ceylon, and was taken from England to Africa by Mr. Johnstone a few months ago as his servant.

FOREIGN NEWS.

THE OPERATIONS IN BURMAH. MANDALAT, SUNDAY. There is much sickness among the troops at Kurnri. A species of paralytic disease has attacked the cavalry horses. A large number have died. Owing to the disturbed state of the country and the small rainfall, great scarcity is anticipated in Upper Burmah next season. Catceerm, SIINDaY —lt is understood that a concerted and extensive plan for the thorough pacification of Upper Btirmah will be und,rtaken next winter. Large reinforce- ments, including two or three regiments of native cavalry and additional police, will be sent from India so as to bring the garrison of the united provinces to more than 25,000 men, and to enable the troops to traverse the country from end to end. RiNGOO:g, WEDNESDAY.—As Major Anclainleck, with a detachment of the Royal Scots Fusiliers, was returning on the sth inst. from Lepantozs, he was attacked by a party of Bozweh's men, who were lying in ambush in a thick jangle near Thaybyanin. The British troops drove out the rebels, but were unable to come up with them. On the British side there were three men wounded. MORE FIGHTING IN BURMAII—A POST ABANDONED. The second edition of the "Times " contains the follow-

ing : MANDALAY, AUGUST 11.—On the 9th there was a sharp engagement with 250 insurgents strongly etockaded at Lizay, near Sagain. Our force consisted of eighteen of the Hampshire Regiment, and 50 of the sth Bombay, under Col. Poole. Two of the Hampshire Regiment and nine sepoys were wounded. Ten of the enemy were killed. Singoo, on the West Bank, was threatened by 400 Shans and Dacoits. Reinforcements have been sent. THE BATOUM. QUESTION. Sr. PETERSBURG, SUNDAY.—Lord Roeebery, in his Note to Sir Robert Morier on the Batoum question, stated that In conversation with the Russian Ambassador he had dwelt upon the validity of treaties, and pointed out that Russia could not abrogate any single article of a treaty without the consent of the other signatories. THE AFGHAN FRONTIER. MERV, T.—lntelligence received here from Bosaha to the 18th ult. announces that all preliminary surveys of the African Boundary Commission for the delimitation of the frontier between Dukeni Wells and the Amu Dana have been brought to a close. TURKISH MILITARY PREP AR CRON& CONSTANTINOPLE, MONDAY.—The step taken by the Sul- tan in ordering the formation of two new army corps for Macedonia is understood to be due partly to the language used recently by M. Tricoupis in regard to Greek teiritorial pretensions in the province, and partly to the efforts which Russian emissaries are reported to be making to incite the Macedonian Slays to Rebellion. The agitation carried on by those emissaries in Macedonia had become all the more active since the authority of Prince Alexander in Bnlgatia and Eastern Roumelia thwarted their propoganda in those States. The new army corps, if organised on a complete footing, will consist of two divisions, each numbering from 10,000 to 12,000 men ; the total, therefore, being from 40,000 to 48,000 men. THE UNION OF BULGARIA.

soFis, MON Ottoman and Bulgarian delegates for the reviseon of the organic st,tute met to-day at the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. M. Zanoff, the Minister of that departmeet, in his address welcoming the Turkish re- presentatives, said the patriotism of the delegates awl their devotion to the in'erests of their respective Governments, Indicated a successful issue of their mission. THE IMPERIAL MEETING AT GASTEIN. GASTEIN, SUNDAY.—The Emperor of Austria arrived hers at seven o'clock this evening, and was respectfully greeted by the large crowd assembled in the Strawbingor Plate. His Majesty drove immediately to the Chateau des BAIRS, where he was received by Prince William of Prussia, Prince Bismarck, Prince Reuss, and the Emperor Wile Ham's suite. The Emperor at once approached Prince William and embraced him twice most cordially. After warmly shaking hands with Prince Bis- marck and addressing a few words to several members of the German Emperor's suite, his Majesty entered the chateau, where the Emperor William and the Empress of Austria were awaiting him. The two monarchs twice embraced each other most cordially. The Emperor Francis Joseph having warmly greeted the Austrian Empress, their Majesties re- tired to the German Emperor's apartments. GASTEIN, MONDAY.—Aft,m• his visit to the Emperor Wil- liam yesterelay evening, the Emperor of Austria proceeded to the Hotel Stranbioger, where he wee received by Cardinal Mihajlovics, the local clergy, and the Mayor. Shortly afterwards the Austrian Fenperor received a visit from Prince William in the name of his grandfather. At half- past eight the Emperor of Austria, accompenied by Prince William, returned to•the Badeschloss, where they took tea with the Emperor William, Prince Reuss and Prince Hohen- lobe being also present. At about half-past nine the Em- peror Francis Joseph returned to his hotel, accompanied by Prince William, and was again enthusiastically cheered by the crowds assembled in the open space between the Hotel Stranbinger and the Bideschloss. THE CHOLERA. ROME, Si:MEDAL—Cholera has broken ant With great virulence at Barletta, on the Adriatic, where 132 caees and 42 deaths are announced.

RONR, MONDAY. The cholera returns for the last twenty-four hours report 120 cases and 53 deaths at Bar- letta. TRIESTE, SIINDAY.—There have been six fresh cases of cholera and two deaths here during the last 24 hours. FIUME. SUNDAY.—TWO fresh cases of cholera occurred here yesterday. GREAT FIRE IN NORWAY. CHRISTIANA, MONDAY.—The greater portion of the town of Skien, in the district of Bradsberg, was yesterday de- stroyed by fire. Among the buildings burnt down were several large warehouses. The total loss is estimated at four to five million kroner, of which two and a half million are covered by insurance. THE FRENCH ELECTIONS. PARIS, SIINDAY.—Tbe second ballots in the elections of the Councils General took place to-day. Tke results, ae far as at present known, show that 65 Republicans and 16 Conservatives have been elected. The Republicans lost two seats. Polorrrimunn, SHNDAY.—Five of the second ballots for the elections to the Councils Gener.l for this district have resulted in the return of the Republican candidates.

AMERICA.—GIitEAT FOREST FIRES. NRW YORK, TURSDAY.—FOreSt fires are raging for 100 miles along the line of the Wisconsin Central Railway. The village of Spencer has been destroyed, and others are doomed unless rain sets in. The city of Marquettee, Michi- gan, is completely surrounded by flames.--an appeal has been lodged in the Supreme Court of Chihuahua agairst the sentence of one year's imprisonment with hard labour and a fine of six hundred dollars recently passed upon Mr. Cutting. It is reported that Mr. Bayard has made a final demand for his releaee, and the matter will probably be re- ferred to an International Tribune. Meanwhile the war fever on the Mexican border continues unabated. Ten gun carriages have been sipped from New York for Texas. Several men-of-war are understood to be under orders to sail for the Mexican coast, but official information as to their destination is refused. WASHINGTON, TUBSDLY ..—President Cleveland has ap- pointed Mr. James Matthews, a gentleman of colour, to be Recorder of Deeds, an office for which the Senate had pre- viously rejected him. PRUSSIA AND THE VATICAN. Roma, WIDNRSDAT.-1 special convention has been signed between Prussia and the Vatican with the object of terminating all controversies on secondary matters between the contracting parties, and of regulating for toe future the relations between the State and the Catholic Church in Prussia concerning the procedure connected with the presentation to benefices, and also with regard to ecaleeial- tical seminaries.

ICURDISH RAIDS. ST. PBTRRSBURG, WIWNBSDAS.—A despatch received here from Tiflis announces that on the 21st ult. about 200 Turkish Kurds, armed with Peabody rifles, who had crossed the frontier in the Sournaly district of the province of Erivan, attacked some Russian jczjidis near Karadjaran, some miles north of Erivan, carrying off nearly 1,000 sheep. Fighting was carried on between the raiders and the Ras- sians for nearly two days, tilers being several killed and wounded on both sides.

Ten policemen have stated in their evidence that they did not draw their revol- vers until after the bomb had exploded. CLOSE OP AMERICAN COTTON MILLS. Nsw YORK, THURSDAY.—Eight cotton mills at Atlanta, Georgia, have been closed, and 2,738 men are thus thrown out of employment, and committees have been organised for the relief of the unemployed. TERRIBLE FOREST FIRES. NEW YORK, THIIRSDAT.—Tbe forest fires in Wisconsin are abating. About a dozen persons are reported to have perished in the flames, and it is feared that many back- woodsmen have met the same fate. The loss among live stock is terrible. It is believed that in Calumet, Clark, Marathon, and a few of the adjacent counties 500 families liove been rendered homeless.

The Speaker took the chair at 2-15, immediately after prayers. when the process of swearing in members was at once resumed. There was only a very limited attendance. In the first batch of five sworn were Mr. Gladstone, the Marquis of Hartington, Sir William Harcourt, gr. F. S. Powell, and Mr. E. Hubbard. Included in the next two batches were Mr. Spencer, Mr. 0. Coope, Mr. Finlay, Mr. Webster, Mr. R. Cooke, Mr. Gerald Balfour, and Sir Lyon Mayfair. Amongst others subsequently sworn were Sir E. J. Reed. Mr. Tomlinson, Mr. H. Lawson, Sir H. Selwin- Ibbetson, Colonel Makin, and Mr. Mark Stewart. • After a pause, during which no members presented them- selves at the table, the STRAKER, rising, said—l have to ac- (plaint the House that I have received a letter from the right hon. gentleman the Member for tai-Lothian, which I will read to the House :—My dear Mr. Speaker,—l take the liberty of advising you that having been re- turned to Parliament for the county of Edinburgh, or Mid-Lothian, and also for the Borough of Leith, I elect to serve for the county of Edinburgh, or Mid-Lothian.— I have the honour to be faithfully yours, W. E. Gran- STONE. When the oath had been administered to about 30 hon. gentlemen the House beoame empty. In the course of the nest hour several members who arrived at long intervals were sworn in singly. Among them were Mr. C. Villiers,' Mr. L. Cohen, Mr. Johns, Mr. Cozens-Hardy. General Sir F. Filzwywam, Mr. Whitley, Major Dickson. Sir D. Currie, Mr F. H. Maclean, and Sir W. Hart Dyke. On the motion of Mr. Arnold Morley, a new writ was ordered to be issued for the election of a new member for the Burton Division of Stifford, in the room of Sir M. A. Bass, Bait, who has been elevated to the Peerage. The House adjourned at 4-5. HOUSE OF CONIMONS.—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 1-5, when the business of swearing in those members who had not previously taken the oath of allegiance was at once proceeded with. Among the &et to come to the table were Mr. Cabal, Mr. Dixon. Hartland, Baron Dirnsdale, Mr. Gourley, Mr. C. Lewis, Mr. A. Sutherland, Mr. T. Roe, Col. Gunter, Sir E. Lechmere. 1' Mr. J. Corbett, Sir H. Roscoe, Mr. H. C6aplin, and Mr. C T. D. Aclan4. The above were all soon sworn before half- past one o'clock, after which hour the arrival of unsworn members took place at more or less infrequent intervals. They included General Fraser, Col. Blundell, Mr. Cremar, Captain G. E. Price (Devonport). Lord Grimston, Mr. Round, Lord Claud Hamilton, Mr. Gully, Dr. McDonald, Mr. Morgan Howard, Colonel Sandvs, Mr. Labouchere, Mr. Giles, Mr. Justin H. M`Carthy, gr. Haldane, Mr. Gent. Divis, Sir J. W. NEW WRITS.—On the motion of Mr. AKE as DOUGLAS,neW writs were ordered for the Blackpool Division of North Lan- cashire, in the room of Sir F. A. Stanley, on his acceptance of the office of the President of the Coolluittee of Privy Council for Trade and Plantations; anti for the Northern Division of Northampton, in the room of Lord Burghley, appointed one of her Majesty's Grooms-in-Waiting. On the motion of Mr. Akers Douglas, it was also resolved that the House at its rising adjourn to the 19th inst. The House adjourned at 3-50.
