At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before his honour Judge Thompson, the adjourned case of Mrs. Ann Monaghan, a widow, against Mr. and Mrs. William Johnson, was heard. It was an action to recover £5, alleged to have been wrong- fully received from Messrs. J. C. Gamble and Son's sick club on the death of the plaintiff's husband, and also to recover £2 10s, the value of certain clothing which bad belonged to deceased. There was a counter claim for .£9 alleged to he owing by Monaghan to Johnson; with whom he lived some time prior and up to the time of his death. Under the rules of Messrs. Gamble's sick club, of which deceased was a member, .E 5 was payable on the death of a member to his widow if he left one, and if he 1-ft no widow then to another person he might have ap• pointed in writing before witnesses. In this Case the John- sons had got a written authority from Monaghan for the Messrs. Gamble to pay it, and ignoring the prior claim o( the widow. At a previous hearing his honour ordered Messrs. Gamble and Son to be entered as j)int defendants, expressing an opinion that payment to any other person (Fri not relieve them from the liability to carry out their origi- nal onligation to the widow.—On ;Yednesday, Mr. R. W. H. Thomas appeared for all the defendants. and Mr. H. Linden Riley for the plaintiff.—His Honour ordered Messrs. GAm. hh. and Son to pay £5 and cAsts into courr, but out of that 101 would be paid to Mrs. Johnson as a settlement of all matters in dispute. Mr. Henry Irving was entertained at dinner in New York on Wednesday evening by a number of American friends. LORD SALISBURY ON IMPERIAL FEDERATION.—A. depu- tation from the Imperial Federation agee waited on Lord • Salisbury at the Colonial Office, do Wednesday, to urge hint to call a conference or to appoie a R)yal Commission for the purpose of suggesting some pract,cal means whereby concerted action may be taken for placing up,m a satisfac- tory basis the defence of the ports and commerce of the em- pire is time of war, and for promoting direct intercourse, commercial, postal, and telegraphic between the several countries of the empire in time of pmce, and any other means of securing closer federation or union of all parts of the empire. Sir Thomas Brassev introduced the deputation, which included several members of parliament. Lord Salisbury said in reply that the proposition of the deputa- tion was one he could not answer on his own anthority, and he wou!d have to consult his colleagues. The growth of sentiment in favour of Imperial federation had .been very rapid and very remarkable. He believed the abstention from a premature formulation of definite proposals on the subject was very wise, because the questions with which they had to deal were of enormous complication And diffi- culty. The difficulties in the way of settling the question of Imperial defence were in process of being overcome, and the efforts of the colonies would be, met in a corresponding spirit by the mother country. The matter would be fully considered by the Cabinet. MORE RIOTING IN BELFAST
HEAVY FIRING.-MANY KILLED AND WOUNDED.

Further disturbances took place in Belfast on Saturday afternoon near Alexandra Dock and Bally- ; inacrett. There was considerable stone-throwing, which commenced while an excursion party were 'driving through the district on cars. At night the rioting was resumed, and attained more alarming proportions than at any period in the history of the ' present disturbances. The conflicts resulted in in- juries to some 50 persons. In many cases the wounds are expected to prove fatal. The most terrible struggle was on the Shankhill-road, where the police were everywhere made the common object of attack. Stones and pistol shots were discharged at them, causing many serious injuries. The peoplell were consequently fired upon by the constabulary with terrible effect. Some of the men were quar- tered on the premises of Mr. M`Kenna, publican, Old Lodge-road, which was surrounded and at- tacked, shots being fired in reply from the windows. At about ten o'clock matters assumed a quieter aspect. Bodies of military—horse and foot— patrolled the town, and the police guarded all the dangerous localities. A proclamation was issued in the afternoon ordering the closing of all public- houses after 6 p.m. and prohibiting bands of music from parading the streets. The following communication relative to the ; present disturbed state of Belfast, and the further ; measures to be adopted for the preservation of thel peace of the town, was received on Saturday by the Mayor of Belfast (Sir Edward J. Harland, Bart.) from the now Chief Secretary for Ireland (Sir M. Hicks-Beach, Bart., M.P.) :—" Dublin Castle, August 6, 1886.—Sir,—I am directed by the Lords Justices to state that their Excellencies are seriously con- cerned at the condition of Belfast, and consider it imperative that the most energetic measures should be taken with the view to putting an end to the disturbances which have brought discredit and dis- grace upon the town. Every requisition of thel magistrates for extra police and other assistance has been promptly complied with. Further aid of the same kind will be afforded should it be desired, but their Excellencies would earnestlyimpress upon you, as representing the inhabitants of Belfast, that such action onithe part of the Government cannot secure its object without the hearty co-operation of those who are primarily ipterested in its success, and that it is the first duty of all peaceable and law- abiding citizens to afford their active assistance to the authorities in their endeavour to restore order and maintain the peace. Their Excellencies have, therefore, read with great satisfaction the terms of the proclamation which you issued yesterday, and every assistance and countenance in their power will be given to make this step effective. It is for the consideration of the magistrates whether, look- ing to the gravity of the present situation, it may not be desirable to extend the prohibition of assem- blies likely to endanger public peace to processions and bands, and they would call your attention to a proclamation issued by the Mayor of Belfast under similar circumstances on the 19th of August, 1872. It has further occurred to their Excellencies that much advantage might arise from the presence in Belfast at the present time of a civil officer of high rank who should be in supreme control of the move- ments of the police, and they have therefore in- structed the Inspector-General of the Royal Irish Constabulary to proceed at once to Belfast. . . . Their Excellencies do not intend in any way by this step to interfere with the constitutional responsi- bility of the magistrates, but they hope it will tend to secure uniformity of action in the work of restor- ing order, and vindicating the law, and they confi- dently rely upon the magistrates, both local and resident, recognising the advantages which may arise from this arrangement, and upon their heartily co-operating with the Inspector-General in carry- ing out such measures as may be required for this purpose. Their Excellencies have communicated this arrangement to the military authorities, whose cordial co-operation throughout with the ; civil authorities they have much pleasure in recog-

nising." A resident magistrate on Monday left Dublin for Belfast, taking with him warrants from the Castle appointing all the superior military officers at pre- sent at Belfast special magistrates during the pre- sent disturbances. This.step is regarded as the initiative to placing the town under martial law. The state of Belfast is causing grave anxiety to the executive at Dublin Castle: Prince Edward of Saxe- Weimar, commander of the forces, had an inter- view with the Chief Secretary on Monday on the subject, and the deputy Inspector-General of con- stabulary has furnished a report of the state of the town to the authorities.

A Belfast correspondent, writing on Monday, says: —Eleven deaths and 130 wounded, many seriously, are the results of rioting since Satuiday. Nearly all the casualities were due to the fire of the police. Rioting was renewed this morning in the Grosvenor- road district. The police were again compelled to use their arms, with the result that several persons were wounded. In Killen-street some boys were collected alongside a school, and were, it is said, fired on by 'the troops. One of the boys had hist right hand blown off, and the soldier who fired the shot was at once arrested and removed under escort to the barracks. One thousand infantry and 200 cavalry arrived here this morning from Dublin and. the Curragb. Shots were fired on Monday night in Grosvenor Fields-road, Durham-street, while an unsuccessful attempt was made by the mob to wreck the houses in Gibson-street. The homeward journey of the workmen from Queen's island led to some rioting in North-street and Old Lodge-road, but the fighting was promptly quelled by the appearance of infantry and cavalry on the scene. Serious stone throwing occurred on Newtonards-road. The rioters, how- ever, were dispersed by a troop of Dragoons charg- ing down the road. It was here that District In- spector Bull was badly wounded by a stone which struck him at the back of the head. According to the official list, nine deaths have taken place, but if later accounts of the fighting at Springfield are to be credited, the loss of life must be considerably greater. Eye-witnesses of the ferocious fighting state that it was carried on between the rival mobs in this district in the early hours of Sunday morn- ing and again on Sunday night. They estimate the killed and wounded at sixty. The latest accounts describe the rioting there as being of a most deadly character, the combatants being well armed with rifles and revolvers, and taking up positions behind breastworks. On Monday a party of men with rifles assembled, but were dispersed by the cavalry. ' Military reinforcements, both infantry and artil- lery, continued to arrive all day, and troops were concentrated in the area of the recent riots. Shank- hill and Old Lodge-roads, Percy-street, and sur- rounding thoroughfares are strongly guarded by troops and constabulary, who completely overawe groups of. sullen-looking men who are idly saunter- ing in the streets. Shortly after noon on Tuesday there were 4,000 soldiers on duty. On all sides. are to be seen evidences of the wreck and ruin effected by the rioters. Both sides did their utmost to con- ceal from the police the results, which were not as disastrous on the Protestant as on the Roman Catholic side. The dead and wounded were huddled together and hurried home, so that the full results are never likely to be known unless there is the strictest in- vestigation. A public subscription is being raised for the relief of the sufferers and the families of the killed. We understand that the Catholics will not hold their usual outdoor demonstrations in Belfast next Monday, which is usually observed as a high holiday. At Belfast, on Tuesday, John McKeown was sen- tenced to three months' imprisonment for having a five-chambered revolver in his possession at about one o'clock on Tuesday morning in Conway-street. Patrick Sullivan and William Martin, for attacking a man in North-street, were committed to gaol for two months.

A telegram, dated New York, Tuesday morning, says :—Mr. Michael Davitt, who has just arrived here on his way to Chicago, has been interviewed by a newspaper reporter in regard to the Belfast riots. Mr. Davitt said he did not think the riots materially affected the political situation, except that they would show the absolute groundlessness of the English boast that the Orangemen are the friends of law and order in Ireland. The Orange- men, added Mr. Davitt, tried to provoke a general fight, and, having failed, they felt bound:to fight any- way, and therefore they arrayed themselv6 against the police. There was more rioting at Belfast on Tuesday, accompanied by the loss of one life. The fatality took place under most disagreeable circumstances, as advantage was taken.of the funeral of the lad Devlin to fire shots at the 300 Catholics who fol- lowed the body to the grave. One man was fatally wounded, while in the scuffle which preceded the arrest of the ten persons from whom the firing proceeded another man was seriously injured. A i third case occurred in Grosvenor-road, and lies n a precarious condition. A scrimmage with stones took place at Sprmgfields between two large mobs, which had to be separated by the military. div.head: LORD SALISBURY AT THE MANSION
div.p: LORD SALISBURY AT THE MANSION
HOUSE.

Her Majesty's Ministers were entertained at the Mansion House on Wednesday night. The Secretary for War and the First Lord of the Admiralty, in res- ponding to the usual toasts, referred to the "demand.' which the country has recently put forward that its money shall be well and wisely spent. • Both Ministers seemed not unwilling to admit that the country had a right to have an efficient army and navy; and promised to do their best to carry out reforms. Lord Salisbury, in replying to the toast of Her Majesty's Ministers, said there were two circumstances in the recent elections which were not strictly of a political character, but to which he was bound to refer with gratification. One of them was that in constituencies of a thoroughly demo- cratic character, dealing with one of the most im- portant questions which it was possible to submit to judgment of the people, as well as in other con- stituencies of an opposite character, all classes had pulled thoroughly together. They had only to cast their eyes over the City to see examples of the answer that had been returned to the endeavour to set class against class, and to see also that the trust the various classes of the country reposed in each other had not been undermined. The Afghan and Egyptian problems, which Were unsettled when lie last spoke at the Mansion House, were still unset- tled ; but he thought there was a more general desire for peace among the peoples of the world. The greatest achievement of the last 13 months was that a continuous policy had been restored to the country; and in proportion to the continuity of that policy would be the influence of England. The news that had reached us from Ireland showed that the population of that island was far from being a homogeneous people. It would be too soon to say what would be dune in that island; but one of their first duties would be to free the loyal subjects of the Queen from the restraints which were over them. He spoke of the duty of the Government to exhaust every effort to secure peace to the loyal sub- jects of the Queen in their vocations. Previous Go- vernments had only succeeded to an imperfect extent, but the present Government had the advantage of being the bearers of a mandate from the people, de- ciding irrevocably the question which had wrecked the peace of the neighbouring island. The question of the independent government of Ireland had been referred by the most powerful. statesman of this century to the only tribunal that could determine it without appeal. The people had given answer which was emphatic and unequivocal. The minor- ity would not have been even what it was but for the personal influence of Mr. Gladstone, and it was not superfluous to- note that if England had decided alone the majority would have been far more over- whelming than It was. The Lord Chancellor and Mr. Stanhope responded for the Houses of Parlia- ment. Mr. Stanhope expressed the hope that the present Government would set in order the dis- organised finances of the country. •

div.head: "ST3OTINi.3-" THE NIAGARA,
div.p: "ST3OTINi.3-" THE NIAGARA,
RAPIDS.

Late on Sunday afternoon, two coopers named Potts and Hazlett started on a trip through the Niagara Whirlpool Rapids in a torpedo-shaped bar- rel. They were an hour going from the foot of the Cataract to the mouth of the river, a distance of eight miles. The barrel was built of oak staves an inch and a half thick. It is ten feet long, with a round prow covered with sheet iron. The keel runs the whole length. The stern is flat, and about two feet in diameter. A twelve-inch propeller wheel, worked by hand, is inside the barrel; and a small iron ruddet, worked with wires, projects from the stern. The greatest diameter of the craft is three feet. The length inside available for the occupants is six feet, the front being headed of, so that if stove by the rocks the occupants would be safe. There is a turret-covered opening just large enough for one man to get into the craft at a time. In it were two thick glass bull's-eyes, and an inch-and-a- quarter iron pipe through which air was taken. The whole contrivance was bound with twenty two-inch iron bands, and the wheel was protected by iron rods. The preparations for the trip were completed by carefully ballasting the boat with 3001bs. of sand, and putting a large piece of ice in to keep the air cool. Potts and Hazlett fastened themselves to the bottom so securely that they could not be thrown about inside by the action of the waves. On starting the craft was carried down the surge of the first breaker and hurled stem fore- most over the swell towards the next big wave. Surging currents coming together in the centre of the gorge in the vortex turned the craft ove- . When she righted for a moment before being caug it in the next breaker it was seen that the American flag which had been fastened to the stern was not torn away. The craft dashed on in the surf, being twirled about, pitched first forward, then down- ward, and finally the last ;wave tossed it into the whirlpool. It had been in the rapids for a few seconds less than four minutes, and was carried so near the shore in the outer swirl of the malestrom that Potts put out his head and hand. They had ' escape(' the worst of the whirlpool, and said after- wards they could have gone ashore. In two minutes they were close to the second series of rapids, and were caught by the waves and tossed along. Several rocks were grazed, and the craft got a worse shaking than before. Some water poured through the air pipe as they were sucked under by the swell near the Devil's Hole, and the passage was longer and harder, lasting sixteen minutes. The propeller and rudder were of no use whatever. When they reached the smooth water the men were fatigued but unhurt. They crawled out, and sitting on the top of the barrel were towed ashore. They were drenched by the water through the air pipe and from the melting ice. The wheel and rudder were uninjured. The flag was still flying. Fully ten thousand people witnessed the feat. Graham, who went through in the barrel previoutly, says he will go through with his head out of the barrel, and challenges Potts and Hazlett to do the same. He declares also that he will, about August 19, get into the barrel, and di-op from the old Suspension Bridge into the river, a distance of 190 feet, ending the performance with the whirlpool trip. If he does this safely, Potts and Hazlett declare they will arrange for a trip over the falls.

The Queen's Prize at Shoeburyness was on Wednesuay won by the 4th deracninent of the 2nd Middlesex, and the Prince of Wales's Priz3 by the Coester ant Carnarvon Artillery. THE SHOOTING OF THE VOLHNTEERS.—The Adjutant- General, Lord Wolseley, on behalf of the Field-Marshall commanding-in-chief, has juet issued a General Orthr mak- ing very great changes in the musketry regulations ot the Volunteers, and to which they must in future confor.m in order to earn the cavitation grant. The new scheme , ~.omes into force at once except in the case of those corps • ..vnich have completed or commeoced the course for the cur- tcnt year. CONFESSION OF MURDER. A man narri9,4 Frederick PA.RNES, 31 yeals old, was found behind a h,dge :it Grove- hill, Camberwell, With a leaded revolver in his possession, 0,,r1y on Thursday morning, and when brought before the Lambeth police magistrate he said he was " on his way to give himself up " for murder. The man was remanded, sod in the course of the afternoon he made a statement to the effect that between one and to o'clock on the morning A the 23rd June he threw his wife and child over Lam- Lath Bridge, and that he was sure they were drowned.

div.head: POLICEMAN.
div.p: POLICEMAN.

At an Occasional Court, held at the offices in Bank- street, Warrington. on Wednesday morning, a farm labourer named Thomas Flaherty was brought up on remand, before Mr. Maroon, charged with inflicting bodily haftn upon Police Constable Stead, of the Lancashire constabalary, in the township of Hoighton, on the night of the Ist August. Mr. Longton defended.—Superintendent Weir said that at 10.30 Sergeant Barnes and P.C. Stead saw some fireworks being let off near a farm yard, and the sergeant gave the constable instructions what to do. The constable went to the place and saw three men, who used threats to him. Shortly afterwards prisoner ran at the constable, and com- mitted the assault complained of, particalars of which were given in evidence. _

Dr. Smith was the first witness called. He said that on the 2nd mat, about two a.m., Constable Stead was brought to his surgery in a cab. He was suffering from very great nervous shock, and apparently from loss of blood. His clothing was saturated with blood. Witness examined him, and found him suffering from a jagged laceration extend- ing from the right angle of the mouth downwards and out- wards, even below the jaw. There was also a second lacera- tion, extending along the red part of the lip. The lining membrane of the month was also very much lacerated, an& hung in folds. He was, as well, suffering from a recent bruise on the right cheek. Witness dressed his wounds, and had been attending him since. Superintendent Weir : I suppose you foand it necessary to stitch the wound ? Yes, I put several stitches be- lieve you did not consider him fit for any duty; 1, you ordered him to remain off duty? I told the sergeant he would not be fit or duty for a week or more.—He is not yet fit? No.—Was there any danger arislig from the wound? There was danger of erysipelas and ale° of blood poisoning,—Would a thumb put into the constable's moutb, violently out.:ards, piodnce the injuries lyou found? I think it would.—Mr. Longton ; You say his clothing was' saturated with blood. You are not prepared to swear that the blood was his own blood. Supposing two men had been cut, and were bleeding with a struggle. some of the blood relight have been that of the other man? Yes.—Might not the wound have been caused by a blow? I think not. I think a blew from an instrument to have caused that wound must have unseated two or three of his teeth, and very

likely fractured the jaw as well.—Would not the flesh have cut against tbie teeth? Not such a length as that, The ; wound was about 21 inches long.—Could it have been 1, caused by a man falling on a sharp substance, such as a m4cadam stone? I think not —l3v Mr. Weir: The con- stable was suffering from loss of blood, and was quite blanched. I had to give him restoring draughts. Police-cm3stable Thomas Stead, stationed at Croft, said that be was on duty at Houghton Green in company with Sergeant Barnes, on the first of the month, at about 10 30 in the evening. He saw what appeared to be small fireworks let off near a farmhouse at Houghton Green. In consequence of what the sergeant told him he went to the place. He there saw the prisoner Thomas Flaherty and two other men. He said, " Which of you have been throwing up those fireworks." Prisoner said "It's none of us; you can search me if you like. I have neither pipe nor matches." Witness pat his foot on the burning fragments of the fireworks, and prisoner then said "Lock me up; no b-- policeman can lock me up, or sergeant either. If you do Pll knock your b head off. Let's go into him." Witness heard the sergeant say You had better i go away, and never mind threatening anyone." Witness said "-If you don't go away you will get locked up." Pri- soner then rushed at him, and bit him on the right side of the face with his fist. He was striking at him again, and witness struck his arm with a walking stick and parried the blow. Prisoner then got hold of him, and they struggled. They fell to the ground together, witness en the top. Wit- ness tried to get the handcuffs from his pocket. Before that prisoner got his thumb in witness's mouth; and tore his right cheek a little. Witness tried to get his handcuffs out of his pockets, and prisoner overpowered and got on the top of him. Prisoner put his knee on witness's ct est, one hand on his throat, and got two Of his fingers into hs (wit- ness's) mouth. He tore his mouth as hard as he could. Witness heard some one call out "Tom, Tom ;" and prisoner sa:d "Stick to him, boys, I'm working. I've done for one." He then got off him, and witness felt a blow on the nose. Witness was rendered partially insensible. Witsess got up sometime afterwards, and found the sergeant trying to handcuff the prisoner, several people assisting him. Pri- soner was secured, and Dr. Smith afterwards dressed the wounds of witness, who had suffered a great deal of pain, and had been off duty since the assault. There was a great deal of blood on his clothing. Sergeant Eward Barnes spoke to being in company, with Stead on the night in question. Having given corrob)ra• tive evidence regarding the assault on Stead, witness said that while prisoner was being assaulted by Stead be was attacked )yt the other two men, and a struggle ensued. Afterwards, at the police station, witness charged prisoner, who replied, "I did nothing."—By Mr. Langton: Stead did not strike or push the prisoner, before prisoner struck him. Michael Flaherty did not endeavour to separate them. Other corroborative evidence having been given, prisoner was committed for trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Ses- sions.

Prisoner Thos. Flahertyand a second prisoner named Mid. Flaherty were then conjointly charged with assaulting Ser- geant Barnes, at the same time and place.—The Sergeant stated that he went to the assistance of Stead, when prisoner Michael and another man rushed at him, and he struggled with them. Thomas Flaherty struck the sergeant in the face whilst he bad held of Michael, and afterwards jumped on his back, put his arms round his neck, and tried to put his thumb into the sergeant's mouth. Witness struck the nrisoner with his stick, and they hit him several times. With assistAnce he succeeded in taking Thomas into cus- tody, and Michael was arrested later on. After other evidence bad been taken, prisoners were com- mitted for trial.

DISGRACEFUL SCENE AT A PRIZE FIGHT.—At Pontypridd, Evan F vans, one of the principals in a fatal prize fight on Eirw Mountain; William Hohnan, and Griffith Evans, seconds, and Thomas Williams, plate holder, have been charged with the manslaughter of John Jerfkins Jones, last Sunday morning. A quarrel arose between the decea•ed and Evans on Saturday night, and, after a protracted struggle, they determined to settle their disagreement by a pitched battle next day for 5s a side. At four o'clock on Sunday Imorning the four youths assembled on the mountain, and fighting was re-commenced. Both men fought desperately for an hour and a quarter. As one fell he was picked up by the other and the combat was instantly renewed, the struggle continuing in this way until 36 rounds were fought. Both were severely wounded, and Jones was thoroughly exhausted towards the close, and was bleeding terribly. Both shook hands after the fight, and Jones shortly afterwards dropped senseless to the ground and died. The casewas adjourned. LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE RAILWAY COMPANY.—The half-yearly meeting of the Lancashire Railway Company was held on Wednesday. The Chairman (Mr. P,arson), in moving the adoption of the report, said that in 1872 a divi- dend was paid of 8i- per cent, but since then there had been a gradual decline to that which the directors now recom- mended, which was 3 per cent. During the past half year, owing chiefly to the depression in trade, there lied been a falling off in the receipts of £24,666, but be thought that under their peculiar circumstances they had reason to be satisfied With the result, as, in addition to that falling off, they had had to find £23,579 for interest on additionalcapital. The number of passengers carried had fallen off in all the classes, but there was an increase in the number of con- tract tickets sold. Savings had been effected in the main- tenance of permanent way and in other items, while the stock of the company was now so much improved that the directors felt justified in reducing the sum test aside each half year for replacement by £lO,OOO. In the future, as in the past, every effort would be made to economise. After some discussion the report mils adopted.
GENERAL NEWS.
Mr. Rnekin is so much better that no further bulletin will be issued.
For refusing, when requested, tr) assist the police to con- vey a prisoner to the station, Mr. John Geraghty, a member of the Bootle Towa Councii, was on Monday committed for trial.
Lord St. Oswald has again returned the tenants cn his Nostell estate twenty-five per cent. of their rents. A similar abatement has been made by him:for the past six years. _

- The "Journal des Debats " publishes a communication from Rome representing that his Holiness the Pope is seri- ously ill, and that the nature of his malady is such that his life Is despaired of. The Dorset Regiment, ordered home from E..rypt on account of sickness. arrived at Portsmouth on Sunday. The regiment was stationed at Shelland, twelve miles beyond Assouan, and in five months 80 men died from fever and dysentry.

FATAL ACCIDENT WITH FIREARMS.—On Sunday, whilst Mr. William Atkinson, a broker, who was on a visit to his larother, Mr. Thomas Atkinson, West Derby, near Liverpool, was handling a gun, it accidentally exploded. The charge struck Mr. Atkinsoa in the mouth, fracturing his jaw and terribly mutilating his face. He was taken to the Royal Infirmary, where Ise died soon after admission. ACCIDENT TO CARDINAL MANNING.—In tbo Church of English Martyrs, Tower Hill, Londonron Tuesday morn- ing, Cardinal Manning consecrated the Right Rev. Anthony Gaughron as Bishop of Priene and Vicar Apostolic of Orange Free State. On retnrning to Westminster a wheel of his carriage came off. Though he was shaken, it is not be- lieved the Cardinal was injured. He drov:. home in a four-, wheeled cab. ATMOSPHERIC PHENOMENON AT EOLTON.—.5.'oon after twelve at noon on Tuesday Bolton became enveloped in midnight darkness, and the gloom continued for more than an hour and a half, when heavy rain fell for a few minutes. Subsequently, while the sky to the west of the town showed a brilliant luminous glare, the east portion remained thickly overcast, this continuing until shortly after two o'clock. The temperature was close and oppressive. EXTRAORDINARY DROWNING ACCIDENT.—An extraordi- nary incident was related on Monday night at Corwen, at an inquest on Clement Roger Poston, who was drowned in the Dee. The deceased entered the water to assist his Master's son, who was struggling in deep water, when he was himself swept away. In his struggle:. the artificial teeth became wedged in his throat, and he was immedi- ately drowned. Tbe jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

A TRAGEDY.—On Saturday, in a suburb in Pestb, a man who has been weak ef mind for several weeks suddenly went mad in the street. lie attacked a woman with his knife' and when on her calling for help several men ap- proached, his father-in-law being among them, he ran his knife three times into the breast of the latter, and injured the others set iously. The womAn was killed. Meanwhile more people came up and tried to secure the madman, but without effect. At last they beat him with cudgels until he was fairly overpowered.

Tax TIRE tXPIdDITION.—Six arrests were effected on Friday, and without any collision between the authorities and the islanders. One of the men voluntarily surrendered himself. They arrived in Oban on Saturday morning, being conveyed in the steamer Negel, in charge of 36 policemen. Each man was landed haodcuffed to a policeman, and they were lodged in the police station until the departure of the train at ten o'clock at Inverarv. A large crowd assenabled to witness their departure at the station, cheer after cheer was given for the Crofters, while three groans for the Duke of Argyle were called and responded to with much demon- stration of feeling,

CAPTURE oF Comens.—On Sunday the Birmingham police made a raid on a small brass-caster's shop in a back court in Wrentham-street. Two men, father and son, who gave the name of Johnson, were discovered at work coining. The son was melting white spelter in a pot, and the father was attending to an electro-plating apparatus, in both of which were four base florins being plated. All the apparatus for milling and polishing the coins was found. Twenty farina unpolished were also found in the father's pocket. The prisoners are said to have emissaries in different parts of the country for dispesing of base coins. They were on Mon- day remanded for the Mint to prosecute. . AN IMPRISONED CLERGYMAN.—The Rev. Mr. Levs, the venerable minister of the First United Presbyterian Church cortgregalon, Strathaven, who more than a fortnight since was sentenced at Edinburgh to imprisonment during the pleasure cf the Court, for refusing to deliver op his gran 1' children to their father, still remains in Calton Prison, Edine burgh. Mr. Leys's case is exciting much sympathy and keen controversy throughout the country. A petition askine for the release of Mr. Lea's was forwarded on Saturday to Colonel Holier,the Conservative member for South Lanark. shire, who has written saying he has seen the Home Secre- tary and Lard Advocate, and will spare no effort on behalf of the imprisoned clergyman. ALLEGED GROSS LIBELS ON SIR W. ARMSTRONG AND CO. —ln the Queen's Bench en Saturday, before the Lord Chief Juetice and Mr. Justice Denman, Mr. Walton made an ap- plication, on behalf of Sir W. Armstrong and Cti ,to restrain , Captain Annit, editor and printer of ihe Admirety and Horse Guards Gazette, from the publication, pending an action for libel, of certain defamatory matter, alleging that memtiers of plaintiffs' firm, by reason of their connection with the Government and with the War Office, corruptly influenced the Ordnance Select Committeet.grenting large contracts to plaintiffs' firm.—Mr. Walton said the libels were continued tomi week to week, and were of the graFs2sr character, charging several distinguished persons with cor- ruption and c,nspiracv, and the firm with incompetency.— Their lordships refused the injunction on the ground that the alleged hods were privileged, and if they were true it was of the utmost importance to the Country that they should be made known. EXECuTION or THE ASHTON POISONER. Mary Ann Britland, c.indemned to death at the last Manchester As- sizes for the murder of Mary Dixon, at Ashton-under-Lyne. was executed on Monday morning within Strangeways Gaol, Manchester. Berry was the executioner. The woman was partly pinioned within :he cell, from which she was conducted to the scaffold a few minutes before eight. She was much distressed, and as she walked across the corridor was supported by two female warders, the male warders coming behind. She was accompanied by the chaplain, reading the burial service, and the usual gaol officials, and the execution was witnessed also by a magistrate from Ash- ton and four reporters. The scene as the procession moved to the scaffold was very painful. The voice of the chap- lain, as he read the usual prayers, was drowned by the screams of the woman, "Oh, Lord, have mercy! Oh, Lord, forgive m, ! " she piteously cried out. While standing on the scffild Mrs. Britlend was supPortsd by the warders, who left her side just before the drawing of the bolt. When once en the scaffold the necessary details were at once com- pleted. and when the bolt fell the woman appeared to die instantly. A drop of seven feet bad been allow, d. T,e woman is reported to have made a full confession of her guilt of the first crime, and when asked by some reletivi s who visited her on Saturday whether she had done away with tier husband and daughter she hung her head and did not deny it. During Sunday night the convict, who I,el listened to the ministrations of the prison chaplain wit'i gratitude, was greatly excited, and at midnight she was heard singing snatches of hymns. On Monday morning, when offered refreshment she was unable to take it.

Teta TRADES UNION CONGRESS —The ".Final Notice" of the Nineteenth Annum Trades Union Congrese, which is to be held at Hull on Monday, September 6, and five fol- lowing days, together with the " Ptoposed Parliamentary Programnie for the Session 1886," was issued by the Par- liamentary Coenmittee of the Congress on Saturday. AP- pended to the " Final Notice " is first "The Order of Business," which is as follows :—" 1. The Chairman of the Parliamentary Committee will take the chair at 12 o'clock prompt on September 6th. 2. Election of officers for the Congress. 3. Election of Standing Orders Committee. 4. Parliamentary Committee's Report. 5. Reports of Standing Orders Committee on the credentials of delegates. 6. Prestdent's opening address." The following is the "Proposed Parliamentary Programme for the Session of 1886" :—" 1. Employers' Liability Act (1880.) 2. Cer- tificates of competency for men in charge of steam engines and boilers. 3. The -desirability of increasing the numher of factory and workshops inspectors. 4. The right of the relatives of deceased miners to be represented at coro- ners' inquests. 5. Co-operation and i.e rehtion to trade unionism. 6. li, presentation of labour in Parliament. 7. Codification of the criminal law. 8. Codification of the laws summarily administered in petty sessions. 9. Re- form of the land laws. 10. Public inquiry into sudden and accidental deaths in Scotland. IL Mines reguletnon reform. 12. Law of Distraint Amendment Bill." In a foot- note it is stated that the programme in relation to subjects to be discussed "is not foal, and can be aAded to or amen- ded as the Congress may think fit," providing the questions to be submitted are "in harmony with the conduct of the Congress." EXTENUATING CIRCUMSTANCES.—The Assize Court of the Seine (France) has just dealt with a man convicted of a dou- ble murder in a manner which exemplifies the merciful dis- posit;on of French juries. The prisoner, Jean Weigscheider, a waiter, aged 39, was formerly in the service of a widow, Madame Genest, who kept a wine shop at Passy. Their relations were of a very intimate character' but after a time the woman broke off the intimecy, arid became the com- panion of a man named Leonard. Furious at his rejection, Weigscheider armed himself with a revolver and threatened his old mistress and Leonard. For creating a disturbance in the streets be was sentenced to four month's imprison- ment. On being released he breught against Madame Gen- est a charge of stealing a gold watch chain, but the accusa- tion was dismissed. Then he decided to kill the widow and her partner, and for that purpose he provided himself with a beg knife, and waited about the house for a favourable , opportunity. On the evening of May 6th, as the two were walking in the Rue Marseille. Weigscheider sprang from a doorway and stabbed Madame Genest twice in the back. She fell to the ground exclaiming, " I am killed," and Le- onard raised his stick to strike the assassin, who, however, rushed forward and plunged his knife into Leonard's bady. A concierge named Collet, attracted by the cries, ran up and tried to seize Weigscheider, but the latter ag tin used his weapon with terrible effect, burying the blade four times in the man's chest. He was then seized and bound by other passers-by and handed over to the police. Leonard end Collet died tbe following day, but Madame Genest recovered. In the dock the prisoner denied that there had been any pre- meditation on his part. He wept copiously and dectertd that he had no recollection of the crime. The jury returned a verdict iu accordance with which the prisoner VMS CO,ll- - to incarceration for life, with hard labour.

The match b-Awe.-n Nottinghamibire and Lancashire, for , the hen,fit ‘..f Barlow, alth.ugh it ended in a thaw, will be memorable for the large number oi p•ople who paid to see tht, game, and ffflr the fact that Nottinghamshire were only saved by time and the we.lllier from a severe defeat. On Saturday morning rain fell for some hours, and at noon the wicket was saturated to such an extent that the game could not be resumed until really half-past one. Notwithe:aud- ing this there was a large gathering of spectators at noon; and at three o'c'ock, wilen the sky had cleared, a very large crowd had formed mond the ground. There could not bays •E a fewer than 12 000 persons on the ground, and the ag- gregate fo, the three days of I era ,ns wt.e had actually parsed through the turnstiles was 26,010. Ater three days' criesit the march between the Austra. liens and Glouceelersbire at Clifton on SAturclAy ended in a ! drew. very much in favour of the horns side, the Augralians let th 9 finish with five wicke!s to fall wantinz; no fewer than ! 195 runs to win.

& most successful Canterbury Week was brougbt to a close on Saturday, wh.n Kent defeAted Yorkshi:e with six wickets to spare. Except on the nvenin, thy the weather waa brie t and pleasant. After Friday's tel..y there was little doubt as to the result. as Yorks )ire, with ono wicket down in their second innings, were still 157 runs in ar- rea,s.

In consequence of hoavy rain, the match between the Australians and Warwickshire at Birminzham could not be pruceeded with. Both teams were on the ground at noon on Tucsday. but at that timo the wicket wit: almost under water, and it was decided raa abandon it. as a drawn game. The overnight score Australians: First in- nings. Iq7 ; second inninirs, 5 for three wicket. Warwick- , shire : First innings. 70. Though the Sussex men at Brighton on Wednesday bad a. full innings to play and wanted only 72 runs to win, they found a t-.ek by n.) means easy. 'Etre matlh ended la a victory for Sussex by four wickets. The result delighted the spectators, and Jesse I-I:de was warmly cheered for vigorous c•ick,,t. Rain at Sheffield completely rained the return match be- tween Yo,kshire and Notts, and ;' ended in a thaw in favour of Notts. as at th-t drawing of stumps Yorkshire, with six wickAs down in their second innings., were still 23 runs in arrears.

The weather was b,autifully fine at Leyton on Weclue.s. day, when Essex continu.d tira innings againßt Derby- shirdtand thal.ka Oie vigorous hitting of ai round and the stea )y cricket of Silcnek the total r2ached 202. Tie two proftssionals put on 77 rims fr tho sixth wicket. Being 191 behind, Ess.x followed on at a quarter to f,,tr, ano. started so badly that five wickets were down for 45. The remaining wickets fell rapi ily and the inaings closed at six o'clock for 113, Dabyshire thus wir.ning by ml in,ings and 78 rune. At Gloucester on Wednesday .Middl-s,x gained a mnst Idecisive victory over Gioucestrshire by an innings and 87 runs.

div.head: SATURDAY, AUGUST 14, 1886.
div.p: SATURDAY, AUGUST 14, 1886.

THE Electors of the Ntwton Division of South-West Lancashire are called upon to select a fresh representative, owing to the elevation to the peerage of Sir Richard Cross. Another opportunity is afforded them of showing their minds on the great question which is before the country; and it is to be hoped that the Liberals, now that a good chance is given them, will see to it that they are at last represented by a Liberal. Sir Richard Cross as the man in possession of the seat was bad to dislodge, for possession is sometimes nine points of the case in elec- tioneering as in law. But he is now out of the way; he has been elbowed out of the House of Commons, and is taking his fare- well of his late constituents. Speaking in the Newton Town Hall, on Monday. Sir RICHARD CROSS said —" Connected with that high office of Secretary of State for India, it had been conveyed to him that it was necessary he should accept a generous offer of Her Majesty, viz., a seat in the Howe of Lords." It is pretty well known that he didn't for some time see that all this was "necessary," and that he thought it was anything but " generous " to give to another man what he regarded as his post as Home Secretary. But Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL was inex. orable, and the elect of the Newton Divi- sion has been sacrificed. The Conservatives, alive to what was going on, have had a can- didate ready in the person of Mr. W. T. LEGH. He is a young man who would never have been heard of in connection with this or any other constituency if it had not been for his interest in a large slice of the sod' in this part of the country. England re- quires above all things a reform of the land laws; but the landlord class stand in the way of all reform; and they are the last people that either tenant farmers or working-men should think of to represent them in Parliament. They have an interest in keeping things as they are; high rents and huge royalties are exactly what they wish to preserve in order that they and their children—from generation to generation--- may live in idleness and luxury. They are-- The drones of the community; they feed On the mechanic's labour; the starved hind For them compels the stubborn glebe to yield Its unshared harvests, and yon squalid form, Leaner than fleshless misery, that wastes A sunless life in the unwholesome mine, Drags out in labour a protracted death To glut their grandeur. The world is a very good world as it is to the landed gentry. It is no wonder that they wish to be in the House of Commons—it is the best club they can find; and it enables the few to keep the whip hand of the many. The wonder is that a section of the many should be such fools as to play into the hands of those who would take everything and give nothing in return. Let the electors

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: of the Newton Division ask themselves what they are likely to get if Mr. LEGH should be sent to Parliament and have his way. Let them look at his Address; it is pretty long, it is true, but it is a mere array lof "words, words, words." Mr. LEGH would "give to Ireland similar laws to those extended to England and Scotland;" but what does this amount to? Nothing, when we know that he IS not in favour of allowing the people of Ireland to manage their domestic affairs in a Parliament of their own. He would not 'enture to say that he would refuse anything that was demanded by three-fourths of the representatives of the peopie of England or of Scotland, and yet, under the plea of equality, he would deal thus unequally with Ireland. It is crass ignorance, or gross sub- terfuge to talk of having a law applicable to the whole of the United Kingdom." There are already differences in law as applying to England, Scotland, and Ireland—differences Which rightly harmonise with differences of Peoples, and what is wanted is Home Rule for each of these countries of such a kind as Will be most suitable to the people living in these countries.

Mr. LEGH promises, in vague general terms, to give his "special attention to all questions affecting the mining industry ;" but he is careful not to commit himself to any particu- lar thing, and he hasn't a word to say about that which goes to the root of the mining in- dustry—the question of royalties. Contrast this with the specific reference of Mr. FRENCH, the Liberal candidate. Elf; says : "I think the question of the mining royalties now payable to landowners in many parts of the country should be inquired into and dealt with in those cases where it stops the working of mines and interferes with the em- ployment of the people.' But, as might be expected, it is on the land question that, When weighed in the balance, the Tory can- didate is most found wanting. This feeble little paragraph is all he can bring himself to lay before the electors:—" I deplore," he says, "the present depressed state of trade and agri- culture, and I venture to hope that some course will be found to bring this state of things. into a more satisfactory condition." lie ventures to hope—what a wonderfully bold Venture !—that something—he cannot sug- gest what—will be done to mend matters: and this flimsy allusion is supposed to be sufficient for the electors! It is a little dust Which is being thrown in their eves, but it is So very, very little, even as dust, that it will scarcely interfere with any of them seeing that Mr. T. W. LEGH cannot be counted on to vote for those radical changes in our land System which are so necessary for the pros- Perity of the farming class and the well being of the whole community. We are glad to see that Mr. FRENCH, as a Liberal,, fully re- cognises the problem of the future, and that he is prepared with a solution. He says : The Land Laws in England stand in great need of reform. lam in favour of the abolition of primo- geniture, and the system of entailing land, which creates great estates, and interferes with the acquisition of small holdings by people of moderate M i Means. Any changes should be n the direction of facilitating and cheapening the transfer of land, so that every man may have an opportunity of acquir- ing an interest in the soil in the country in which he lives and labours. The position of English farmers is at present so unsatisfactory, that I thould gladly support any- measure for giving full security for fixity of tenure an I compensation for improvements. In this direction I think relief is to be found in the depressed state of agriculture, and I should strongly oppose any scheme for taxing the food of the people, which would be really in the landowners favour. Mr. FRENCH, as his Address and as his Speeches show, is a sound Liberal who would Move on the broad Liberal lines of "trust in

the. People." Mr. LEGH is a Tory whose lines have fallen in pleasant places and Who is content to say or sing—" As it Was in the beginning is now and ever shall be." It is for the electors to decide on Monday next which of the two shall be their representative in Parliament. Let the Liberals work, and work unitedly, and they Will see the Liberal candidate at the head of

the poll. The battle was lost last month because some of the rank and file—and some leaders too—contented themselves with look- ing on and taking no part in the struggle. Victories are not won in this way; and there is, besides, a change in the circum- stances. With a Tory Government in power, there is every need of sending such a Liberal to the House of Commons to strengthen the hands of those who will have as much as they can do to keep the Tories from Meddling and muddling as they did in Afghanistan, with a loss, without the slight- est thing to show for it, of thousands of lives and over twenty millions of money. There is, too, political immorality in high Places when a mountebank like Lord RAN- 130LpH CHURCHILL is installed as leader of a Party; it is immorality which all true men Should set themselves to resist ; and that resistance can be best offered, so far as New- ton is concerned, by electing Mr. FRENCH on Monday next to represent the Division.

THE fatal • riots at Belfast will supply material for a chapter in Irish history which Will be as deplorable as it is disgraceful. Here are two sections of a people who pro- fess to btlieve in a religion of love and peace, hating each other with a deadly hatred, and maiming and killing each other when they come in contact. It is terrible to think of
_ the way in which both Protestants and Catholics have resorted to firearms, and then
proceeded to shoot each other in the most deliberate fashion. Policemen and soldiers

have been called in to keep these rival sects from slaying each other, and have them- selves been assailed in uch a barbar- ous fashion as to be compelled to fire in self-defence. It is • always expected that the representatives of the law will be slow to anger, but it is not in human nature to stand to be shot at. It is their duty to repress disorder; and the sooner it is done and the better for all parties. It is a case of being "cruel only to be kind." There should be .flo temporising with mob law; riotous Belfast triust be subdued even if it takes an army to bring it into subjection. It is a matter of course, whilst the mischief is being done, that each party should blame the other; but it is not to be lost sight of that Otangemen are in the ascendant in Belfast, and that in every other part of Ireland Where the Catholics are in a majority there is Peace. Nor is it to be forgotten that men like Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL have in- cited the fanatics of the North of Ireland to rebellion. Mr. GLADSTONE took his lordship gravely to task for the extraordinary doctrine he had been preaching. He foresaw that by sowing the wind it was possible to reap such a whirlwind as has now come upon the Orang.emen of the city that ridiculously prides ilself upon its loyalty. The present leader of the Conservative party in the House of Corn- Mons was told, when he made his speech, that he might incite others to fight, but would Drobably take care to be cut of harm's reach When blows were being given and taken.

div.head: aalL
div.p: aalL

And so it has happened; but if justice was done he would be under arrest for inciting to riot. There are many people lying in gaol at Belfast for their misconduct, and it would have a wholesome effect if Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL were amongst them.

• , MR. HENRY MATHEWS, the new Home Secretary, has after all been re-elected with- out having to fight, out and out, for his seat. Mr. Alderman Como was prepared to combat the constituency on behalf of the Liberal party; but only on condition that there was evidence of his being supported by all sec- tions of Liberals. It seemed at first that the 'Liberal Unionists were about to sink their differences on the question of Home Rule; but evil councils prevailed, and Alderman COOK, finding that, instead of getting the support of the Radical Union, he was likely to meet with its opposition, • wisely de- clined, on Wednesday, to allow himself to be nominated. The Home Secretary may there- fore be said to have been returned unop- posed; but the encounter, short though it has been, has brought into prominence the fact that Mr. MATHEWS, unless he has changed his mind, is quite as much a Home Ruler as Alderman Coox, In 1874 he con- tested Dungarvon, and in his formal Address to the electors, he said : The question of Home Rule is one on which your opinions were hardly elicited in 1868. The country has now demanded that an Irish Parliament shall legislate for Ireland under conditions which were laid down at the recent conference in Dublin, and which many leaders of public opinion concurred in adopting. I consider that a demand so made is one which your representative ought to support, and I have become a member of the Home Rule League formed to carry out the views of the con- ference. What the public have a right to know with regard to the Home Secretary is whether he is still disposed to support the demand that "an Irish Parliament shall legislate for Ire- land." If he is still a Home Ruler, the Liberal Unionists of Birmingham have been curiously hoodwinked in giving him their sup- i port ; and the further question arises whether it is honest in him to occupy a place in a ' Ministry which is pledged to oppose Home Rule. If Mr, MATHEWS has become con- verted on this question since he addressed the electors of Dungarvan, it is of importance that he should say how and when he came to the conclusion that he was preaching a dangerous doctrine when he was "a member of the Home Rule League." He cannot let the matter rest where it is, if he has a reputa- tion which is worth preserving.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

it is announced that Mr.. Bourke, M.P., has accepted the office of Governor of the Presi- dency of Madras, which will be vacated by Sir M. E. Grant Duff in the ensuing autumn. As Mr. Bourke is the brother of Lord Mayo, who did so much for India, he will be wel- compd to India for his name's sake.

It seems that the Chairman of the Runcorn Burial Board has been complained to—and no wonder—about fowls being allowed in the Cemetery. There is a placeffor everything, but the place for the scratching hen is not on the grave which loving hands have adorned with flowers. Apart from the damage fowls do, their very appearance in a cemetery is an impertinence.

Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P., has suggested that the Conservatives should nominate Mr. Goschen for the vacancy at King's Lynn, caused by the appoinment of Mr. Bourke as Governor of Madras. But it won't do • a telegram received last night states that A. W. Jarvis has been adopted as the Tory candidate. The Tories like Mr. Goschen—at a distance; it "lends enchantment to the view."

The question—" What is whitebait ? " has never been satisfactorily settled. Two of the inspectors of the Scotch Fishery Board say it "consists entirely and at all seasons of young sprats and herrings, which vary in size and in the relative proportions according to the season of the year and the place of cap- ture." This will be a sort of "come down" tp the epicures ; but at the same time it sug. gests that people other than Her Majesty's Ministers will have easy access to whitebait.

The Fishery Board, in their annual report, say Turning from the food of fishes to the consideration of fishes as food, the Board regret having to confirm the belief that fish are not appreciated amongst the working classes as much as they ought to be." There- is a good reason, however, for the working- man not taking to fish as a general article of diet; he cannot afford to have a dinner of several courses, and he knows from experi- ence of an aching void that a dinner chiefly ,of fish is a hollow mockery. --- Sir Richard Cross says the country "had eleced a Parliament distinctly for the pur- pose of putting a Government into office in order to defeat the bills of Mr. Gladstone and to have a policy of their own." Just so, but what is that "policy of their own ?" It is a pity Sir Richard, who always professes to be "in the swim," doesn't reveal the nature of the policy. Can it be that the Government regard it as so entirely smething of "their own" that they mean to keep it entirely to themselves?

Mr. Chaplin, in the course of a speech at Sle tford, on Monday evening, said "he thought Lord John Manners had told him that he had been in Parliament longer even than Mr. Gladstone." Tory orators have a way of letting fancy take the place of fact. Lord John was born in 1818, and was four- teen years of age only when &Ir. Gladstone was fist returned to Parliament in 1832. It may be granted, as Mr. Chaplin puts it, that his lordship is hardly fit for "the labouring oar," but it does not therefore follow that he has worked either as hard or as long as Mr. Glad- stone.

-- Mr. Chaplin has been " sold" once by his party through not having a seat in the Cabinet, and he makes it pretty clear that he will not be fooled again. He was put up to speak on behalf of the Tory Government, when the famous allotments motion of Mr. Jesse Collings was under discussion. His cue was to talk about glebe lands, but Mr. Balfour, who spoke later on, let it out that the Cabinet had had the question of allot- ments under consideration. As Mr. Chaplin pathetically observes :—" The discrepancy in their speeches was the subject, of course, of general remark."

At Carnarvon, on Thursday, Griffith Lewis, late secretary of the Nantlle Vale Building Society, was committed for trial on several charges II f embezzlement and theft. His de- falcations amounted to over £1,500. Damage to the amount of £2,000 was caused on Thursday by fire breaking out in the mizin.-roorn of Messrs. Barnes's cotton mill at Farnworth. On Thursday also a chemical works at Crieff was almost destroyed by are. The 1039 is estimated at £B,OOO.

LOCAL NEWS.

Sm. R. A. CROSS'S PEERAGE.—It is stated that Sir Richard Cross has signified his intention of sitting in the House of Lords by the style and title of Vis- count Warrington. There was a former bearer of

RUNCORN SALTATION ARMY.—Captain Moor has been re- moved to Wallsend-on-Tyne. OPEN AIR CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—The Mill Brow Brass Band on Wednesday evening performed a capital programme of music in the Market-place, Runcorn. FIRE AT HALE BANK —A haystack belonging to Mr. Richard Sutton, farmer, Halebank, was totally consumed by fire on Tuesday afternoon. The damage is estimated at £lOO. The hay was accidently set on tire by a young son of Mr. Sutton's. RUNCORN FOOTBALL Cum—This club has arranged a splendid list of fixtures for the approaching season. Amongst other noted clubs who will visit Runcorn is that hailing from the Welsh town of Cardiff. Th,e data of the fixture is November 3rd. TRIPLE BIRTH AT WtDNES —The wife of Mr. John Woodward, of Eleanor-street, Widnes, a workman at the Widnes Alkali Works, was on Wednesday morning de- ltvered of three children, one of whom has since died. Dr. O'Neil attended the mother. _ _ _

LECTURE AT WIDNES.—The Rev. L. P. Jones, on Tues- day eyenink, delivered a lecture in the Welsh Wesleyan Chapel, Cromwell-street, the subject being " Celestial ar- chipelagoes and continents.'' The lecture was a description of stars and planets, and the audience was much interested. Mr. Thos. Hughes, of Fern Lea, Sankey, presided. TELE ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—The conveyances of Mr. Smith, of the Griffin Inn, Fern worth, arid Mr. Parkes, Cen- tral Hotel, Widnes, came into collision at Sirum's Cross on Tuesday, and the occupants were thrown into the road. Fortunately they all escaped unhurt, but the vehicles were considerably damaged. RuNCORN BONE WORKS COMPANY —Tee annual treat to the employees of the Runcorn Bone Works, Sutton, was given by Mr. Owen Reilly, the proprietor, on Saturday, when upwards of 20 men and boys, accempanied by their friends, visited the Liverpool International Exhibition. The Great Eastern and Mersey Tunnel were also inspected. A pleasant day was spent. THE SHOCKING SUICIDE AT CRONTON.—Mr. W. T. Hus- band, on Saturday, held an inquest at the 'Unicorn Inn, Cronton, on the body of Robert Ellaby, 66 year of age, a toolmaker, who resided in Chapel-lane, and who committed suicide on Thursday, under circumstances previously repor- ted A verdict that the deceased committed the act whilst temporarily insane was come to. SCHOOL TREATS AT WIDNES —The children attending the Welsh Wesleyan Chapel, Cromwell-street, had their annual treat on Saturday. when they spent a pleasant after- noon is a field at Halewood. The scholars of the Anne- street and Hutchinson-street Catholic Schools, to the num- ber of 1,500, went in processional order to a field kinely placed at their disposal by Mrs. Deacon. They were beaded by the Young Men's brass band. BLUE RIBBON GOSPEL ARMY, RUNCORN.—MiSS WOMerS- ley, who has had charge of the Runcorn Branch for some months, has been appointed to the direction of a branch at Boodet Lane, and she took leave of her Runcorn friends on Monday evening. A well-attended tea party and public meeting was held, under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Cooke. Mr Joseph Santley, on behalf of the members, pre- sented Miss Womerslev with a purse of gold. STAR OF WIDNES LODGE, No. 261.—At the weekly Ses- sion of this bAge, held on Wednesday, the following offi- cers were installed for the ensuing quarter :—W.C.T. Bro. G. Turton, W.V.T. Sister H. M. SLeadMan. W.Sec. Brother E. Andrews, W.F.S. Brother E. Evans, W•Treas. Sister S. E. Pearson, W.C. Sister S. J. Davis, W.M. Brother, A. Greig, W.T.G. Sister S. E. Smith, !W.Sen. Brother J. Davis, W.D.M. Sister H. Greig, r.w.c.T. Brother H. Smith, W.A.S. Bro. W. Routledge. There were two candidates prepared for initiation, and two initiated. FARNWORTH FACTORY.—The old factory at Farnworth, which has been unoccupied for many years, is now being re- paired and altered, preparatory to being opened by Mr. Wm. Milne, of Bowdon and Manchester, and Mr. John Wright, of Frodshatn, under the title of the Fernworth Pith Company, for the manufacture of that article. Owing to the extent of the alterati, ns, and the putting down of new machinery, it will be some weeks before the work of manufacture be- gins, bat when the works are on full swing they are ex- pected to find employment for a large number of hands. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. H. S. Halt and Mr. H. Gasket', jun., at Widnes, on Thursday, Francis Gaynor, a young man, was charged with being drunk and disorderly and with assaulting P.C. Lowther Thompson. On Monday night the prisoner was drunk and disorderly in Ann-street West, and he was apprehended. On the way to the police station he was very violent. He struck the officer on the mouth with his fist and then threw himself on the ground and kicked the officer several times on the legs. The prisoner was ordered to pay 25t 6d or go to gaol for 17 days.

NILSON-ST.I/En SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. The annual sermons in aid of this school were delivered on Sunday morning and evening in the Camden Chapel. The Rey. Sydney Mees, formerly of Runcorn, preached on both occasions to good congregations. In the afternoon Mr. George Hazlehurst, of Rhyl, gave an address to the teachers and scholars and friends. The choir, under the conductorship of Messrs. S. Bazley and W. Tickle. ren- dered specially selected music in a manner which called forth many ealogiums. The collections and donations amounted to is) 10s, and the committee return thanks to the numerous generous subscribers. DEATH OF A WIDNHS SCHOOLMASTIIR—Mr. Davil W. Hunter, head master of the Warrington-road Beard Schools, Widnes, died at his residence, Saxon-terrace, on Thursday morning after a brief illness. During a visit to France and Germany, during the summer holidays, Mr. Hunter slept in a damp bed and caught a severe cold, which ultimately de- veloped into pleurisy and congestion of the lungs. The deceased, who WAS in his 29th year, was a native of London, and had occupied his position as head master of Warring- ton-road Schools since 1879. He possessed the confidence of the School Board, the love of his pupils, and the e•teem and regret of a large circle of friends, and his early demise is the cause of deep regret._

THE EARL OF bHE9TER'S RIFLES AT RHYL.—The vol- unteers of the 2nd C.R.V., which include the Runcorn com- panies, concluded their week in camp on Saturday. On Friday the annual inspection was held by Colonel Patton, of the 22nd Regimental District, who, in addressing Colonel Ashton, officers, non-commissioned cancers, and men, said he could not conclude without expressing his extreme satisfaction at the way in which they had acted that day. They had been very steady, and their drilling was very creditable. Their march past was good, and they handled their rifles in perfect style. He was particularly pleased with the silence observed in the ranks. He congratulated Colonel Ashton upon having so fine a battalion. THEFT .FROM THE RUNCORN RAILWAY STATION.—At R.ncorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Patrick Lavelle, an Irishman, was charged with stealing a parcel addressed Unsworth Brothers, containing a coat and vest and two pairs of trousers, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Co. The parcel was put off the half-past ten train from Liverpool on Saturday, and was shortly after- wards missed from the platform. Philip Turner, a porter, saw the prisoner take the parcel off the platform and place it under his arm.—Tne prisoner stated he had been over- carried from Speke.—Evidence was given by Philip Turner, porter, Thomas Park, the booking clerk, Wrn. Nit "cutter out" to Mr. Unsworth, and P.C. Riddlesworth. The prisoner, when charged, said the parcel wet "kicking about the platform" for about a quarter of an hour and he picked it up as he did not know who it belonged to. The prisoner was committed to the quarter sessions. Assatrurmei THE POL/CE AT WITYNES.—At Widnes Police Court on Monday, James Fleming, Bedford-street, and Lawrence Keating, Bern-street, labourers, were charged with having on Saturday night assaulted and resisted P.C.'s Laing and Dean,whilst apprehending a prisoner for drunken- ness in Water-street. James McCormick was charged with obstructing S .rgeant Robinson whilst in the execution of his duty at the same time and place. About eleven o'clock on Saturd ty night Laing and Dean were taking a man into custody for drunken and disorderly conduct, when Fleming came up and struck Lung a savage blow on the mouth, and knocked his helmet off. Keating then rushed at Dean, and struck and kicked him, and during the struggle the man escaped. Prisoner McCormick next interfered, seized hold of Keatina, and tried to rescue him from the custody of Sergeant Robinson, who came to the first-named officers' assistance. All the prisaners, however, were eventually aecured.--Keating and Fleming were committed to gaol for 14 days each, and McCormick was fined 2s. 6d. and ,elqtA.

RUNCORN BuntAit. Boum. The monthly meeting of this Board was 11-1 d at the Cemetery office, on Wednesday. Mr. W. Mellor presided, and there were present—Meesre. Coleburn, Imison, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary.)—The Chairman reported that during the four months ending July 25th. there were 89 interments ; corresponding period last year 127, decrease 38. The fees received during the same period amounted to £95 193 61; last year £l3l se, decrease £35 51 6d.—Mr. Imison read and moved the a,lop. tinn of the Finance Committee. The month's cash account showed total receipts £26 2s 10d, paid away £l2 33 21, leaving a balance of £l3 193 8d to be paid into hank. Ac- counts amounting to £3 14s 3d were recommended for pay- men,..—The Chairman said that several complaints had been made to him about fowls being kept in the cemetery. He did not see that there was any particular harm in keeping there within bounds, hut he thought it was contrary to the ordinary rulrs of any cemetery or burial ground that fowls should be in the place. Several people had complained that their graves had been damaged by the fowls, and he thought it would be as well that Mr. Salkeld should see Ford and ask him to discontinue the practice.—Mr. Cole- burn said Ward had frequently f ,wls in the yard of Oie parish church, and he remembered that 30 or 40 years ago sheep were regularly, in the churchyard. He had heard of damage done to a certain grave in the cemetery by t',.#3 fowls.—Tbe Secretary said he would see Ford about the matter.

THE EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY ACT.—At the St. Helens County Court, before Mr. Registrar Tyrer, on Wednesday, a case under the Employers' Lia- bility Act, in which Patrick Lawlor, a labourer, sought to recover compensation from Messrs. A. a Kurtz and Co., chemical manufacturers, was heard. Mr. 11. L. Riley appeared for the plaintiff; and Messrs. Cooper and Sons, of Manchester, for the de- fendants. On February 3 last the plaintiff was en- gaged tarring the roof of a building at the works, when one of the rungs of the ladder upon Which he was standing broke, and he was thrown vio- lently to the ground. He was incapacitated from fol- lowing his employment for some weeks. Judgment was taken by consent for £2l.

Jogeph Connolly said he had worked kr Mr. Mellon close on 12 months. On Monday night seven weeks ago he was in Mrs. Mellon's house, helping her to pack up some furniture and other goods. Mr. Mellon came home for his tea, hut there WAS nothing for him, and there was nothing for him to sit down upon. He went out and came in about half-oast ten, when everything was packed up. Witness did not hear Mrs. Mellon put him out. Mrs. Mellon was drunk only a few weeks ago. He had heard her sing at Runcorc—By Mr. Knowles: Mr. Mellon did not break in the door. The Bench' retired to consider their decision, and upon returning into court after a brief absence Mr. Hall said the magistrates ordered the defendant to pay 105 per week to- wards his wife's support, and also to pay costs, which included lOs 6d, the advocate's fee.

WATER POLLTJTION AT NEMERLEY.

The Chairman, speaking with reference to the polluted ditch at Netheriey, said he had visited the Huyton and Roby sewage farm. The thole affair was only 20 acree. and to call that a farm aiteared to him a misnomer. He went with Mr. Jump along the ditch and round the farm, and the whole thing, to him, was most unsatisfactory. Mr. Jump stated that the Board had improved his land by pumping water at Netherley. If they did not take steps to prevent the pollution of the larooks then there was no doubt that the water supply woeld be polluted. It behoved the Board to adopt most strenuous means with this end. The Clerk (Mr. Allen) had communicated with the Author- ities, and he (Mr. Gossage) had had a conversation with a friend of his from Roby, who was an indluential man, and he had premised to take the matter up. There was no de- sire, he said, that anything wrong should be done. He had also heard that a deputation of the Huyton and Roby Local Board had visited Mr. Jump, and everything had been done to cill the attention of that authority to the matter. It rested with the Huyton and Roby Loma Board to suppress the nuisance. and it was for the Widnes Local Board to see that they did it.—The minutes were passed.

- The minutes of the Finance Committee contained the fallowing:—" Main Sewer Loan—Letter, 2nd July. kern Public Works Loan Commissioners, agreeing to a futther advance of £1:750 at 31 per cent, repayable half-yearly by way of annuity; and letter, 30'h July, consenting to con- solidate existing bane, and to accept repaym.nt by h& yearly instalments of £552 10s by way of annuity, the last payment to be madeen the 11th April. 1912."—Mr. Rrndiev moved the adoption of the minutes and said this system of repayment would kiff-ct a saving during the next twelve months of £245.
