At Shoebtirvness, on Th,arsdav, the Canadians beat th, let Cheshire (representing British artillery) in a 64-pounder s,wll contest, and also won the special repository prize as against England. "SOME HINTS ON CONJURING APPARATEN."---Thift is the title of a series of articles now appea,log in "A mate Work," the author being Mr. D. B. Adamson, of the well-known firm of Urquhart and Adamson, cabinet makers, B di-street, Liver- pool. The number for July contains a very clever article on the construction and manufacture of " the marvell.ms birdcage." It is easy to see that Mr. Adallson has made a study of the subject of conjuring and conjuring apparatus. and the plain and practical manner in which his ,xptana- lions and " hints " are given will leave no excuse for failure on the part of the merest tyro who desires to pr4fit by the instructions. The details of the construction of the bird- cage illusion are lucidly given, and the article is elaborated with working drawings of the essential parts. The articles are made all the more readable by the modicum of conjurors "patter," which is woven in with the more solid t.-xt. They nrornise to form a valuable contribution to " Amatnar Work" of the recreative sort.'

div.head: BIRTHS AND DEATHS IN RUNCORN AND DISTRICT.
div.p: BIRTHS AND DEATHS IN RUNCORN AND DISTRICT.

It appears from the Quarterly Return of the Registrar. General that there was a decrease in the mortality of the town and sub-district of Runcorn in the last quarter, for the deaths were only 90, against 108 in the first three months of this year. These 90 deaths corresponded to an annual rate of 17 2 per 1,000 of the population, estimated to be in tie middle of this year 20.648, showing a growth of 1,445 on the total of the last census. Ihe rate was again a low one, for it was 11 below that of the 50 great towns in England and Waes. There is almost always a close competition be- twek it and Widues. The latter is assumed to have this year 33,115, being an increase of 5,420 since 1881. and as the dea,hs in it were 147 they yielded a rate of 179, which in this instil-lee was 0-7 more than that of Runcorn. Again. it is seen that Chester. with a population of 49 820. had 230 thaths and a rate of 185, and Warrington, with 48,319, had 209 and 171 respectively, so that the rate of 172 in Run- corn was less than either of those.

The births in Runcorn were 200 in the quarter which has just ended, and they comprised 97 boys and 103 girls. This is not so large a total as the 214 in last March, but again in Dec. it was only 177. The average of the first period of 1893- 4-5 led us to expect in that of this year 108 deaths, and as the actual number was 94, they were 13 less. In June of last year the total wag 119, but in that of March, 1885, it was as much as 151. This was an exceptionally heavy mortality, and wits the greatest in the last two years. Run- corn has lately suffeied a great deal from scarlet fever. In last Decembq it was fatal in 22 cases; in 7 in March, but this report has not any. Whooping cough was credited with 11, and diar, hese with 2. The 90 deaths in the latter in- cluded 47 males and 43 females; and of the total 29 of them were those of infants under one year, and 11 referred to adults who had attained 60 years and upwards. There were 2 deaths from violence, inquests were held on 2 bodies, mad 8 persons died in the workhouse. The births in Frod- shaM and Kingsley in the last qaarter were 70, and as the deaths were 32, the total was 3 less than what was antici- pated. It is a much better report than that for last March, when there were 53 deeths. Budworth had 25 births and 14 deaths, Daresbury 26 and 14, Widnes 320 and .147, and Warrington 432 and 217 respectively. With the exception of Widnes, the mortal;ty in each of them was low. The principal zymotics were not iepreeented by one in Budworth and Daresbury, and there wes only one of diarrhoia in Fred. sham.

div.head: TILE WIDNES THEATRE PROPRIETOR AND HIS
div.p: TILE WIDNES THEATRE PROPRIETOR AND HIS
WIFE_

Before Messrs. H. S. Hall and Mr. H. Gaskell, jrinr., at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, Mr. George Mellon, proprietor of the Vislidnes Theatre Royal, was summoned by his wife, who was smartly dressed, for having deserted her and refused to maintain her. Mr. Knowles said the defen- dant was summoned under an Act of Parliament, dated the 25th :Tune, which gave the Bench power to make an order for maintenance upon a husband who deserted his wife, to an amnunt not exceeding £2 per week, and it might be en- forced in the same manner as an 4ttiiiatinn order. Some seven weeks ago last Monday defendant left his wife and Went to live at the Mersey Hotel. He gave her no money, and. she hal to pawn her jewellery and wearing appatel. In years gone by she had been in affluent circumstances, and had earned as much as .129 a night as a singer. Some twelve months ago she caught a bad cold, and as she had boat her voice she bad been unable-to earn any mouey. She and her sister and her niece had kept defendant for years, he only having got up the programmes. Defendant had been making £3OO a year. All complainant asked for was 20s per wee,;.—Complainant was called to corroborate this 'statement. She stated that she had earned as much as £2O ' a week. Her husband had been looked up for assaulting her at Glasgow. Her voice was originally injured by defendant holding her over the bar of a public-house and almost choking her. In crose-examinatian, witn?ss said she had been married six years in September. He bought the theatre lie at present owned with money she had saved. She did slot lock him out the other night or refuse to let him in. it was not true that she backed him out of the house. She went-to him for some money, and he gave her the magnifi- cent sum of sixpence. She bad pawned her wedding ring for Ss, and she was sober when she did so.—Mr. Husband : I believe there is no doubt that you occasionally glt over the line? Yes, the same as my husbred.—Witness went on to say that she had also pawned her two dress rings and a satiii dress. It was not true that her voice bad been spoiled t.y taking drink.—Mr. Husband, for the defence, said it was positively true that his client had been locked out of the house. Complainant p Acked all the furniture and said she would go away. Unfortun itely, he was obliged to tell their worships that Mrs. Mellon could not keep sober. It was quite ant-rue that there had been any desertion, and Mrs. Mellon was quite capable of keeping herself if she would only not take drink. Defendant was called, and maintained that his wife was in the habit of getting drunk. She had told him that he could go away if he would only leave her in peace. At Whitsuntide she had £6a week at the Hay- market Theatre, Liverpool. At Warrington they had to drop the curtain becanee she was not saber, and at Wigan they could not get her out of the dressing room. Cross-examined by Mr. Knowles : He was not drunk last Tuesday evening. He was a little bit inebriated. He never kicked her. He did not on one occasion send a fork through her chin. He had not been drunk during the past seven weeks. [ls drove over to Prescot, hut it was in a convey- ance which had been lent to him. A gentleman from Liver- pool now managed the theatre for him. He was engaged by him, and paid on commission. He paid income tax last year on £l5O, but he was going to appall against paying it again, did net sing himself. He got up the pro- grammes, and his wife and his Wife's sieter had sang for him, but not above two or three times. He had never re- ceived anything from them since he had been in Widnes. He did not give his wife 6d, as she bad stated. Ho had struck her when there had been cause for it. It was not true that he had offered a man named Kelly a situation of £1 a week if he would swear that ha had committed adul- tery with Mrs; Mellon.

div.head: OUR 'I )ON LETTER.
div.p: OUR 'I )ON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

The scene at the Mansion House last night, when the Lord Mayor entertained Her Majesty's Minis- ters, was very striking. All the Ministers were in full dress, some of them assuming it for the first time. Beyond this there was a considerable sprink- ling of civic fuli,-dress, military and naval uniform, whilst the presence of ladies added grace to the scene. With the exception of Lord Salisbury's speech, the dresses and the dinner were decidedly the best part of the entertainment. The Lord Mayor is not endowed with oratorical gifts, and he made one fatal mistake that would perhaps have been openly resented but for the sacredness of his character as host. Though, of course, Conservatives preponderated, there was a leavening of Liberals, and it was a departure from the high courtesy usually preserved on such occasions for the Lord Mayor to run out of his way to state that in view of the political leanings of the lifinistry he had pecu- liar pleasure in welcoming them to the Mansion House. An unfortunate arrangement was that which left the reply to the toast of the House of Commons in the hands of Mr. Stanhope. The Man- sion House is a very had place to speak in, and Mr. 'Stanhope is even in the House of Commons, physic- ally, a poor speaker. He has in the most favour- able circumstances a habit of rising to a squawl. Last night, battering against the acoustical de- ficiencies of the Mansion House, Mr. Stanhope went off in a series of squawls that were positively distressing. As for Lord Salisbury's speech it was in many respects admirable. Listening to him and noting his manner, it was impossible to resist comparison with what Lord Randolph would have said and done in similar circumstances. Grave in manner, moderate in tone, and courteous towards the adver- sary, Lord Salisbury fulfilled all the expectations of a great statesman speaking at a critical epoch. It is a pity Lord Randolph was not there to profit by the example. But, probably to the relief of his colleagues, the Chancellor of the Exchequer had petulantly declined the invitation, some said be- cause he objected to appear in circumstances where he must have played a subordinate part to Lord Salisbury. However it be, his chair was empty, and Sir R. Cross, Mr. W. 11. Smith, and Lord Iddes- leigh ate their dinners in peace. Wkilst a great deal may be said for Lord .Salisbury's speech, it was marked by one characteristic which is likely to have important effects upon the situation. It seemed for some time that he was going to avoid altogether the question of Ireland. But after dis- posing of other topics he was bound to admit the existence of the skeleton in the cupboard, and took it out for a few moments' contemplation. But all Lord Salisbury had to say on the subject was limited to one aspect. It was all coercion ; not a word of conciliation. It would have been so easy on this festive occasion to drop in a' reference, howsoever common-place, to the desirability of meeting, or even considering, the national demand. That Lord Salisbury should have avoided doing so indicates a deliberate resolution which portends much. The House of Commons stands adjourned till next Thursday. To-morrow there is to be a Cabinet Council, at which decision will be arrived at with respect to the course ot the session and the scope of the Queen's Speech. If next Thursday Ministers!, are not able to say more than Lord Salisbury uttered last night, we may look forward to a pro- longed sitting. There is no disposition in any part of the House, not excepting the Irish camp, to enter upon obstructive policy. Mr. Gladstone personally deprecates such a course, and Mr. Parnell is not dis- posed to assume it. But if the Government have to offer the eighty-six representatives of Ireland no- thing but this dry crust of coercion, it is pretty t er- tain that the struggle for the estimates will be ; prolonged and angry. The assumption of such an I attitude would be incredible but for the evil augury ; of Lord Salisbury's speech last night. Still there is hope. The Conservative Government are bound to deal with the question of Home Rule, and will scarcely go out of their way to increase the diffi- culty by attempting to ignore the question at the outset. Sir Charles Forster made a pathetic figure as lie 1 hobbled across the lobby on Monday just in time to be sworn in. He is better than he was at the end of last session, for now he gets along without the aid of a stick. But he is woefully broken down, ! and the great green shade he wears over his eyes ; adds a new oddity to an appearance always strik- ing. How different from his former self the hon.. baronet is was indicated in the fact that as he crossed the lobby his hat was on his head. For 34 years Sir Charles has represented Walsall in the House of Commons, and for at least 20 years he has been looking for his hat. Two generations of legis- lators have known this familiar hatless figure, I roaming about the corridors, or pacing up the floor ! and gangways of the House of Commons, looking ! for his hat. On Monday he had found it, and it ! seemed to add a touch of increased depression to ' • his general appearance. Sir Charles is one of Mr. ! Gladstone's baronets. He raised him to that dignity ! in 1874, presumably in !To:ignition of his ser- vices as Chairman of the Committee dealing with ; private bills. Sir pharles's gratitude has since been shown in a somewhat embarrassing manner. In his ceaseless round of search he has frequently ; found Mr. Gladstone snatching a few moments t repose on the Treasury Bench, or writing his letter to the Queen. Overflowing with kindly feeling to- ' wards his patron, it has been Sir Charles' custom to seat himself beside Mr. Gladstone if there were room on the Treasury Bench, if not to gain his own seat immediately behind, and therefrom intrude upon the great man's privacy with inopportune remarks. Mr. Gladstone, who like everyone else has a sincere regard for the grotesque little man, was accustomed to bear these intrusions with marvellous patience. But sometimes he turned and snapped, after • which Sir Charles, with opened Vliouth and widened eyes, sat staring into his face; .for a moment or two till he had mastered the situa- tion, when he fared forth once more in search of his; hat, lie is in his seventieth year now, and is getting I a little feeble. But he has a strong 'conviction that ! the private business of the House of Commons could ! not get on without him, and he means to stick I to it. - I

Our Colonial guests are really beginning to clear out now, many of arm having already turned their faces homeward. This is a most desirable consum- mation even in their own interests. They are for the most part stoat well-made men of powerful ! constitutions. But even an iron physique could not stand for more than four months the incessant and invariable succession of daily guzzling to which , they have been subjected. Early in the season, and in spite of political disturbances, it became the fashion to fete the colonials. They were made the 1 occasion and the excuse for all kinds of gatherings which included an enormous dinner or, still worse, a fearful midday feed. The orgie was well conceived, and has been handsomely carried out. I dare say it will do good as drawing closer the colonies to the ! mother country—that is if no fatal consequences follow and our guests get safely home with consti- tutions not undermined. Still there is, I think, a I general feeling of satisfaction that it is at last ' over. Sir Thomas Brassey must, by this time have deeply repented the temporary weakness that made possible the appearance ;upon the scene of his ancestor, Le Sire John de Bressey, of the family of Bressey, in Lorraine, who came over with the Conqueror. It has been received with a burst of laughter that threatens to he inextinguishable. London society and the commercial world never before heard of be Sire John de Bressey, whilst it has the keenest re- collection of Sir John Brassey's father, the burly, honest, hard-working old man, who, beginning life with a pickaxe and shovel, dug and cleared his way to the position of a millionaire. It would be in- teresting to hear "old Mr. Brassey's" views on his ancestor, who came over with the Conqueror. Sir Thomas Brassey, in addition to his father's wealth, inherits much of his common sense, and there is a general disposition among those who know him best to acquit. him of active agency in the creation of this romance. Lady Brassey is an energetic, ambitious lady of a literary turn. Rightly or wrongly it is the author of "A Voyage in the Sun- beam" who is credited with the creation of be Sire John de Bressey. It is pleasant in contemplating our old nobility to turn aside from such as Earl Lensdale, and dwell upon the personality of Lord Crewe. The name , will not be familiar to the general reader; for Lord Crewe, though he votes straight, is not known in politics or in public life. But he is very well known in London society, which he much frequents, and where he holds a unique position. His titie is one curiously Thackerayan in its sound, and its present wearer is just the man Thackeray would have de- lighted to sketch. Though past three score years and ten in age, his lordship is still a handsome, dis- tinguished looking man, and if he would not persist in takimg his hat into the reception room, would he an addition to its ornaments. But wherever Lord Crewe is, there is his hat also, and in the crush of tthe London season a hat held in repose somewhere

iin the neighbourhood of the spine necessarily comes to grief. When Lord Crewe is not standing in the I middle of the room with his hat behind him talking to himself, he is sitting on a couch or sofa fast asleep. He never talks to anyone but Lord Crewe, and as far as I have observed no one attempts to break in upon the conversation. But-his lordship seems to enjoy himself, and that I suppose is the object of his being invited.

div.head: ALLEGED LAND GRABBING BY A WIDNES IRISHMAN.
div.p: ALLEGED LAND GRABBING BY A WIDNES IRISHMAN.

The following is an. extract from the "Dublin Weekly News" of last Saturday : Boyle Organising Committee—Meeting on Saturday last —Mr. Patrick Shaikey, P.L.G., Presiding. Delegates at- tending from the following branches :—Bailinarneen, Bree- dogue, Boyle, Crogban, and Killaraght. Ms. Mary Dockery, of Ballinameen, brought forward a charge of land-grabbing against Mr. Thomas Drury, t•eaeurer ot Widnee branch, Lancashire, Eng!and, which was before the committee at the last three meitings. A vote of censure was passed on Thomas Drury for the unfounded statements made use of in his last letter against Mr. Jern,s Connor, boo. sec., Bal- linarneen branch, and for showing a had example to the country by paying a heavy fine for land for the purpose of having a grass farm, which was tbe cause of evicting four honest-, industrious tenants, including Mrs. Dockery. Re- solved:—" '1 bat we record a vote of thanks to Mr. James Connor, hon. sec., Balinaineen branch, for his noble exer- tions in bringing this case before the committee, and that a copy of these resolutions be sent to Dr. O'Keeffe, president, Widnes branch, Lancashire.—John Higgins, hon.sec. The statement made above has caused a great sensation amongst the Irish population of Widnes, amongst whom Mr. Drury, who is a foreman in the employ of Messrs. Muspratt and Sons, is well known. Strong doubts are entertained as to the justice of the accusation, and a strict investigation into the matter is being made by the officers of the local branch of the league.

div.head: DROWNIM FATALITY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: DROWNIM FATALITY AT WARRINGTON.

On Sunday afternoon a boy named John Picton, 11 years of age, whose parents reside in Hamilton- street, was drowned in the river Mersey opposite Latchford lock. Deceased, in company with another boy named Joseph Percival Whittaker, 10 years of age, also of Hamilton-street, went to bathe, and de- ceased got out of his depth. He was drowning when William Massey, aged 14, son of John Massey, of 25, Birchall-street, attempted to rescue him. Massey pulled off his coat, trousers, and shoes, and jumped in the river. He got hold of the drowning boy, but was compelled to let go his hold to save himself. The river was afterwards dragged, and the body of the deceased was recovered and taken to his home.

Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an in- quest into the circumstances of the death, on Wed- nesday afternoon, at the Old Crow Inn, Fennell-st. Evidence to the following effect was taken :—Sarah Fairbrother, mother of the deceased, said that the body seen by the jury was that of her son, John Pic- ton. Witness had been twice married. Deceased went to Sunday School on the afternoon of Sunday. His body was brought home at about 8-30 in the even- ing.—William Alassey, Birch all-street, off Batters- by-lane, a boy, said that he was on the river side at about 6-30 on Sunday evening. He saw some boys bathing in the river. A boy told witness that de- ceased was drowning and he pulled off his clothes and jumped in. Deceased was struggling in the *ater, and witness was compelled to leave go of him. Witness could swim, but was not strong enough to get deceased, who pulled him towards the bottom of the water. William Bancroft, Dye Houses, llowl4y, deposed that on Sunday evening he was on the river in a boat Find heard that a boy was drowned. Witness grappled, with the aid of two young men, and recovered the body of the de- ' ceased from the river.-The Jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased was accidentally drowned and expressed the opinion that the witness Massey had acted in a very plucky manner.—A collection: was then taken upon the lad's behalf.--The Coroner- remarked that perhaps the police would call the at- tention of the Humane Society to the case, as it , deserved recognition.

div.head: LOCAL BOWLING.
div.p: LOCAL BOWLING.

MATCH AT PADGATE.—On Monday afternoon, on the bowling green at the King and Queen Inn, Pad- gate, an off-hand match was played between Mr. William Bolton, of Warrington, and Mr. L. G. Royle. of Manchester, for .E 5 aside, 21 up. The green was in good order, the weather was fine, and there was a good attendance of spectators. • The game resulted in a victory for the local bowler by 17 points. MAIN OF BOWLS.—On Saturday a main of bowls. was held on the green of the Warrington Cricket and Bowling Club, a number of prizes being com- peted for. The following gentlemen carried off the .prizes:-1, Mr. S. Kenyon; 2, Mr. W. Jones; 3, Mr. G. Pilling ; 4. Mr. Henshall ; 5, Mr. F. Howard; 6, Mr. J. Chidlaw. The game was a very sue-ossful one, and was witnessed by a large number of spec- tators. MAIN AT THE BULL'S HEAD INN.—A handicap main of bowls was played on the bowling green attached to the Bull's Head Inn, Church-street, on Saturday afternoon. Mr. J. Evans, the proprietor, gave a copper kettle. Thirty-five players com- peted, amongst whom were Messrs. James Bridge, G. Ball, J. Holbrook, and several other well-known bowlers. The handicappers, however, were at fault in making the limit two, as there were many players who have had better starts in similar affairs, and been unable to show prominently. Mr. W. Wood, the winner, played with remarkable judgment throughout the contest, and cleverly de- feated Mr. R. Wilcock and Mr. James Bridge in the tllird and fourth rounds. In the final round Mr. Frank Berry was his opponent. BOWLS AT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB.—On Satur- day afternoon a main of bowls, the first for this season, took place on the new green attached to the Conservative Club, Sankey-street. There were 60 competitors, and some good play was witnessed. The ground was in fair condition, and the contest was witnessed by a considerable number of spec- tators. Four-handed games were played, and al- though the match was commenced at two o'clock in the afternoon it was not brought to a conclusion till nearly 8-30 p.m. Some of the games were ex- ceedingly well contested. The prizes were distri- buted to the successful competitors in the first-class billiard room of the Club by Mrs. Reynolds, wife of Captain Reynolds, J.P., Chairman of the Conserva- tive Association. They were awarded as follows Ist, timepiece, T. Ogden; 2nd, timepiece, G. Ogden ; 3rd, bowls and jack (ivory mounted), John Leather- barrow ; 4th. bowls and jack, Henry Hayes; sth, a copper kettle, F7trh, ankpipTe, J. Thornton;uryer;6th,u 8t umbrella, knives lla,ll irviel- lm ia Gleave; and forks. Henry Potter. At the conclusion of the distribution a vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs. Reynolds, on the motion of Mr. John Roberts, seconded by Mr. .1-ason ; and also to Captain Rey,- nolds for his presence, and for providing the Ersr and second prizes, on the motion of Mr. john Dew- burst, seconded by Mr. Watson. A vote of thanks to the Bowling Green Committee brought the pro- ceedings to a close.

The troopship 'Ritual-Iva was in collision on Thursday in Queenstown Harbour with the racing cutter Wraith, which sustaintd some damage. Thera was a gale at the time. • A sal,smap na.meil o.,kes,who was injur•-•d in the Finktry Park collision last FtbruarY, on Thursday recoved £6OO damages from the Great Northern Railway Company.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MoNDAY—Before the Nl:4yor (Alclerman Harrison), and

Aldermen D ivies and Holmes. DRIINUENNESS —William Conroy. le- being drunk and disorderly in the Market-place, on Saturday afternoon, was fined las and coets.—Bridget McDonough, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Palmyra-square, on the pre- vista morning, was fined 2s 61, including costs.—Henry Glover, a stranger, was charg-d with being drunk and dis- orderly in Buttermarket-street, was allowed to go on promis- ing to leave the town —Thomas Taylor, John Lee, and Ralph Taylar were summoned for being drunk and dis- orderly in a yard cff Town's End on the Tuesday previous. They wars each fined 5s arid clsts.—Elizebeth Leyland and Sarah Riley were each fined ss. including cost 9, for the same offence ; and Catherine Mellor was ordered to pay the costs. _ .

CRETELTY.—WiIIivn Bennett was fined 10a and costs for working a horse that was not in a fit condition, and the Mayor complimented P.C. Williams for the manner in which he had detected and taken notice of the offence. THEFT.—Divid Warrener, fo-ge labourer, Stamford-street, was charged with sealing a hen and chicken, value 4, the preperty of Henry Augustus Powell, who keeps the Vulcan Beerhouse, in Dallam-lane. The theft was committed on the 7th. Prisoner was fined 403 and colts, £3 2s in all, to undergo a month's imprisonment in default of payment. LAZY VAGRANTS —James Casey, Richard Williams, Ed- ward Calloway, and Sidney Kershaw were charged with re- fusing to perform their tAsks of work whilst casual inmates of the vagrant ward at the Union Workhouse —Prisoners pleaded inability to perform the tasks, and Casey said that the stones, which were like millstones, should be boiled. They required softening.—The Mayor : Do you think boil- ing would make them softer ?—Casey : Yes.—Chief Con- -stable Hunt: He b as' had a lot of expericnce.—The Bench sent the men to prison for seven days. CHEATING A RAILWAY COMPANY.—John Baguley was charged with riding in a third-class carriage from Wigan to Warrington, on the London and North-Western Railway, without a ticket, on the 7th inst. He was also charged with assaulting Detective Harvey and one of the railway officials. Prisoner arrived by train at Bank Quay about midnight. He had no ticket and said that he had not travelled, but he had been seen to get out of the train. He was taken into custody and then committed the assault. The magistrates sent him to prison for a month with hard labour. A SFArLTING A P ARAISIOUrt.—Henry Wilson, a young man, was charged with assaulting Bridget McDonough, a young woman with whom he had been cohabiting for the past ten weeks. Complainant said prisoner got hold of her by the hair, tore her clothes, and violently kicked her. THREATS. - Patrick McDermott, charged with using threatening language to his wife, was ordered to pay the cost.. _ . .

DETRACTING THE RAILWAY COMPANY.—BeRiIMin Atik- land. f,f Powys-street, was fined lOs and costs for riding on the London and North-Western Railway without hav- ing paid his fare on the 7th inst. 'Detective Harvey proved the case. MAINTENANCE CASES. Samuel Brandwond was sum- moned for not koeping; up payments for the maintenance of his wife, under an order obtained by her against him. The order was reduced from 64 to ss, as defendant pleaded in- ability to pay the first amount. James Ernson was ordered to pay is &1 net week towards the maintenance of his boy on the ship "Clio."
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MOSlM.Y.—Before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. G. L. Davies. DRUNKENNESS.—Ambrose Bate, Margaret Hancock, and Thomas BLakernore were each fined for drunkenness. _ _ _ . .

. - Poo AT LARGE.—William Rudd was charged with having his dog at large in Bridge-street on the 29th July, in contra- vention of the order of the justices.—The case was proved by P.C. Smith and a fine of is and costs 9s 6,1, was im- posed. GAMBLING—Peter Ha:yes, Alfred Cotterill, John Hulse, John Cavanagh, Robert Collins, and Austin Garritty, young men, were charged with playing pitch and toss on Sunday, the 25th July. Cetterill did not appear, Hulse pleaded guilty, and the rest ple4d.d guilty. The case was proved by P.C. Barker and P.O Riddlesworth, and Superintendent Hollingsworth said there had been numerous complaints about tne game being carried on on a Sunday. Hulse, against whom there was a black list, was fined 103 and costs 113 Cu, a warrant was granted for the apprehension of Cot- terill, and the remainder were each fined 5s and costs, 93 6d.

It appeared that on that day-Wat.on was travellincr from Liverpool by the 4-25 train, which is advertised tO stop at Bryn when required. When the train approached the station, deceased was undoer the impression tbat it was not as it got. to the platform he sideways and fell on his head. The railway going to stop, and jumped out officials went to his assi,:tance, and thinking he was not seriously hurt, allowed him‘ to walk home himself, which took him six hours, although the dis,,ance is little more than a mile. THE POLITICAL SITUATION. MINISTERIAL RE-ELECTIONS, &C. The Irish party, it is stated, intend to move an amend- ment on the Address, calling upon the Government to take ateps to secure the revision of rents and the prevention of eviction!. The Press Association says :—We understand that Lord Weymouth will move, and that Mr. Whitmore will second, the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne on the 19th inst. Mr. Chamberlain has, it is reported, declared that he will give no vote which will bring Mr. Gladstone back to power as long as that right hon. gentleman adheres to his present views on the Irish question; and this represents the generat sentiments of the party. The " Daily News" says :—The question of a November session still remains in abeyance. The tendency noted for the project to be dropped gains force. Lord Hartington has declared, with the approval of his friends, that he will assist Lord Salisbury in resisting any attempts to compel him to disclose his ?risk policy till such a time as he may deem it convenient. This places Lord Salisbury in a posi- tion in whick he will be able to disregard the request of the Liberal party for information on this point, and defer the introduction of his measures till February. The National Liberal Federation has issued a circular, signed by Sir James Kitson, Bart, its president; Mr. R. W. Foster, Mr. W. H. Hart. the members of the Emer- gency Committee; Mr. Sehnadhorst. and Mr. R. A. Hod- son, reviewing the results of the general election. It con- cludes as follows :—We venture, therefore, to impress upon Liberal associations the necessity for close attention to the registers, and the extreme importance of extending and perfecting their organisation. The future even of this new Parliament is wholly uncertain, and it behoves us te be prepared for any emergency. The Press Association understands that the Queen's Speech will be remarkable for its brevity. Beyond a refer- ence to our relations with Foreign Powers, there will prob- ably be no subject of importance touched on. The final de- cision with regard to an autumn session will be taken at the Cabinet Council on Friday. It is believed that the arrangement agreed to at the Carlton Club will be altere,4. Sir 'Richard Cross has appointed Mr. Clinton E. Dawkins to be his assistant private secretary ; and Sir John Gorst (Parliamentary Under Secretary of State let India) has appointed Mr. Richmond Ritchie to be his prelate secre- tary.

The nomination for the Burton-on-Trent Division is fixed for Monday, and the polling on the following Friday. Mr. Splnsy Evershed is the Liberal candidate, and he will be opposed by Mr. Gerald Hardy, Conservative. BRIGIITON.—At Brighton, on Wednesday, Mr. Marriott, Q.C., Judge-Advocate General,was proposed by Dr. Tindall Robertson, Mr, .J. W. Howlett, Mr. W. P. Box 411, and five others, seconded by Colonel Yerrall, Alderman Lamb, Mr. Cheesman, and others. There being no other candidate, Mr. Marriott was declared duly elected. SOUTH PADDINGTON.—Lord Randolph Churchill, the sew Chancellor of the xchequer, was on Wednesday nomi- nated for South Paddington. No other candidate was pro- posed.

SHEFFIELD.—Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett was on Wednesday re-elected for the Ecclesall division of Sheffield on his appointment as Civil Lord of the Admiralty. The pro- ceedings were purely formeJ, and Mr. Bartlett did not attend. BRISTOL.—The nomination for Bristol West took place oa Wednesday. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, Conservative, was proposed by Mr. James Inskip, and seconded by Mr. Geo. King Morgan. Ni other candidate was nominated, and Sir Michael was declared duly elected by the High Sheriff. The proceedings were purely formal, it being understood there would be no opposition. HA-3IPSTE.ID.—Mr S G Ratcliffe, returning offieer, on Wednesday attended at Hampstead Vestry Hall to receive nominations. The only candidate was Sir Henry Thurston Holland, Bart., Vice-Preeident of the Committee of Council on Education, who was proposed by Mr Thomas Sinsome Preston, 7econded by Mr John Thomas Taylor, and re-elected without opposition. PLYMOUTH.—Mr Edward Clarke, Q.C., was on Wednesday returned unopposed for Plymouth, on seeking re-election aa Solicitor General. TOWER HAMLETS.—In the St. George's division of the Tower Hamlets, Mr R Eves (Liberal Gladstonian) and Mr C T Ritchie (Cuneervative) were on Wednesday nominated. Both parties are actively engaged in canvassing. LoNnoN.—Mr W H Smith was on Wednesday nominated for the Strand division of London, and in the absence of any other candidate wee declared to be elected. EAST MAJZYLEBOIII3. Lord Coarles Beresford was on Wednesday re-elected without opposition as member for the East Marylebone divisioe of the Metropolis. LEWISHAM—Lord Lewieham was on Wednesday nomin- ated for the Lewisham division of the metropolis, and was returned unopposed. CROYDOS.—The nomination of a candidate for Croydon took place on Wednesday. The Hon. Sidney Herbert was the only gentleman proposed, and be was declared to be elected.

WesT Dower.—Lord Arthur Hill has issued his address to the electors of West Down seeking re-election. Eas-r MaNcHusTEE.—The Mayor of Manchester (Mr. Alderman Goldsohmidt) attended on Wednesday at the Toe n Hall to receive nominations for the seat vacated by the Right Hon. A. J. Balfour on his acceptance of office. "Arthur James Balfour, 4, CAdton-ga, dens. London. S.W., Privy Councillor, and Secretary for Scotland," was nomin- ated by Stephen Cheaters Thompson, Higher Ardwick, seconded by Hugh Kerr, Brunswick-street, Manchester. The nomination of no other person was forthcoming, and at two o'clock the Mayor declared Mr. Balfour duly elected. LIVERPOOL (WALTON DIVISION).—The Right Hon. J G. Gibson, the new Solicitor-G-eneral for Ireland, was on Wednesday re-elected without opposition for the Walton Division of Liverpool. The large majority which the right hon. gentleman obtained over his opponent at the recent election served to discourage the Liberal party from any at- tempt to contest the seat on the present occasion. BLACKPOOL DIVISION.—On Wednesday, Mears. Wilson, Wright, and Wilsons, the acting under-sheriffs, at Preston, received the writ for the election of a member of Parlia- ment to represent the Blackpool division. The High Sheriff has fixed Monday the 16th inst. for the nomination, and Friday the 20th inst. for the polling. It is believed that the Liberals will not contest the seat, as the party are divided in opinion—one section being in favour of a Glad- stonian candidate, while another would have a Unionist, and a third section has no desire for a contest at present. At a meeting of the Central Conservative Association for the uivision, on Wednesday afternoon, Sir Matthew White Ridley was unanimously adopted as the Conservative can- didate to succeed SirAFrederick Stanley. Sir Matthew was then introduced, and accepted the invitation. EAST BIRMINGHAM—Mr. Matthews, the Home Secretary was the only candidate nominated on Wednesday for East Birmingham. Mr. Alderman Cook, the Liberal candidate at the general election, who had intimated his intention of con- testing the seat, has issued an address in which be says:" I only placed my services at the disposal of the party in order, if possible, to restore the Liberal representation. During the last few days I have received most gratifying proofs at the continued confidence of my friends, but I have also found that the division in the ranks of the party still exists, and under these circumstances I retire from the contest" The commotion in Birmingham when it was announced that Mr. Cook had retired from the contest is is said to have been simply indescribable. Some of the bar- rieters at the assizes led a demonstration outside the Coun- cil House, when it was known that Mr. Mat- thews Neal returned unopposed. A correspondent says it has transpired that during Wednesday morning Mr. Cook had a conference with some of his leidiny., supporters, including Mr. Schnadhorst, and it was generally admitted that, in the present divided state of the Liberal party in Birmingham, be would have no chance of success. The knowledge that the Radical Union intended to issue a manifesto against Mr. Cook had something to do with the decision. The decision to withdraw come from Mr. Cook himself, and he admitted that it would be unreason- able to expect under the circumstances a different result from that of five weeks ago. Mr. Matthews addressed a large open-air meeting of his constituents on Wednesday. and, responding to a congratuletory resolution, said he felt that Mr. Cook had been made t play a part which was is )t his own. He claimed his election as a triumph for the cause of the Union. The moral be drew from this election was , that the elect4rs of Birmingham should rely less upon poli- tical organisations, which 11(1 made the town famous and exercised an influence destructive to all honest declaration of OPillioll. The Press Association understands that Her Majesty, who proceeds to Edinburgh early on Wednesday next to visit the Exhibition, will hold the usual Queen's Speech Council at lOsborne next Tuesday, Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, who had arrived iroLoeden in the morning from Dublin, to attend the Cabinet Council which is to be held at the Foreign Office, had a short inter- view on Thursday afternoon with the Prime Minister, who had previously received a visit in Arlington-street from Mr. W. H. Smith.

The Council representing the guarantors of the Jubilee Exhibition to be held in Manchester next year met in the Town Hall, on Thursday, and adopted the plans of the i Exhibition buildings sent n by Messrs. Maxwell & Tuke' architects, of that city. The guarantee fund now amounts to £ll5OOO. 'rho six crofters who were arrested in Tires, for rioting and "deforcing " messengers-at-arms have been released on bail from Inverary prison. They travelled by steamer to Glasgow on Wednesday night, and their arrival was made the occasion of a considerable demonstration on the part of their friends. Two MEN KILLED —Four men were buried by a fall of earth which took place on Wedrisclay during some exc Iva- dons in connection with the extension of the Dublin. Wick- low, and Wexford Railway. near New Ross. Two of the men were killed, and the third was so seriously injured that he is not expected to recover. Gas EXPLOSION AT BOLTON.—At the Bolton Corporation Gasworks. on Wedn-sday, an alarming accident occurred, which narrowly missed cansint, most disastrous results. The explosion took place in the meter-house, through which all the gas passes, and had not immediate disconnec-. tion been made with the gasometers and retorts the result would have been terrible. The building was completely gutted. The damage is estinaated at £l,OOO. No one was injured. The in inufacture of gas is stopped in consequence of the explosion.

Earlestown; Mr Simon Hazel- ton, Earlestown; and Mr John Lambert, Earlestown. SELECTIi)N oF A LIBERAL CANDIDATE. A hastily summoned meeting of the Lib4Pral 300 of the Newton Division was held in the Viaduct Insti- tute, Earlestown, on Monday night, to consider the selection of a candidate in the Liberal interest. The meeting appeared to excite much interest, and many rumours were afloat as to the probable candidate. Several names were prominently mentioned, including local gentlemen as well as others residing at a die- tance. There was a very large attendance of repre- sentatives from every part; of the division, and the proceedings throughout were of a very enthusiastic character. 'The chair was occupied by Mr. Charles Pilkingtou. J P., who was Anpported by Messrs. G. W. Rawlins (R.tinhill), W. D. Burdis, B. Harrison. P. Hall, 31. Birkhead, L. T. Foulkes, R. Yates (Got.. borne), A. J. Rawlin4on (Newton), C. E. Parker (Penketh), S. Barlow (Warrington), J. Taylor (Hay-

. was not true. (Applause.) The founittion of their policy was that in order that the empire might he maintained strong and vigorous, and upon a ssolid and firm basis, it was necessavy that every part of the empire in its turn sold be wisely and well governed so as to he prosperous and to b e contented. (Cheers.) He referred to the chine made by Mr. Chamberlain, who endeavoured to inculcate uoon the labouring lasses of England that by granting Home Rule to Ireland the effect would be to bring from Ireland an increased emieration of the labeuring clas- see, thereby cheapening labour in England and overcrowd- ing the labour market. His (Mr. French's) answer to that charge was that it was not true—it was abeolut^lv falla- cious. (Applause.) Did they think it likely that with a well ordered system of government in Ireland, with the domination of the landlord gone, and the people wrekimr ' for themselves and managing their own affairs with in- creased prosperity, increased enterprise, and increased em- ployment for the people in their own country, they would emigrate to Englamd ? (" so," and applause.) Tee working 1 classes need not fe,ar that by assenting to the measure of jost:ce they would in the slightest -degree injure their owe interests, but on the contrary they would be , doing what was right. what was just, and at the same time would he serving their own intemits. (Applause.). The charge that if Home Hole was passed the Catholics ifrould oppress their Protestant fellow-countrymen was a wicked prophecy not based upon meterials to justify such a charge. (Applause.) It was for the people to consider what had occurred in the past, what was occurring now, and whether in their judgment the time had come for a wise change, and a Liberal measure of local self-govern• ment for Ireland, which would satisfy and pacify that country, at the same time reserving to England and to the empire its full integrity and full Imperial powers. (Ap- plause.) Other questions of a grave charactn• were now before the country, though they were not attracting urgent

and immediate attention. One related to the law in refer- ence to mine royalties, and he thought that was a subject they would not find his opponent very ready to enter upon. (Laughter and applause.) They knew the reason why. It was that if the question was dealt with at all it would have to be dealt with in some manner affecting the rights of landlords. If they like to elect as their representative a gentleman who represented the landlords they could not ex- pect from him, or from his party, any measures seriously interfering with the rights of the landlords. (Applause.) He (Mr. French) should be glad to take an active part in considering what should be done to give a full measure of relief in the interests of the mining population. (Ap- plause.) There were other questions affecting the miners, which he should be glad to coaeider, and he would support any further legislation for the better protection of miners in the arduous and dangerous lives they had to lead. (Applause.) He said the farmers and the whole agricultural interest were susering at the present time from the great d•pression, and he suggested the ques- tion to them whether it was not time another radical change was made in the land laws. (" Yes," and applause.), He thought the time had come to try another and better mode dealing with the question, to render the English farmer more independent, to give them a better chance of cultivating their farms with a full feeling of security in the possession of his holding, including a fixity of tenurerand full com- pensation. for all improvements he made, and giving him the right to improve, and even taking away from the land- lord the right to increase the rent of the farmer in respect to the improvements that the farmer himself had made. (Applause...) Such things were nothing else but spoliation and legal plunder. (Cheers.) Did they expect those re- forms from the Tory party (" No.") New,. as in times past, if the people wished to ameliorate their condition they must depend upon themselves. The people of this country had it in their hands, by returning members to Parliament, to fashion and guide the course of legislation, and he asked, , in conclusion, if they were willing to reverse the result of the previous election, and strike out a new line by having for their representative a man willing to serve the interests of the people. (Loud cheers.) Dr. T. E, HAYWARD received a warm welcome. He said he could hardly believe that tbe electors of the division would implicitly follow the recommendation of Sir Richard Cross, for, without going into personal condemnation of Mr. Legh be (Dr.. Hayward) thought the most Mr. Legh's inti- mate friends could say about him was that they did not know any harm about him. (Laughter.) Certainly they knew very little about him. (Renewed laughter and ap- plause.) He thought they would decline to accept tke recommendation of Sir Richard Cross, but they would choose a representative for themselves—(applause)—and he had great pleasure in proposing "That this meeting having heard Mr. French, considers him a fit and proper person to represent the Newton Div!sion in Parliament, and pledges itself to use all lawful means to secure his return." (Cheers.)

Mr. INca, in seconding the motion, said he thought there was little doubt Sit' Richard Cross was glad to get to the House of Lords, and be (Mr. lace) was sure the electors were equally glad to get shut of him. (Laughter and ap- plause.)

The resolution was then put to the meeting, and was carried unanimously amid enthusiastic cheering. Mr. Frthrrerre. QC., on rising to respond, was again re- ceived with warm cheers. He said with every question affecting the interests of the working classes he was heart and soul with them, and working, for them, with no love at all and without ninch sympathy for the landlord classes. If the electors and himself (Mr. -French) would work hard and unitedly, he had no doubt they would be able to carry the contest to a triumphant issue. (Cheers.) The meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

div.head: MEETING A T NEWTON.
div.p: MEETING A T NEWTON.

On Tuesdiav evening, after speaking at Haydock, Mr. French, 4C., addressed a gathering of electors in Newton Town Hall, where he was greeted with cor- diality. The chair was occupied by Mr. Urquhart, and amongst those who supported him were Messrs. A. J. Rawlinson, W. D. Burdig, J. Adams; McHardy, Rhodes, &c.—The CHAIEXAN 84id that their late mem- ber had left them suddenly, but he did not think that I the majority of the people' in that district would be I very sorry. He then introduced Mr. Frenah as a good eandhlate to represent the views of the Liboral elec- tors.—Tbe Carmtnarra, who was cheered on rising to speak, said that the contest which they were now engagfd upon was good evidence of the pluck and energy that was pos- sessed by the Liberal electors of that division. In twelve months they had been twice beaten, but were ready again to fight, and see if the verdict last arrived at could not be ceanged. It was no hopeless battle, for there was qtaite a change now to the circumstances of the last elections. After a full consideration of the figures and of the circumstances the leaders of the party had come to the conclusion that in the altered position of things, with Sir itiehod Cross gone and with the new candidate who had been brought for- ward, there was such a large reserve of voting power upon the side of the Liberals that if the electors would work hard and come to the poll they could and would carry the seat. (Applause.) The facts leading up to the present contest reflected yeey little credit on the Tory party. Sir Richard Cross had served his party well for 20 years in the House of Commons, and had represented their division for the same length of time. He did not go to the House of Lords of his own free will. He would rather have remained in the House of Commons, probably with the idea of leading that House,.but Lord Randolph Churchill was evidently determined that the eminently respectable Sir Ricleard Cross should not stand in his way any longer, so Sir Richard Cross was shoved out of the way in order to leave the field clear for- such pranks as that youthful and bold legislator might determine upon (Laughter and applause.) Sir Michael Hicks-Beach had gone to Ireland out of the way, and in fact the process of slaughter was going on at sech an alarming rate that it was impossible to say where they would get to. when Lord R. Churchill stood alone at the bead of affairs with supreme power in his hands. (Laugh- ter and cheers.) Sir Richard nominated his successor in Mr. Legh, introduced him to the electors, and allowed the cloak of the great Sir Richard to fall upon this new prophet. (Laughter.) His shoulders were hardly strong enough to bear it. He (Mr. French) supported Mr. Glad- stone in the great and liberal measure he had introduced for the pacification of Ireland and for the good government of the whole of this great country. (Cheers.) He de- clared solemnly that the charge preferred by the Tories that the Liberal policy in any way aimed at separation, was a falsehood and a slander. No, the policy of the Liberal party was to maintain and confirm the integrity of the Empire by dbing full and absolu,e justice to every portion of Her Majesty's. dominions. He claimed on behalf of himself and those who believed with him the title of real Unionists. The question of justice for Ireland was a practical one—it meant a practical people managing their own affairs, and winning for themselves a full measure of employment. If the people of England would help those of Ireland in this matter it would tend to the benefit of both peoples. (Cheers.) M. Crladstone's policy, be claimed, would bring confidence to the Irish people. Mr. French then spoke on the question of miners, and asked would they prefer a member woo was representative of the great landed interests which drew the large royalties from mines, or would they prefer one who would seek to protect their interests, the interests of the people, upon this question P Would not the interests and sympathy of a landowner be in favour of the right of a landowner to get as much royalty from the bowels of the earth as he could get rent from the surface (Cheers.) The candidate also referred to the subjects of agriculture, primogeniture, and the tying up of land.—Afterwards a reso- lution of confidence in Mr. French was pissed with a few dissentients, on the motion of Mr. BIIRDIS, seconded by Mr. RAWLISSON.—The CANDIDATE thanked the- meeting, and the proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the cliairman. •

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

A meeting in support of the Liberal candidata was held in the Congregational School-room, at Golborne, on Wednesday evening, the weather preventing its being held, as bad been arranged, in Mr. Unsworth's ' field. The room was crowded with an enthusiastic audi- ence. The chair was occupied by Mr. Jahn Davies, of Golborne, who was supported on the platform by Mr. French, Q C., Mr. Johnson Ferguson, of kenyon, late M.P. for the Leuehborough Division of Leicestershire; Mr. C. Pilkington, J.P., fluyton ; Mr. G. W. Ra,wlies, Rainhill ; Messrs. W. Mitchell,-Openshaw, El twkinti, and others.—The CHAIRMAN said that they al Liberals were as confident now as ever they were that they were right and that the object they had in view would be gained—that was the pacifice.eion. of Ireland and Horne Rule for its people. (Cheers.) Mr. FRENCH, Q C., the candidate, on rising was received with cheers. He expressed himself confident that the con, stitueney would reverse the decision, of the former election, and show to the people of Englared that a change hod oc- curred, that the unfortunate divisions in the Liberal party no longer continued to exist in Lancashire, and that all bodies of Lib--eals were united for the purpose. Sir Riahard Cross, as a reward for his services to. the Tory party,, had. been kicked out of the .House of Commons by Lord Ren- dolpb Churchill to his final resting place. It was for the people of England to consider whether in years to come, apart from the Irish .question, the questions affecting the home and foreign relations of this country, and the destiny of the nation, were to be committed to the hands of such a man as Lord Randolph Churchill. ("No," and cheers.) He (Mr. French) stood there as a supporter of the integrity and the unity of this Empire, and he and the friends asso- ciated with him in the struggle, and the whole of the Liberal party, yielded not one jot to any body of Tories, or any body of Liberals, in the deter- mination that the union should be preserved. (Loud cheers ) He resented as an insult the supposition that he stood before an audience of Englishmen to advocate eeparatiOn. (Ap- blause.) Who dared to do it? (" No one,' and applause.) The candidate then referred to theoluestion of mining royalties, and in concluding his speech urged every elector to go to the poll en Monday next, and to taken personal int-rest in the contest. Doing that they would succeed. (Cheers.) • Mr. R. OPLINSITAW (Ciolborne) proposed a resolution pledging the meeting to use all ;awful means to secure the return of Mr. French, QC. (Cheers.) The Liberals of the Newton Division, he said, could do it if they would. It depended upon the working cleafies. The power was in theirhands. • He asked them to use that power, and show the landlords and squires that they wanted a man of experience and -commonsense to represent them. (Cheers.) They wanted a man with judgment, one who would look after their personal interests.—Mr. BetwietNs (Golhorne) seconded the resolution, and said be would never consider the electors of the Newton Division enfranchised until they had returced a Liberal as their member. (Applause.)—Mr.

KBRNBDY (Birkenbead), in supporting the resolution, cnn. gratulatod the electors upon having such a candidate as Mr. French. He was confident he would do good service for the Newton Division if he was returned to Parliament. (Ctieers.)—The resolution was also supported by Mr. dom.; FRuoirsos, and was carried amid loud cheers; and the meet- ing closed with a vote of thanks to the chairman. _ AS HTON. _

A second meeting on Wed—ft-ea-A-ay. evening, in support of the Liberal candidate, w.as held in the Congregatival Schoolroom, Ashton. Mr. French, Q.C., drove from Got. borne to Ashton, where he met with art enthusiastic recep- tion. The large schoelroom was packed to its utmost capa- city, while a large number of persons were unable to gain admission. The chair was occupied by Ir.T. Mitchell, and he was supported by Mr. French, Q.C., the candidate, Messrs C. Pilkington, G. W. Rawlins, W. Kennedy. J. Latbam, ' T. Roberts, W. Boardman, Walkden, Clough, J. McGeever, Jsc.—The Chairman, Mr. C. Pilkington, J.P, and the Candi- date add' ssed the meeting.—Mr. T. ROPORTS moved a resoluti- of confidence in Mr. French as the Liberal candir' ..e, and pledged the meeting to use every legitimate effort to secure ti return.—Mr. WALLDBN seconded, and Mr. KIiNNED" ,riirkenhead) supported the resolutiou, which was earriec. with cheers. STUESHAW CROSS. On Thursday afternoon Mr. French, Q.C., the Liberal candidate,. drove round by Simm's-lane-ends, Fourfooted Cross, anct Stubstraw Cross, and at each place he addressed a meeting.

- MEETING AT EARLESTOWN, On Thursday night a crowded and enthusiastic meeting of Liberals, in support of Mr. French, Q.C., was held in the Viaduct Institute, Earlestovrn. Mr. C. Pilkington, J.P., I presided, and among the gentlemen on the platform were Messrs. Frencb, Q.C.. F. F. Kennedy, Birkenhead ; J. E. Barlow, Manchester;. G. W. Rawlins, Rainhill ; J. Prescott, M. Birichead, A Gooding,. B. Harrison, G. Ratcliffe, F. A. R. Neill, B. Corlett, L. T.. Foulkes, T. J. Clarke, P. Hall, W. D. Burdis, J Davies, and T. Morris, hon. sec. of the Earleetown and District Liberal Club; and F. Broadbridge,. election agent.. The CHAIRAwr, who was well received, said that Mr. French was gaining, golden opinions wherever he went. From what be (the chairman) had seen and heard of him he believed Mr. French to be the strongest candidate that they had yet brought out. (Cheers.) It remained for the electors to fight for him even more strongly than they had yet fought for any other candidate. (Cheers.) There was, the chairman mentioned, a trip on Saturday which would take a great many people of that district away to different 1 parts of the country. It would take away many of their II voters, and therefore it was earnestly hoped that those who Gould se far deny themselves for their political feelings and would remain away from the trip. and that those who did not Stay would eudeayour to return in time on Monday next to record their votes. (Cheers.) Mr. Finetron, QC.,.was,received„with enthusiastic cheer- ing. He stated that on Monday night they accepted him with a degree of enthusiasm which even then made him full of hope in the contest upon which they were about to eater. Since then he had been in many parts of the divi- sion, he had met nia,ny classes of the voters, and he was now satisfied if the party would continue to work with the genie heart ancP with the same cordial zeal that they had shown up to the present, they bad every chance of succeed- ing at the poll on Monday next. (Applause.) In some districts on tee last occasion She miners were reported to be indifferentabut that day he had had three large and in- fluential meetings of miners, and they would on Monday 1 next work with them heartily, and if they di el he was told , by men of great experience in election matters that success was assured. (Cheers.), When be last spoke in that ball a contest was taking place in Birmingham, but it I now remained for the electors of the Newton Division to tell the people of England whether a change had taken place, and whether on Monday night they could telegraph to Mr. Gladstone—(cheers)—that the 'tide had begun to turn, ! and that be could look forward, to the time when the people of England, freed from misunderstandinos and the mis- representations of the general election, would see in the true light the great questionrebefore the country, and would give him the support which he needs for the great work. be had in hand. (Cheers.) He proceeded to criticise the ob- servetions•of Sir Richard Cfoss-and hie opponent, Mr. Legh, and said that the Tories seemed to think they could traffic with the people of this division, and Sir Richard Cross bringing forward, this youth by the hand—(laughter)— seemed to thinkhis 20 years-of political position had given the divisien to him, and as the absolute property of the Tories, and that they might pass it on like any other ancestral' position to this legatee —Master Legh. (Renewed laughter and , cheers.) Proceeding, the candidate said, that pressing reforms were needed. One was as regarded the manner in which the land was en he dealt with. (Cheere.), Another was the aboli- tion 'if primogentatire. (Cheers.). Oa each occasion when he had addressed !greetings. he, had thrown a challenge to Mr. Legh upon all the questions of practical importance be' fore the conetituencea such as the royalty question, the Employers' Liability Bill, the claim of farmers as against the landlords. but he had never yet had from him an answer, good, had, or indifferent. (Cheers.) Not a word from him in defence of himself or his position, except that when at Burtonwood and he. mede one answer when he said, and most truly said, that he was identified with the coal interests in that county. (Laughter.) Apart from the great question, of which toe day of reckoning was, to come for the landlords, there were other matters which harassed the people. One was the encroachments made upon common lands. Newton Common was now threatened, au rl the work was already beeun. This systemeticencroachment by the landlords on the rights of the people called for immediate attention, for the public righte of a nation should above all things be carefnlly gnarded. (Cheers.) He was also of opinion that there should be a full iequiry on the royalty question. He supposed Mr. Legh would refer theee and ether matters to the family friend, Lard Werrington. , ( Laughter and cheers.) The oracle had been consulted, but had not yet,spoken, and he would think twice before he gave an answer that would, he in any way injurious to that admiieale body of persons, the English landlords. (cheers.) Were net, he asked, the landowners of Eneland already sufficiently represented in the Parliament ; and did not they in the House of Lords monopolise the whole 'representation.. They had now got rid of ,a powerful Tory representative,, one of great local influence. The constituency was now open to a full and free exares- sion of opinion, And he asked them to give that expression ia his favour, and in favour of the gooa cause that he advo- ca(e3. (Cheers.) Mr. J. E. Bantow; J.P:, of Manchester, and the unsuc- cessful candidate at the election for the Knutsford Division of Cheshirealist November, proposed "That this meeting considers Mr. French a. man well qualified to represent this division in Parliament, and pledges itself to use every legi- timate effort to secure. hiareturn." He referred at some length to the land question, and pointed out the amendments required in the Land Acts to beta fit the farmers for improvements carried out on the land they occupied, commented upon the injus- tice of titbeseand said the people would have no sitisfactory solution of the land question until they fully recognised the fact that the land of England was made to maintain Vie people—(cheers)—that private rights must give way to ; Public rights, that no law could be just which threw the land of England out of cultivation, and prevented it being cultivated and giving that employment and susten- ance for the.people of the country to which they were en- ' I titled. and which was prevented for the sport and amuse- ment of the privileged aristocracy. ("Shame" and cheers.) IHe urged reforms were required in the taxation of ground' rents, in the system of local government, and in speaking of Ireland urged- they should have fair play all round, arid they should not have this ceuntry's business choked and blocked up by Dinh people who could not get their business attended teeeither. (Applause) He asked them to make up their minds to support a progressive policy by voting for Mr. French, who would well represent them in the House of Commons, and English industries would flourish, they ' would have unjiest restrictions taken off their trades,, and they would have the country more happy, more 'prover- , ous, anchnore contented. (Loud cheers.) , Mr: L. T. Fotiokos (Earlestown), in seconding the reso- lution,, said on Monday next they would have to say ' whether they approved of the Cabinet to rule this country, ' se.ecited by Lord Salisbury, and whether they approved of such a man as Lord Randolph Churchill—(hisees)--as leader of the House of Commons. The Liberals were afraid that the interests of the country would not be best served in the hands of quell a politician as Lord R. ' Churchill, and he for one protested against that appoint- ment (Cheers.) He asked if they were going to tell Mr. Legh that they were pleased with the manner in which he had treated this division, and where they going to send Mr. Legh to represent his own interests? Their interests were bread and butter for themselves and their families, and just and eqeitable laws by which they were to be governed, and they should not betray them by sendiug a man to Parlia- mer t who was unfit to represent them th'ere. (Cheers.) Their buqine-is was to be determined to return Mr. French to Par- liament, and be no longer bambeozied by any Tory mem- bers, unfit for any place. (Loud cheers.), Mr. F. F. KRNNRDY (Liverpool) in a stirring-addrese, sup- Darted the resolution, which was carried amid prolonged cheering. Mr. Fitateen, Q.C., responded, andsaid he felt confident that on Monday next, with the earnestness they bad hitherto shown, they would succeed if the Liberal electors would only go to the poll. (Cheers.) He moved a cordial vote of thanks to the chairmaneaad paid a tribute to the services of Mr. Pilkington, Mr. Rawlins, and other workers of the Liberal party in his behalf. Mr. T. MORRIS seconded the resolution, which was cor- dially passed. The CHAIRMAN briefly acknowledged the compliment, and the meeting concluded.
MR. W. T. UGH'S CANDIDATURE. DOWNALL GREEN, &c.

On Saturday Mr. T. Woodhouse Legb, Conserva- tive aandidate, a.ddressed a number of Con.servatives at Ashton, where he had a gool reception. Tie sub- sequently proceeded to Stubshaw Cross, and spoke to a small gathering of miners. Having also visited Park Lane, Mr. Leal and his friends went to Dowuall Green, near Wigan, where a meeting was held in the school-room. The chair was taken by Mr. M. B. West- head, and there was a' moderate attendance,— he CrutrixaN explained the reason why the constituency was again called upon to elect a representative, and said that after due and deep consideration the Council of the Ccinservative Association had arrived at the conclusion that the beet iuterest cZ tie party i.e that division wogid, he

serval by inviting Mr. Legh to come forward as their can* didate. He called their attention to the address of IVA'. Legh. who said that, having for seven years barn con Lected with an embassy in France, he saw how deeply neceesary It was for the foreign policy of this country to be firmly and consisttntly maintained. Mr. Legh's address also referred to Colonial Federation, and to miners, with whom Sir R. A. Cross had the greatest sympathy, and for whom he had worked so hard. Mr. Leah, if elected, would gladly accep.t the honour, but would not despise or eschew the responsi- bilities which ke knew would devolve upon him as a member of Parliament. He urged them to do their utmost to secure Mr. Legh's return.— file CANDIDATE then addressed the meeting. They were, be said, parting with an old and valued representative—a man whom any constituencY would be proud to be represented by. They could not. probably, find another man so qualified to represent that part of the country as Sir Richard Cross. but in one sense . what they lost would prove a gain in another place, for. the experience of Sir R. A. Cross would be given to the LPPer , House. Still, with that elevation there must linger a cer- tain feeling of regret. The separation from that con- stituency, ha was sure, must ba a severe pain to Sir R. A. Cross. He (Mr. Legh) could not presume to offer himeelt as a satisfactory Substitute for their late member, but, al- though he was young and inexperienced, youth was a thing that would cure itself before long, and inexperience aught change to experience. He did not then know whether or not there would be a contest, but, should there be one, he felt somewhat confident as to the ultimate result. ge could not believe that within so-short a time they had seen reason to change their opinions. He had some experience in tble diplomatic service, and was assured to a certain extent that the foreign policy of England should be a fi'm and resolute one—not one of truckling; or of the strong bullying the weak. He could not pretend to a close or intimate know' ledge of local matters. but should it ba his good fortun's to be returned he trusted that he should never give theni.se opportunity to regret the confidence they had placed in bun. He did not advertiee himself as being a success, but be would do his best to deserve their esteem, and should never give them cause to regret the day upon which they lrflia their choice. (Cheers.)—The CHAIRMAN then propel't a resolution expressing the opinion that Mr. Legh was a u 4, and proper person to represent the division in Parliattlen't and, this haying been seconded by Mr. G. F. CLAIM, it earned with one dissentient.—Mr. LEGE briefly replied, amid the meeting then terminated. NEWTON.----SPEECH OF SIR AICITARD'CROSS' A meeting in support of the candidature ofr. 14. T W. Legh, the Conservative candidate, was held gl the Town Hall, Newton, on Monday night, when there was a lame attendance. The chair was °cell.

The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, eta" ted that at a council meeting of the Conservative Associa- tion of the Newton Division, a resolution was passed env bodying the sentiment that they wished to thank Sir Richard Cross for his past services, and that while the' had not the satisfaction and the pleasure of retaining hiT as their member, they had the eatiefection of knowing that his services had been secured to their Queen and the'. country. (Applause.) The selection of u suitable canoe date in the Conservative interest then fell upon the gentle' man on his right hand (Mr. T. W. Leek)). who, as having a great and deep interest in this particular neigh' bourhood, would very probably he able to represent all their individual interests, whether they were Radicals, e! Liberals, or Conservatives, and who would be able to col up to his duty by maintaining those principles which badd been submitted to the people of the country, and which ha pieced Lord Salisbury in power. (Cheers.) Mr. T. W. LEGai was received with warm applause. lie remarked that in their late representative they had 10at ya man of whom any constituency might be proud, and Sir Richard Cross had been the recipient it high dignitY• (Applause.) He asked them to bear in mind that although, they had not got the same man to represent them, they still had the same principles to decide upon, as well as the Bain° questions. Lie said questions, bat he ought properly to sal queeton, as it was the one eternal question—the Irish problem—which was now before them, as it was not -100 g ago. Upon that question they. in common with the grail majority of the constituencies of the kingdom. express their opinion not long ago, and they had expressed that opinion in no unfaltering toile. (Applause.) That opinion; he felt confident, if they were called upon, they weahi repeat again. (Hear, bear.) Practically speaking, the question amounted to this—Were they prepared, before the. menace of the dynamiter and at the point of the dagger ol the assassin, to consent to the disintegration rn the empire? (Groaes ) Their answer at the Isa.,.t election was "No," and he firmly believed ',l* would be so should another occasion arise. (Applause./ Proceeding to speak of foreign affairs he said a foreign Pr): tiny, in order to be successful, should be firm, just, ana ready to support the interests of England abroad, such a pelicy they might confidently expect from the present Con- servative Government. (Applause.) HS held that ell right-thinking Englishmen. and especially the working classes, trona whom our colonies were principally recruited, should give tbeir utmost support to a measure which tended to bring the colonies and the mother country into closer union. (Applause.) In reference to qn ‘stions of local in' terest, be would not profess any deep-seated knowledge 00 questions affecting the mining industries of this countrfr but it should be his great aim and object to acquire suCh knowledge of those matters ie far as might be useful to hirer and in acquiring suck knowledge how could he act better than by endeavouring to follow as well as he was able the conduct of their late representative. (Applause.) The 9 could not expect him to keep pace wrth Sir It'cbard, but would endeavour laboriously to follow in his footsteps. (Ar" plause.) Ira conclusion, he thanked them for having asked him to come forward to represent them. SIR RICHARD CROSS, who was cheered, said his first intY was to thank them for the support which they bad so gene- rously given him at the last election—(applause)—and be must congratulate them not simply u.on the result of the election in that division, but . upon the result of the general election •throughout the country. (Applause.) When the elections gave such a decided voice against the Prime Minister, the question cline to be decided who wes- t() form the next,Government. He was one of those who would have been glad if Lord Hartington could have seen his way to form a Government by himself, not upon Cone servative principles alone, but upon Unioaist principles. But Lord Hartington and hie friends—wisely or unwisely be' said nothing about—came to the conclusion that the,' should stand aloof, promising a perfectly independent lent cordial support to the Conservative party. (Applause.) It' had been stated that Lord Salisbury hid great difficulty in' forming this Government ; that personal ambition stood in his way; and that be Wee hampered by the individual claims - or his colleagues. He should like to give the most positive' and absolute denial to that st itement. (Appl iuse.) In the- formation of this Government it so happened that he (Sir Richard) had been called by command of the Queen to take. the high station of Secretary of State for India. (AP- plause.) He took up that position with the utmost di dence in his own powers, but with determination to face the difficulties, and treating this matter in no party spirits to do all he could for the welfare of those millions upore millions of their fellow-subjects in that distant country. Connected with that high office of Secretary of- State fer India, it had been conveyed to him that it was necessali he should accept a generous offer of her Majesty--vize a seat in the Hoene of Lords. ( Applause.) He could net without pain to himself leave an assembly to which he WO first elected-thirty years since. He not only left the Hoaca of COMMOUN but he left a constituency of which any meat' her might he proud. There was no constituency equal t° the South-West Division of. Lancashire, which be had ea long the honour to represent. When that division 033 broken up. be came to thatepart—N. wton—with which. he had been, connected by. residence and material in- terests for 25 years. He c tml to them, and they most generously came forward and supported not only rile principles which he held, but himself, as a representative ofe, those principles. (Applause.) They could rely upon his aesietaece during the remainder of his lifetime upon any occasion where his services might be found useful to the-electors of that constituency, for whom he had the warmest regard. (Anplause.), ha bidding them farewell, be did ea thanking them from the bottom ef his .heart for all the I;:ndness they had shown him, and so long as life should last he would continue to take a great interest in the constitaency and in all that concerned them. (Applause.) He had made many friends in that part of Lancashire, and he was not aware that he had ever made 0 eingle enemy. (Applause.) Although they had elected MO as representing their principles, let them met forget that it was the principles they were fighting for and not the man ; and though he might depart frcm among them to a differ" ent sphere, he urged them to Let those principles remain 39 sacred as they aver were. He urged them to work bard, to secure the return of Mr. Legh, and said if they were going to elect somebody instead of Mr. Legh, then tbelc would put a dagger into the present Government and a nail in its coffin, and they would band over that division to Gladstone's policy. He moved—" That this meeting hci's with satisfaetion the elicXeSS of the Unionist candidates er the late genarat election,. and having heard the views a rdr: T. W. Legh. the Conservative Unionist, is of opinion that he is a fit and proper person to represent the Newton Diyi" sion in Parliament, and pledges itself to use all legitimate endeavours to secure his return." (Applause.) The Eton. W. GEIINPD seconded the motion, which oaf' carried, and the meeting terminated with a vote a! thanks ta the chairman.
