div.p: FIXED !---" I am a lawyer's daughter, you know, George dear," she said, after George had proposed and been accepted, "and you wouldn't think it strange if I were to ask you to sign a little paper to the effect that we are engaged, would you ?" George was too happy to think anything strange just then, and he signed the paper with a trembling hand and a bursting heart. Then she laid her ear against his middle Test-button, and they were very, very happy. " Tell me, darling," said George, after a long dehcious silence, "why did you want me to sign that paper? Do you not repose im- plicit confidence in my love for you?" " Ah, yes," she sighed, with infinite content, "indeed I do! But, George dear, I have been fooled so many times I" It has I low,"' been considered that a person can be more politely insulted in Paris than in any city in the world. 1 A gentleman who undertook to speak in public there recently expressed himself in such a low tone of voice that the audience were unable to hear him. He was lecturing upon a geographical subject, and copies of a map about three feet square had been generally dis- tributed. Presently one of the audience rolled up his map in the form of a very long and attenuated lamp- lighter, inserted the small end in his ear, and turned the other end towards the speaker. It was a rather ludicrous performance, but not a laugh was heard among the polite assemblage. In two minutes, however, every map in the house was turned into an ear-trumpet, and the speaker saw himself confronted with a sort of mammoth porcupine whose nearest quills almost touched his lectern. He at once spoke louder. The father of Erastus Corning was a candidate once for Congress and the regular nominee of the Democrats. Eli Perry, another Democrat, was running indepen- dently. Perry was a character in Albany in his day. He had been a butcher, and was a butcher still, although he had grown wealthy and was engaged in banking. He was a big man, full of rough animal spirits. Corn- ing was smaller in stature, and had a lame leg, which made him walk with a limp. The two men had an ap- pointment for a joint meeting, after the fashion of the day, at Clarksburg. Corning made a finished speech. He was considered a good talker. Perry knew that he could not answer the speech because he was not in the least degree an orator. But lie knew his hearers; and, *en Corning had concluded, he called a fiddler out of the crowd and made him tune his fiddle. Then he got up on the platform, and said, "Gentlemen, I can't make a speech, and you all know it; but I can dance a break- down better than Corning any day lie lives, and I will dance one now." He proceeded to execute the break- down amid the shout of the assembly. Perry carried the town by a large majority.

div.head: ADVENTURFS OF A WARRINGTON
div.p: ADVENTURFS OF A WARRINGTON
FOUNDLING.

On Monday morning Mr. Shearer, relieving offi- cer, applied to the borough magistrates for an order for a boy named John Warrington to be committed to the ship "Clio." The lad is a foundling, and has caused no little anxiety in the institution where he has been brought up—the industrial school at Pad- gate. Mr. Shearer said that the boy was incorrigible. He had run away from the school seventy-five times, and had had narrow escapes of being killed. He had got into all kinds of trouble. On one occasion Mr. Mines (the superintendent) said to him that he would, if he ran away again, be sent to prison for stealing Workhouse clothing, and when he next ran away he left the clothes behind and made off wiith nothilig on but his shirt. He that time cabled at a gentleman's house, and had breakfast. Not long since the youngster rode to Liverpool on the buffer of a train. He was brought back, and when attempting to perform another journey in a similar manner, he feli off the train at Glazebrook station, and was hurt. The "Clio," Mr. Shearer said, seemed to be the best place for him, as he would far rather work than attend to schooling. He might make a good sailor.- - The Mayor: He does not seem to be short of courage.—Alderman Davies: Would you like to be a sailor? The lad replied that he would.—Alderman Davies: We can sympathise with the captain of the " Clio " on his acquisition. (Laughter.)—Mr. Shearer: He is a good natured boy.—Mr. Mackay (workhouse mas- ter) said that the lad required firmness. He had no difficulty with him.—Alderman Davies: Would you like him for yourself? (Laughter.)—Chief Constable Hunt: He might lead someone astray. I sent a new constable to the school with him once, and he took him round by Woolston—anywhere but the Pad- gate Schools? (Laughter.)—Aldermv Davies: The policeman would be at a disadvantage with such a clever chap.—Warrington, in answer to a question, said he would like to be a sailor.—The Mayor: You are going to the ship "Clio," and I hope you will be a good boy there. Try and learn to be an accomplished sailor, and you may do well yet, You are a clever lad, I have no doubt, with plenty of brain, if you will only use it in a proper manner.—Mr. White (magistrate's clerk) : Too much brain. (Laughter.)—The magistrates gran- ted the application.

like it. In answer to Mr. Woods, witness said that Wolmer distinctly asked him up to fill up the paper in favour of Mr. Woods. He believed it was at Wolmer's own suggestion that the paper should be filled up.—Mr. Woods: Did you think Wolmer was legally signing the paper.—Witness: Yes, at the time I did.—Mr. Darbyshire remarked that there was a course to be pursued, directed by the Local Government Board, by the voter who could write, and another cokirse to be pursued by the voter who could not write. In this case neither one nor the other course had beenpursued.—Mr. Woods: I submit that Wolmer did write. —Mr. Henley said there was no dispute that the pen was touched, and it would be for the Local Government Board to decide.—Chaplin having been recalled said that there was a gentleman in the room at the time Wolmer's paper was signed, but that gentleman was not present at that inquiry.—The case of Michael Lally was then gone into. Lally stated that he was a gardener and lived at Grappenhall. He had had a voting paper delivered to him, and between six or seven o'clock in the eveni,ng he was passing i the Rain's Head Inn, and he went n and asked Mr. Chaplin if he would fill in the paper for him as he had not his "specs." Mr. Chaplin filled it up on the table, and he -(witness) put his hand on the pen and a cross was made.—Mr. Henley (handing the paper to witness): What has become of the cross.— Witness looked at the paper, and not finding the cross, seemed to be rather confused.—Mr. Darby- shire called the attention of Mr. Henley to the fact that Lally had said he put his hand on the pen while the cross was made, though there was no cross.—Mr. Woods: I suppose he means the initials. —Mr. Henley: That is what he means.—Mr. Woods (to witness) : Was it your intention to vote for me.—Witness: Yes.—ln answer to Mr. Henley Lally said that Mr. Chaplin suggested that he should put his hand on the pen. He had his hand. on the pen when Mr. Chaplin began writing, but he believed he took it off before he finished. He knew the paper was filled in for Mr. Woods, and he took it home with him.—Mr. Chaplin was then again called, and corroborated the statement of Lally with the exception that he deposed that Lally never touched the pen whilst he was filling the paper up. He did not think that in either case he suggested that the voter should touch the pen.—ln answer to Mr. Woods he said he could not swear that Lally did not touch the pen, but he did not think he did. —Mr. Henley having inquired if there were any witnesees to call, Mr. Darbyshire said he had not been quite sure whether the inquiry would be confined strictly to those two cases so that he had caused other witnesses to be sum- moned whom he did not wish to call upon, because their evidence did not particularly bear upon those cases. Peter Mather, one of these witnesses, was the gentleman who went round with the deliverer of the voting papers on Mr. Wood's behalf.—Mr. Henley: You don't wish to call him.—Mr. Darby- shire: No, not if the newspaper question is not be- ing gone into. Mr. Darbyshire then said he should not like the Witnesses who were not called to lose their day's work without being paid for coming there.—Mr. Henley said that all the witnesses who had been summoned by him would have . a prima facie claim to their expenses, but the Local Govern- ment Board might say that certain witnesses were not required, and therefore disallow their expenses. So far as that inquiry was concerned it was closed. He would report as soon as possible to the Local Government Board and ask them to give their de- cision.—Mr. Woods and Mr. Darbyshire then ex- pressed their thanks for the manner in which he had conducted the inquiry. The latter gentleman observed that if there was to be another inquiry he should press some of the other charges which he had made to the Local Government Board. ; There were other circumstances of the election which the inspector could not very well notice at , that inquiry, but which he (Mr. Darbyshire) should press.—Mr. Henley said it would be well to remem- ber that the Local Government Board were de- barred from determining any case of general cor- ruption or illegal practice unless so far as to deter- mine the validity of any vote. That was for another court altogether, and there were penalties 'attached to corrupt practices. He thanked them for the assistance they had given him that day.— The inquiry then concluded.

The proceedings of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society, for the session 1885 6, are is- sued in book form, and make a capital volume, as the papers, which are printed in full, are of more than ordinary interest. It is noteworthy that of the six papers time of them are Shakesperesa. Mr. Joseph Adams deals with The Dramatic Method of Shake- spare " ; Mr. Robert Davies with "The Trilogy of lEschylus and Shakespere's Hamlet; and Mr. John Dun with "The Character of Hamlet." The other contents of the volume are as follows A Flash of Lightning," by Mr. J. J. Webster; "Energy." by Mr. W. Thompson; and "Chester Cathedral," by Mr. W. Owen. They were all reported more or less at length at the time they were given; but those who heard them will be glad to have them in this complete form.
The ninth series of Health Lectures delivered in

Manchester is published in a one shilling volume by Mr. John Heywood. Tee lectures of this series are confined to the subject of Food and Drink; but the information which they give is invaluable. The first lecture, which is "On Diet," is by Mr. Arthur Ran. some. M.D., M.A., F.R.S., and President of the Society. The Manchester lectures have had a powerful effect in stimulating scientific authorities in other large centres of population, and the result is that lectures of a like hind are now given during the winter season in Edsnburgh, Glasgow, and Birmingham. "Holiday Notes in East Anglia is the title of a little volume which sets forth the merits of the plea- sure resorts of Norfolk, Suffolk, and Essex. The
sketches, for such they may be 'called, are for the

most part pleasantly wiitten-; and they are accom- panied by bright illustrations. The views include Yarmouth, Lowestoft, Southwold, Cromer, Than- stanton, Clacton-on-Sea, Felexetowe, &c., and cer- tainly set the reader longing to be in the fashion by paying a visit to some of these places by means of the Great Eastern Railway. "The Official Guide to the isle of Man," issued by the Isle of Man Steam Packet Company, is a capital sixpenny worth ; there is no wonder at its reaching a third edition. There is a coloured map of the island, and numerous illustrations of the more im- portant places, and a full account of the history, legends and antiquities, with full details as to routes, fares, &c. The guide is well printed, and well arran- ged, and written in a readable style. Cassell's Magazinefor August is particularly attrac- tive, and, like the summer number, "Mistress June," it is just the thing for those who are out holidaying. Even Parliament is made light reading in the chap- ter on its " Gaieties and Gravities." "The pleasures of Mountaineering" are well described by Mr. W. T. Mainprise, and "The Glens of Ochils " is another admirably illustrated paper. "The Physiology of Diet" is dealt with by the Family Doctor; Mr. George Weatherly contributes a story in rhyme en- titled "Ned ;"while the serial stories fully preserve their interest. "The Quiver" opens well with two line illustrations "The Convalescent.* and "The Un- known Martyr." "Sundry Musings in the Lake District "is the title of an interesting article by the Rey. H. Dinnis ; and there is a paper on " Working- men and the Sunday Question," by Rev. Dr. Tres-- trail. "The Lights along the Shore" deals with the sailor folk; and a paper on "The Pleasures of Boy- hood ". introduces some choice quotations on a fav- ourite subject of the poets. Besides "Short Arrows there are other articles and stolies of interest. The current number of "Little Folks" bac a pretty fron- tispiece" In the Meadows ; " but the colour in this instance scarcely harmonies with the subject ; it is green, but not the green of the meadows. As a whole, text and illustration are delightful; and the rhymes, stories, jottings, and puzzles are everything that young readers can desire. "The Magazine of Art" for August is enriched with a noble engraving of Mr. Thornveroft's statue of " The Sower." "Art in Australia" is the title of the leading paper. which is suitably illustrated. "Some New York Theatres" opens the door to several charming bits in the way of architecture. "The rapid Spey" has justice done to it; and there is a second article on "Current Art." Under the title of "The Romance of Art" we have an account of the career of Quentin Meteys ; and there is an instruc- tive and amusing paper (illustrated) on "Female Head-gear." Part 7 of " Cassell's Illustrated Shakespeare" brings "The Comedy of Errors" to a close, and carries the

reader on to the second act of " Much Ado about Nothing." The editor preserves all the fine features with which it commenced. Part 12 of "Gleanings from Popular Authors" completes the first volume of this work which is destined to become increasingly popular. The selections and the illustrations are alike admirable.

Toe Life and Times of Queen Victoria" (part 3) is another venture by Messrs. Cassell which promises to be a great success. It is history of the best kind, with the very best illustrations. Issued in monthly parts, at 7d each, it is. as it should be, accessible to all classes. The Dandelion and Hyacinth are the inely finished coloured plates in the current issue of "Familiar Wild Flowers." Part 28 of "The Book of Health" deals with "The Skin and Hair," Baths and Bathing," &e., and gives valuable advice while furnishing the latest scientific knowledge. We have also to hand part 31 of the incomparable Ency- clopedic Dictionary; and the following volumes (3d each) of " Cassell's National Library," "Life and adventures of Baron Trenck," Cowley's Essays, Sir Roger de Coverley and the Spectator's Club, and "The Diary of Samuel Pepys." " Income Tax : How to get it Refunded" is a useful work by Mr. A. Chapman, of 16. Artesian- road, London, W. There are many tradesmen and professional men, who, looking back at their income for three years, know that they have paid too much income tax; but they do not see their way to get- ting what is due to them from the lion's mouth. This work shows how to set about the task, and the instructions are of such a kind that he who runs may read. The price of the book, which has reached a third edition, is one shilling. The current issue (part 21) of Messrs. Ward and Lock's Technical Journal deals with such varied topics as the grazier and cattle breeder, the young architect, the calico printer, the stonemason, the land .drainer, the steelmaker, &e., whilst the technical dic- tionary is carried to the letter S. We have also to hand the August number of "The Season"—which is now published in two editions, one at is and the other at tixpence ; "The MonitPur de la Mode " is; " Myra's Journal" 61 ; and " Myra's Threepenny "—all oi which are admirable in their way as glasses of fashion, with a view to being moulds of form.

div.head: SHOCKING KICKING AFFRAY AT
div.p: SHOCKING KICKING AFFRAY AT
RAINFORD SPORTS.

At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, before ' Messrs. R. Pennington, jun., and J. C. Gamble, a young man named John Cowley was under remand charged with unlawfully wounding Frederick Antro- bus, market gardener, 40, Church-street, Farnworth, whilst they weie at Rainford sports on the 3rd inst. Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for complainant, and Mr. J. 0. Swift defended.—Mr. Riley stated that com- plainant was arguing with a man from Liverpool about son.° bat he had made. when defendant, who was one of the sur- rounding crowd, said "Don't pay him a:copper." Com- plainant asked him why he should interfere, as he bad nothing to do with it. Defendant said, "I'll let you know," and immediately struck him violently in the mouth and .knocked him to the ground. When he tried to get up pri- soner made a running kick at his head, and so serious was the kick that complainant was rendered insensible. He was carried to the Golden Lion Hotel, and attended by Dr. Murdoch, The next day he was taken home to Farnwortii, and there attended by Dr. O'Neil. Complainant bad not since done any work, and he was told that he would have to be careful for some time to come.—The prosecutor then gave evidence, and, in reply to Mr. Swift, said he was quite sober. He had been at Rainford sports before. He was there la6t year, but he was not turned off the field. He didn't create a disturbance, but he got mixed up with one. He was not mixed up with a disturbance th. year before. He had not to be ejected frem the field both last year and the year before. This was not the third year in succession at Rainford sports that he had managed to get into some row. He did not challenge defendant to fight or give him any provocation.—Joseph Corbett, 20, Higher Parr-street, St. Helens, Thomas Sexton, Tontine-street, St. Helene, and Henry Glover. Westfield-street, gave corroborative evldence. The latter said •defendant took two steps bickvrards and then gave complainant a kick in the jaw, which rendered him insensible.—P.S. Smith stated that when prisoner was charged with kicking prosecutor on the face, head, and jaw, he replied, " No ; that is not right."—Mr. Swift asked the Bench if they considered it a case in which, if defendant paid complainant a substantial sum for compensation, the case could be withdrawn. Defendant admitted t" at he hit complainant after provocation an after he had NW ,ed a blow, but denied that he bad kicked him.—The magistrates considered it a case which should go for trial.—Dr. Mur- doch, M. 8., C.M., said he found complainant lying oh the field apparently recovering from insensibility. He was suffering from a contused wound on the upper lip, and com- plained of severe pain in the head. His condition was apparently very serious, and be bad him removed to the inn and attended him several times during the evening. The symptoms were such as he wonld expect from the injuries described.—ln reply to Mr. Swift, the doctor said complain- ant had had a little drink.—lnspector Whittaker said he received prisoner at St. Helens when he was brought in from Rainford. In reply to the charge of unlawfully wound- ing, he said, "I will tell you the truth about it ; I did kick him once on the top lip."—ln reply to the clerk, he said, "I am not guilty ; he hit me first."—Prisoner was then committed to the next sessions for trial. Bail was allowed in £3O, and Mr. Harrison, of Rainford, was bound for another £3O.

A DISTRACTED SWEETHEART.—In Dublin the registrar of the Common Pleas Division has sat with a jury of six to assess the damages in an action for breach of promise to marry. The plaintiff was Margaret M'Kee, and the defen- dant Bernard Raffertv, from whom £5OO damages were claimed. The plaintiff, a girl of 18, said that the match was arranged by friends. Subsequently the defendant agreed to marry her on.receiving £lOO from her father. The wed- ding dress was procured, friends invited, and a priest en- gaged, when defendant's sister prayed to have the match broken off, as another girl had become distracted on learning that defendant was about ta marry the plaintiff. The plain- tiff cried, and her father laid the £lOO down on the table to induce defendant to keep his promise, but he refused, and married the distracted girl.—The jury awarded plaintiff £l2O damages. DRUNKENNESS OR TEMPERANCE IN BATIEEtSBY-LANE.

Sir,—Could I, as a resident in the above lane, draw the attention of our licensing magistrates and the Temperance and Band of Hope "'llion Committees to the notice posted up in our midst of an in- tention to !apply for an inn license at the coming licen- sing thy. We have already two licensed houses within sixty yards from each other in the lane—one holding a spirit licease--vet they want to plant another in between these very two houses, to farther destroy the peace of our neighbourhood, and give further convenience to the dread- ful vice, evidence of which we already see about here. Again, we have no less than eight off-licenses and four ion licenses, all within a distance of four hundred yards from the proposed site, and this, I believe, is sufficient ac- commodation for a new neighbourhood. Trusting that the property owners about here will oppose this matter for their own benefit and that of their tenants, I remain, yours, (Le.,

div.head: RESIDENT.
div.p: A RESIDENT.
THE NUISANCE IN MARKET-PLACE.

Sir,—l am very pleased to see that the nuisance in Market-place is being taken up by men of high character. On Saturday last it was something disgusting; to hear the language usrd inside tke Place. Surely a more suitable spot could be found rather than put it opposite a row of shops, when the trade depends upon the passers-by. If the nuisance is to stop there, we may expect before this time next twelve months to see the whole row of property empty. I am sure Alderman Burgess, and the rest of the committee, are not aware what they are doing; but wonld Alderman Burgess I i li- one opposite his shop door at Bridge-foot? How. ever we may keep ear ears open, as there is sure to be some- thing said at the next Council meeting. If the nuisance mentionell is not removed shortly, perhaps we shall have to wait mill one or two large fires have taken place, and the people cannot find the fire bell. Just fancy the committee putting a urinal inside the fire-bell place. But ratepayers will remember those gentlemen when they have to ask for an election of councillors by vote.—Yours. Warrineon. T. L.

ANTI-VACCINATORS AND THEIR CHAMPIONS. Sir,—After reading the report of the proceedings of the Guardians at their last meeting. re vaccination, one can hardly nrlp coming to the conclusion that the anti-vaccina- tore of Eirlestown are somewhat unfortunate in their cham- pions. At the previous meeting the Guardians showed, if net sympathy with the anti-vaccinators, at least an unex- pected tol,rance of their views, and at the last meeting a letter was read f-om the Local Government Board actually telling ne,Guardians in almost so many words that it is no use proercuting people under the Vaccination Acts unless prosecution rs lik-ly to have the effect at inducing them to vaccinate thei. children. Surely here was an opportunity for the representatives of the anti-vaccinators on the Board which, if "taken at the flood," might have led on to per- fect immunity from fines and penalties. What coeld have been easier than to point out what is perfectly well known to everybody that no amount of prosecution will induce a confirmed anti-vaccinator to have his children vaccinated, and that ther4ore the Guardians in refraining from prosecu- ting would be only following the dictum of the Local Go- vernment Board itself. But the anti-vaccinating Guardians did not do this. They contented themselves with putting for- ward a resolution which meant nothing, unless indeed it meant that the Board was to go on pros 'eating as it bad alone heretafore. A wonderful outcome this of having special representatives of anti-vaccination as Guardians. There will now surely, be no more grumbling among the anti-vaccinatots at Earlestown when their own champions went out of their way to move a resolution that the Guar- -dians should act towards anti-vaccinators exactly as they lad Leen acting all along. Warrington, August 11, 1896.
J. T.

div.head: "THE OLD GANG."
div.p: "THE OLD GANG."

Sir,—l suppose we ordinary folk ought to pay due respect to the powers that be ; but I think I shall not be far wide of the mark when I sty that at least one piny in the State are doing their best to bring into conternptthe ruling power. Ever since the article entitled " Elijah's mantle" appeared in the Fornightly Review," it has been clear that Lord R. Chureall Intended, by book or crook, to be the Disraeli of his party. It has been matter of great regret to this lordly bantam that the enajority of one hundred which so demurely followed Lord Beconsfield should have collapsed, and the strongly expressed opinion that Toryism would be in power for a qaarter of a century should have been falsi- fied by succeeding events. Yet so it is, and the disciple of " Opportunism" seeks to find a remedy. What so natural, to one who ignores political truth and honour, as to kick out "the old gang" and replace it by a gang willing to sweat by a descendant of the traitorous Duke of Marl- borough?

First on the programme was Sir h. Northcote, openly , denounced because be had "no go" in him; he was forced into "another place" where the weary, the intractables and the ileapsbleq, fled their appropriate resting places. In Sir Stafford's place, as leader of the House of Com- mons, arother was foisted (Sir M. H. Beach) against whom the same complaint was charged Between the two leaders there was this difference—Sir Stafford Northcote could not 4orget that he was an English Tory, neither could he sink his own independence of character, and suffer himself to be snubbed and bullied by a young upstart who was trying to wriggle into "Elijah's mantle." Pliableness was required for a short time; Sir Michael was at hand, and a bargain was struck, the result of which manceuvring is that Lord Randolph appears as the leader of a party pledged to the country to be so full of "go" that they have none to spare for the Irish, who, poor fellows, must stand still. Since this terrible denenciation was first burled at poor Stafford's head, I have often wondered what was meant by it. It seems such a c .rioas thing to charge Conservatives with having "no go " in them. Coming from Coneervatives we are obliged to believe it, yet the same thing has been said a thousand times by the Radicals. How many times have we in Warrington expressed eur surprise at the amount of enthusiasm that could be raised for Sir R. A. Cross? Yet, as a member of the "old gang," he has received the pro- verbial Irishman's promotion. Since Lancashire Tories went mad over the !lista Church, and turneel out Mr. Glad- stone in their efforts to resist men fall of "go," Radicals , all over England have been stating that Sir S. Noi-thcote was a muff. This statement has received its confirmation in the least of all expecte I manners. Wbv, it is enough to make one burst with laughter—Lord Randv-Pandy the leader of Sir It A. Cross! Talk of turning out the "old gang," this is doing it with a vengeance. But what a disappointment it must be to our Tory friends round about Warrington; poor fellows, thee thought they were voting for a Home Secretary, when all the time their leader had doomed him to be a humble follower of his in some wild Indi in policy, and join company with the select few of the Old Gang" who had already gone where the weary are at rest. It but remains to remove that beautiful specimen of "our old nobility," Lord John Manners, and the House of Commons will be clear of the "old gang." Lord Randolph will then be at liberty to give us a sample of his Toryism. People who are hoping for the hest say that Lord Saliabury will keep this wild ••unkennelled fox" in order. I have no faith in this, there is not one member of the Cabinet that dares now to oppose him. He has set be- fore him the tesk of bringing back to his party "power, place, patronage, and glory." To accomplish this it was necessary to have men with "go" in them. These he has got, but they must receive their inspiration from the wearer Of " Eli j th's mantle." CLIFFORD DIX.
THE EARLESTOWN ANTINACCINATORS.
Sir,—Your issue of the 7th inst reports an interesting dis- cussion at a meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, also a letter signed "Justice," on which I should like to make a few remarks.

It is a pleasure to note that the Guardians take a lenient view of the law-made crime of non-vaccination by p oceed- ing only once against defaulters, and that the magistrates also temper justice with mercy by imposing a mitigated penalty ; but still the injustice remains of treating as law- breakers and criminals God-fearing citizens and loving parents, whose only offence is that of refusing to bow down to the dictates of a medical priesthood, and to submit their children to certain disease and possible death. Mr. Harrison referred to " Jenner'a discovery," which was no discovery but merely the appropriation of a local tradi- tion. taught him by the dairymaids, and which farmer Jesty had put into practice years before. He next stated as a reason why vaccination must be a good thing" that they found very rarely indeed any medical man venture to oppose the practice." Mr. Harrison must be strangely ignorant of the history of medicine to talk such rubbish. Did he ever know any profession to reform itself? Did doctors abandon bleedine, salivation, inoculation, excessive purgation, or any other of the "destructive arts of healing" until the stir erior intelligence of the public revolted against such murderous blunders and compelled them to do so ? History answers no. Does he imagine that they will new voluntarily give up a nostrum which the State in the blindness of ignorance has established and endowed, and which yields them an annual income of over a million pounds sterling, unless they are forced to do so ? Let a member of their own profession reply. In vol. viii. of "The Medical Observer," London, 1810, the editor gives details of 97 fatal cases of smallpox after vaccination, and of 150 cases of injury arising from vac- ciliation, together with the addresses of ten medical men, including two professors of anatomy. who had suffered in their own families from vaccination. Concerning these re- markable evidences, Dr. Maclean observes:—" Although numerous, they are few in 'comparison tc what might be produced. . . . It will be thought incumbent on the vAccinators to come forward and disprove the numerous facts decisive against vaccination here stated on unimpeach- able authority, or make the amende honorable by a manly recantation. But experience forbids us to expect any such fair and magnanimous proceeding, and we may be as- sured that under no circumstances will they abandon so lucrative a practice. until the practice abacdons them," Now for tbe anonymous writer who, under the signature " Justice," upholds the vilest injustice that ever desecrated the name of law, or trod mercilessly under foot the most of human and parental rights—the crying injustice of com- pulsory vaccination, a law which none but tyrants could have passed; which none but slaves should obey. When a law comes into conflict with reason, right, and truth, re- sistance, not servile obedience, is the duty of every citizen. 'roe responsibility of Guardians and Magistrates to God and man is above their responsibility to the law of the land, which, as in the else before us, may be vile and corrupt and oppree'd to the commonweal. " Justice" need not fear that "the structure of anti- vaccination will be scattered to the winds." It stands on too firm a basis for that. Already. the law is virtually a dead letter in Leicester, Keighley, Dewskury, and other towns; whilst house to house canvasses Tonducted in 40 towns and villages hive attested the fact, long known to the leaders of the agitation, that over 90 per cent of the adult householders of those towns are opposed to compul- sory vaccination. And if " Justice " survives a few years more he may possibly see the same fate befall vaccination as happened to the antecedent medical delusion inoculation, which, after a reign of 120 years, was in 1840 made a penal offence.—Yours very truly,
WM. YOUNG. The London Society for the Abolition of Com- pulsory Vaccination, 77. Atlantic-road, Brix- ton, S.W., August 9, 1886.
FRODSHAM.

OPEN AIR CONCERT.-1)n Saturday afternoon the fifth open air concert was held in the main street, Frodsham, when the Ellesmere Port Brass Band gars the following selection, namely :—Pas Redouble. Belphegor," E. Brep- ; Fantasia, " Pastorella," E. Villiers; Valse, " Britan- nia," H. Round; Selection, 'Bohemian Girl," Balfe ; Solo Cornet, "Lost Chord," Sir A. Sullivan; Polka, "Paul and Virginia," H. Round; Finale, "God save the Queen."

OPENING OF A CHURCH OF ENGLAND BOYS' HOME AT KINGSLEY —An interesting ceremony took place in the quiet village of Kingsley, near Prodsham, on Saturday, thd occasion bemig the opening of the fourth Boys' Home in connection with the Cnurch of England Central Seciety for Providing Homes for Waite and Strays. The society has, in addition to the Boys' Homes above referred to, eleven homes for girls, including one at Sherbrooke, Canada, and and it is intended to extend the system to each diocese, and considering that the society only commenced operations in 1982, it has already made great progress. The arrangements in connection with the Home at Kingsley have been success- fully carried out by a local committee, consisting of Mrs. Kay (Davenham), Mrs. Whytehead (Norley), Miss lascelles (Norley), Mies Woodhouse (Norley), Miss Simpson (Frod- sham), 'Miss Wilbraham (Delamere House), Mr. C. T. Gar- fits (Rube), the Vicars of Frodsham, Norley, and Kingsley, and Mrs. A. P. Reynolds (Kingsley), bon. sec. The Com- mittee have secured on lease a commodious house, plei- santly situated at Kingsley, which has for many years been occupied as a high-class school by Mr. Overton. Eleven boys are at present located at the Home, two being from the county of Chester, and tho remainder from various Darts of the country. There is ample accommodation for 50 boys, as there are twelve rooms, two at present being comfortably fitted up as dormitories. Tbe boys will attend the village school, and are to be instructed in useful occupations by Mr. Lett, the master, assisted by his wife, who acts as ma- tron. The proceedings on Saturday commenced with a ,special service in Kingsley Parish Church. An address was delivered by the Rev. J. W. Horsley, M.A., Clerical Secretary to the society/ from the woids "To the poor the Gospel is preached." An adjournment was made to the home when the Bishop of Chester stood at the front entrance and after askinga divine blessing upon the undertaking, declared the Home open.—Dr. Waters (Chester) moved a vote of thanks to the Bishop of Chester, for his kindnEss in attending the proceedings.—The motion was seconded by the Rev. H. B. Blogg, and carried —The collection in the Church amounted to £3O 13s 3d.
SUPPOSED LOSS OF 40 LIVES.

On Friday morning, a colliery explosion occurred at the Woodend Colliery, Leigh, belonging to Mr. John Speakman. About 160 men went down the mine in the morning, but only 38 were working in the No. 1 seam where the explosion took place. As soon as it became known, exploring parties went down, and many persons were found shockingly mutilated. Great excitement prevails in the town. The Press Association Leigh correspondent tele- graphs: On Friday morning about half-past eleven o'clock, at the No. 1 pit of Woodend Col- lieries, Leigh, there was a •very great explosion. About forty men were working in the seam at the time, and so great was the force of the outburst that some portion of the roof was blown down, and thus prevented their escape for some time. In the whole of the mine there were over 150 men, and as soon as it became known that an accident had oc- curred, all who could immediately ascended. An exploring party was soon formed, and, descending the pit, removed the block. On reaching the en- tombed men it was found that many of them were shockingly burnt about the head, face, and body. There are still a large number of miners in the burning mine. Medical men and clergymen quickly arrived on the scene. Up to one o'clock there had been two dead bodies found but it is feared that the number will be largely increased. Telegraphing at 2-15 p.m. a correspondent said:— There is now no hope whatever of saving the lives of about 40 men and boys. The exploring party are stopped at the entrance to the brow where the explosion took place. By 2-30 the mana- gers of other collieries were arriving. These inclu- ded Messrs. Bootle and Barton, of Bickershaw Col- liery, Mr. Walshaw, Astley and Tyldesley, and Mr. Fletcher, Atherton Collieries. They descended at once. Two bodies of lads have been brought up since noon. It will be seen how painful are the surroundings when it is stated that both their fathers are in the exploring party, and both recog- nised the dead before being brought out of the pit; yet they bravely stuck to their posts. There is no immediate prospect of recovering any more bodies. ANOTHER ACCOUNT. On Friday forenoon a colliery explosion took place at Woodend Pit, Bedford, near Leigh, belonging to Mr. John Speakman. The news that the pit had fired, as it is called, spread with the greatest rapidity. The Leigh County Court was sitting, and the intelligence had a shocking effect on several females there, whose relatives were known to be at work in the pit. As we passed through the fields to the scene of the disast6r crowds were hastening to the pit in every direction, and the wails of the women were most heartrending. In has transpired that the explosion occurred on the west side of the four feet mine, and in number one brow. The men on the east side, that nearest Tyldesly, rushed out of the workings to the pit eye. One of them, Henry Hilton. informed us that he was knocked down by the force of the concussion. His wife met him on the way, and gave him a reception of the most touching character. The explosion is said to have ' taken place about eleven o'clock. Only two men, as far as we could asceitain, have come out of what is almost certainly known to be a part of the mine where there has been a serious loss of life. These men's names are John Wooley and P. Board- man. Woolley was badly burned, and he was attended by Dr. Doyle. Dr. Anderton was also pre- sent. Some of the men who came up say they nar- rowly escaped being struck down with after damp. James Ratcliffe and others ran a distance of 400 yards. Several volunteers were soon on the pit bank.

THE EXPLORING PARTY AT WORK. The Central News telegraphs: —lt was soon dis- covered that the explosion had occurred on the west side of the four feet mine, and in N0..1 brow. The miners on the east side, that nearest Tyldesley, rushed out of the workings to the pit eye, and one of them, Henry Hilton, said he was knocked ! down by the force of the concussion. It wasj almost certain that there had been serious loss of ! life in that part of the mine where the full force of j the explosion expended itself. At the time of tele- graphing only two men had got clear of this , section. These were P. Boardman and john Wcolley, the latter of whom, however, did not es- cape without being severely burnt. His injuries were attended to 'by Dr. Doyle, who, with Dr. Anderton, had been promptly summoned to tha colliery. Some of the men who came up from other parts of the mine stated that they narrowly escaped being struck down by after damp. An eager band of volunteers was soon on the pit bank, and an exploring party was quickly organised by Mr. Wm. Sarrobin, manager, and Mr. Calland, under- looker. Among them was Mr. Henry Speakman, son of the proprietor of the colliery, who was him- self unable to be present through illness. Mr. Richard Greenough and Mr. J. Greenough, brothers- in-law of the proprietor, directed operations above ground, and saw that every necessary attention was given to the injured. Cabs were kepi in readiness to convey the disabled miners to their homes. The exploring party made but slow progress, in conse- quence of the after-damp. They, of course, directed their steps towards the number one brow, where the following, among other miners, were known to have been working ;—lliram Pemberton, William Hart, Thomas Hindley, Michael Daniel, Thomas Fair dough, William !Heaton, Allen Hadfield; and William Eckersley. BRINGING UP THE DEAD. After making strenuous efforts the explorers came upon some dead bodies, and the first corpse was get to the bank at 1-15 p m.; it was that of Benjamin Hilton, a boy, and almost immediately afterwards the body of another lad, named William Heaton, was brought up. The former had an arm blown off, and the skull of the latter was laid bare in a shocking manner. The fathers of these boys were among the exploring party, and both recognised their sons at the bottom of the pit, but they con- tinued bravely at their wuk. The bodies having been taken to a shop on the pit brow, and formally examined by a surgeon, they were conveyed to the wheelwright's shop to be laid out. DIFFICULTIES OF THE EXPLORERS. Meanwhile, the scene at the Pit mouth was most solemn and impressive. Outward excitement seemed to have disappeared, giving place to a feeling of profound suspense on the part of the crowd, which rapidly increased as the spreading of the dreadful news brought streams of workpeople from the outer districts. The main way to the colliery was lined by people, and so was every other road and path- way converging upon the spot. Although delay j possibly meant death to the imprisoned miners, it was 1 impossible for the explorers to proceed a yard without carrying air with them by means of bratticing. A ! second great difficulty was the blockage which had ! been caused by the fallingin of large masses of the roof. In the face of these two great inipediments the explorers .were some seven hundred yards dis- tant, from the entombed miners. From the bottom of the shaft there iS a level of three.hundred yards, and then a rise of three or four hundred yards, and it is at the far end of this working that about forty lives are believed to have been lost. Mr. Harry Speakman managed to '(Yet as far as the entrance to the brow. But beyond, the way was congealed with detached rock. Whilst the explorers were trying to overcome the obstacles which beset their path, Messrs. Barton and Booth, managers of the Bickershom Colliery, arrived, and rendered valuable assistance below ground. The staff of surgeons was also reinforced, Drs. Boyle and Anderton being joined by Drs. Jones and Perrin, the last-named of whom has had considerable experience in colliery accidents.

The Liverpool City Council on Wednesday determined to ask the Home Office to consent to the ernpleyment of twelve mounted police for the city. INDEPENDJINT METHODIST 3.-011 Sunday sermons were preached in the Independent Mission Room, Bridge-street, Earlestown, by Mr. Robert Henshaw, of Warrington. There were fairly large attendances, and the addresses were of an impressive character.

div.head: REINFORCEMENTS.
div.p: REINFORCEMENTS.

Among others who descended the shaft at a later hour were Mr. Robinson. of the Wigan Coal and Iron Company, Mr. Gerrard Johnson, formerly underlooker tor Messrs. T. Fletcher and Sons, and Mr. John Walshaw, of the Astley and Tyldesley Coal and Salt Company. Mr. Joseph Dickinson, Chief Inspector of Mines, arrived at the colliery about three o'clock, and at once descended. About the same time Mr. John Smith and Mr. Pearce, the eminent colliery engineers, went to the pit for the purpose of giving technical advice. The explorers, who made, but little headway, were copiously supplied with brattice cloth, and the ranks were constantly being reinforced by volunteers from. neighbouring collieries. Those of them who were stricken down by after-damp were sent to the pit mouth by their fellows, and received restorations at the hands of the medical staff. One of the ex- plorers, Jonathan Pemberton, was so seriously afflicted by the after-damp, that it was deeme d expedient to send him home.

A Cabinet Council was held in Lord Iddesleigh's room at the Foreign Office on Friday afternoon. CRICKET: England, first innings' 434; Australians, first innings, 68 ; second innings, eight for no wicket. The camp of the National Artillery Association was broken up at Shoeburyness on Friday, and everything 'passed off well.
A fire occurred early on Friday morning, in the building sheds of the Harbour Trust at the Prince of Wales Dock, Swansea, and It was not subdued before much damage was dons.
The Rev. C. G. Foster, M.A., senior curate of St. George's, Scarborough. and formerly engaged at a church in South Wales, has just been received into the Church of Rome.

A dispatch from Port Moody, British Columbia, states that the inhabitants of Junean City and Douglas Island, Alaska, have expelled seventy-five Chinamen and are ship- ping them to Fort Wrangel. THE TUNNEL ACCIDENT.—The coroner's jury, in the in- quest of the bodies of the men kill:d by the fall of the tun- nel near Newross, returned a verdict on Friday of wilful negligence against the contractors. The Colonial and Indian representatives concluded their provincial tour on Friday afternoon by a visit to the ex- tensive works of the London and North-Western Railway Company at Crewe, where they were entertained at lun- cheon. MARRIAGE OF MADAME CHRISTINE NILSSON.—Madame Christine Nilsson was recently married in Paris, in the presence of a large number of English friends. The matter was kept very quiet, none of the newspapers noticing the ceremony. The honeymoon was spent in Spain. THE QUEEN.—The Queen, accompanied by the Prince and Princess Henry of Battenberg, will leava Osborne on Tuesday morning en route for Balmoral. Her Majesty will break her journey at Edinburgh, where she visits the Inter- national bxhibition, and thence proceed to Balmoral, where the Court will remain until November.

FIRE AT CHESTER.—ShortIy after seven o'clock on Fri- day morning a fire broke out in smile warehouses situated in Goustall-lane, near the Cathedral, Chester. The flames extended to a house in front of Messrs. Dickson's seed warehouse. The house and back premises were completely gutted, and the staircase of Messrs. Dickson's warehouse burned. The extent of damage is large.

MURDER IN SOUTH WALEST—A horrible murder was re- ported on Friday morning from Llandyssul, in South Wales. It is said that a woman residing at Cefusgarn exas- perated at the confinement of her danehter, placed the baby when a week old in a basket and burned it to death. When charged with the crime, the old woman is said to have ex- pressed regret that she did not burn the bed on which her daughter lay. THE LONDON POLICE AND THE SOCIALISTS.—The trial of Williams and Mainwaring, the London Socialists, for caus- ing obstruction by holding meetings in Edgeware-road, was closed on Friday at the Middlesex Sessions,. Jury returned into court at twenty .five minutes past three o'clock with a verdict of "guilty." His lordship fined each of the defend- ants £2O, and ordered them to find sureties in £5O each to keep the peace for twelve months. He regretted he bad no power to order them to pay the costs of the prosecution. He liberated the defendants until Tuesday to enable them to pay the fine, or else they would be c4mmitted for two months.

SHORT TIME IN THE COTTON TRADE.—A. meeting of the Cotton Spinners' Association was held at Manchester on Friday, to consider as to short time. There was a large at- tendance of members of the committee. The digest of the returns, as prepared by the Secretary, was placed npon the table, and therefrom it appeared that including the Bolton fine spinning district only oce-thira of the mills working sale yarns had consented to adopt short time. Excluding Bolton district, it appeared that the proprietors of only four- ninths of the spindles spinning sale yarns were willing to work short time. As two-thirds of the spinners of sale yarns were required to assent to the proposals before they were acted upon, it is apparent that the proposals will have to be abandoned.

DRUNKENNESS. —At the Newton. Town Hall on SAturday, before Mr. T. J 4., Gidesui-, John Malley, labourer, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Mercer- treet on the previous evening. The case was proved by Police Constable Spencer, and the prisoner was fined 55 and costs.

• QUARTERLY RETURN OF BIRTHS AND DEATHS IN WARRINGTON, According to the Registrar General, there were 230,924 births registered in England and Wales in the past quarter; the birth rate was thus 33 2 per I,ooo* or very nearly 2 per 1.000 below the mean of the corresponding quarter in 10 years. The deaths in the same period were 125.172, which is equal to a rate of 18.0, and this also is very nearly 2 per 1,000 below the mean of ten years. This is the lowest death rate for the June quarter since registration commenced in 1837. This is one of the satisfactory features of the current return, pointing to the existence of an excellent state of the public health in the past quarter. The urban rate is calculated at 18.3, and that of the rural population at 175. neither reaching the average of ten years. With respect to the causes of death, it is in the highest degree satisfactory to find that the deaths by infectious diseases continue far under the average rate; this is apparent on noting that the death rate under this head is 1 6 nes 1,000 inhabitants, whereas the mean of ten years is 2.3. Whooping cough, diarrhoea and measles, as well as fever and diarrhoaa, did not reach the average. Diphtheria happened at the average rate, but scarlet fever was considerably under it. There were 14,030 deaths in workhouse, hospitals, and other public institutions, and 4,013 were due to vio- lence.

The marriage returns for the last quarter of the year do not show much improvement as far as the rate is concerned thus, the rate is calculated at 114, and this does not reach ' the mean of ten years by Pl. The present rate is said to be the lowest one for the last quarter of a year since the commencement of registration in 1837. In the three months that ended 30th June last there were 739 births and 347 deaths registered in the district or union of Warrington. the latter total occurring against an aver- age of 348, taken from the three previous corresponding periods. There were 79 deaths of infants under 1, and 80 took place at 60 and upwards. There were 27 deaths re- corded in public institutions, 22 were inquired into before the coroner, and 16 were due to violence. The fatal cases of the principal infectious diseases were—Measles 3, scarlet fever 3, diphtheria 1, whooping cough 12, fever 2, diarrhcea 6. It is seen that the deaths returned for the past quarter show singular agreement with the average of the three pre- vious corresponding totals, and it is further highly assuring to find singularly few deaths referred to infectious diseases, only 27 deaths coming under this head, most of these, too, being fatal eases of whooping cough. The local re- turns give 83 deaths for the Newton sub-district, 4 more than the average. Measles, scarlet fever, wad fever of another type each caused 1, diarrhea% 3, and whooping cor.th 4. In the Winwick sub-district there were only 4 deaths, 2 less than the average. Not one of these was due to a zymotic disease. In the Sankey district there were 10 deaths, 4 less than the average. Two were fatal cases of scarlet fever. In the Warrington sub-district the births I were 432 and the deaths 217, or two more than the average. Measles caused 2, whooping cough 8, fever 1, and diarrhea 3. In the Latchford district the deaths were 23, or 2 less than the average. One of these was due to diphtheria. In the Rixton sub-district the deaths were 10, or 1 over the average. No death here was referred to as a zvmotic dis- ease. In Lancashire there were 33,245 births placed on record in the oast quarter, as well as 19,514 deaths. The latter do not reach the average by 799, whereas the births show an excess of 521 over the estireate. There were 2.294 deaths in Workhouses, Hospitals, and other public institutions, 897 coroner's inquests were held, and 572 deaths were due to violence, or in other words, they were chiefly fatal accidents. Eight deaths were dne to smallpox. Measles proved the most fatal of the aymotic diseases, having caused 588 deaths: whooping cough following with a total of 460. and diarrhoea with 351. There were 217 deaths by scarlet fever, 154 by other fevers, and 93 by diphtheria. This is, on the whole, a very satisfactory return for the season. Four deaths by smallpox figure in the Blackburn district return. Measles was chiefly fatal in the Ashton, Oldham, Black- burn, and Preston districts. The fatal cases of scarlet fever as well as of fevers of other types, are scattered over the vari- ous districts, but none of the totals are at alltigh. On examining the various district returns, it appears that the deaths from all causes agreed very closely with the respec- tive averages, and in many cases the estimate was not nearly reached.

div.p: the workers ascertained that no part of the pit was on fire.

PROVIDENTIAL ESCAPES. As is usual in cases of this kind some providential escapes are recorded. Thomas Wilcock, of Platt- fold, Leigh, for instance, in the ordinary course of things would have been in the explosion. How- ever, being unwell in the morning, he decided not to go to work. Singularly enough, this man would have been in the Abram explosion had he not been unsu-icessful in an application for employment on the morning preceding the disaster. On the other hand Robert bole, who has a small patch of land, and has been harvesting his hay during the past few weeks, renewed work at the pit in the morn- ing, and is believed to be among the killed. LOCALITY OF THE PIT. The Woodend Pit has been in working order for seven or eight years, having been sunk by Mr. Speakman. Those who know the locality will remember that it is close to the Bedford Branch of the Eccles, Tyldesley, and Wigan Railway, being nearly mid way between Tyldesley and Leigh and Bedford stations.

div.head: MINISTERIAL RE-ELECTIONS.
div.p: MINISTERIAL RE-ELECTIONS.

The remit of the poll in St. George's Division of Tower- Hamlets was declared on Friday morning as fellows :—C. 'l'. Ritchie (C), 1,546; R. Eve (L), 999. The above figures are from the Press Association. The Central News and Ex- change Telegraph Company give the same figures for Mr. Ritchie. but those for Mr. Eve are stated by the former to be 658, and by the latter 888. Lord John Manners was on Friday re.elected for East LPicestershire on joining the Cabinet as. Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster.
The Right Hon. Henry Cecil Raikes was on Friday morn in nominated for re-election as member for Cambridge University. There being no opposition, Mr. Raikes was de- clared elected.

Mr. G. H. A. M•Donald, Lord Advocate for Scotland, was re-elected en Friday afternoon unopposed for Edinburgh and St. Andrew's University. On Friday Mr. Pinnket was proposed for re-election for Dublin University by the Rev. Dr. Stubbs and seconded by Dr. Batten. Mr. Holmes was proposed for re-election by the Rev. Thomas Gray and seconded by Dr. William Moore. The Rey. Thomas Mills proposed, but afterwards withdrew, Mr. Gamble, County Court judge. Mr. Holmes promised to discharge his duties as Attorney-General with strict impartiality and energy. There being no other candi- dates, Messrs_ Plunktt and Holmes were declared elected. Lord Arthur Hill was nominated the Conservative can- didate for West Down Division on Friday. There being no otber candidate. Lord Arthur Hill was declared duly elected.

div.head: BELFAST RIOTS.
div.p: THE BELFAST RIOTS.

The Central News special correspondent, televanhing on Friday moming, says :—Since eight o'clock on Thursday night, the streets have been comparatively deserted. except by the military and police. Rain has persistently fallen. In view of the fact that Saturdays and Sundays are pro- ductive in these times of a censideratile amount of intem- perance, the magistrates Intend. I understand, to issue an order closing all public-houses from five this afternoon until ten on Monday morning. Complaints are still very rife as to the alleged intoler- ance shown by Protestant employers of labour against their Catholic servants, and many instances are quoted in the papers in which such servants have had notice to leave their work. Intimidation is also said to be very rife.

The constabulary and soldiers are getting fearfully fagged by the long hours of duty imposd upon them, while the general trade of the town is suffering great depression. All was quiet in the disturbed districts on Friaay morning. The military and police have been largely withdrawn into the barracks, and it is most satisfictory to be assured that the authorities are not now apprehensive of any further disturhances. Market day wAs held on Friday as usual. It is quits certain that the exict number of killed will never be known, many funerals having taken place privately at night. since the outbreak upwards of two hundred in- jured have been treated at the Royal Hospital, where there now remain fifty patients,

At the half-yearly meeting of the Belfast-street Tramway Company on Friday, it was sttted that considerable damage bad been done to th 3 company's property by the rioters. The question of compensation was under the consideration of the authorities, and it was hoped that the company would n.t sustain much, if any, loss. A dividend of 5 per cent per annum was decLred. A deputation of Ulster ProVstants waited on the Mayor of Belfast on Friday and presented a requisition urging the necessity of a Royal Commission to irquire into the riots.

div.head: HAY WOK.
div.p: HAY WOK.

WESLEYAN BAND• OF HOPE DEMONSTRATION.—The an- nual gala and demonstration in connection with the Hay- dock Wesleyan Methodist Band of Hope Society was held in beautiful weather on Saturday afternoon. The members and friends, together numbering nearly 300 persons, assem- bled at the school, and under the directions of Mr. G. H. Hunt were formed in processional order. The procession was headed by the Haydock brass band, and the band was followed by Mr. Jilin Fairhurst (vice-president of the so- ciety), and Mr. G. H. Hunt. Numerous banners in the procession gave the demonstration a pleasant anpearan,e. They marched down the road as far as the Toll Bar, where they returned near to St. James's Cherch. By the kind per- mission of Mrs. Evans, they next entered the beautiful gar- dens and grounds surrounding her residence,. The Reyes, and on leaving here they entered an adjoining field, which Mrs. Evans had kindly lent for the occasion. During the afternoon those present were regaled with refreshments, in- cluding tea, buns, &0.. The customary sports were heartily indulged in and the company separated at dusk.

div.head: NEW HOSPITAL FOR HAYDOCK.
div.p: A NEW HOSPITAL FOR HAYDOCK.

An interesting ceremony was performed on Saturday afternoon, when Mrs. Evans, whose kind and generous dis- position in all matters affecting deserving institutions, for- mally laid the foundation stone of a new hoinital for the township. For a few years a cottage hospital has been in existence near St. James's Church, but this was found ...two inadequate and inconvenient for the requirements of the neighbourhood, where collieries abound on every band. The cottage hospital has done a great deal to alleviate the suf- fering of those who had met with unfortunate Injuries in the district, and the new institution, it is expected will pro- vide the accommodation required for more extended opera- tions in that direction. About four o'clock on Saturday afternoon a procession of gentlemen was, formed at the offices of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., and among those present were the Rev. James Allatt, Congregational Minis- ter, Newton, D. J. W. Watkins, Newton, Dr. T. E. Hayward, medical officer to the Cottage Hospital, Mr. E. Jackson (the energetic secretary), Messrs. B. B. Glover, Turten, Forest, Baines (members of the committee), J. Billinge, W. Bal. harry, J. Halton, and James Worsley. The gentlemen, pre- ceded by the Havdock brass band, marched to the site of the new hospital, near the vicarage, and shortly afterwards Mrs Evans, accompanied by Mr. C. Pilkington, J.P., appeared on the scene. Round the site of the new hospital a very large number of ladies and gentlemen had gathered. In addition to the gentlemen previously mentioned there were present Mrs. Glover, Mrs. Hayward, Miss Glover, and the Misses Allatt and others. The proceedings were conducted by Dr. T. E. Hayward, who officiated as chairman.. The Chairman remarked it mightseem strange they should associate any signs of rejoicing with such an occasion as that, but they might well rejoice that although there was humble sorrow and suffering existing among them, Provi- dence bad placed within their reach the means fof relieving it. He thought it was very fitting that the foundation stone of that new building should be laid by one who bad shown so much interest in the founding of the hospital. (Ap- plause.) The foundation stone was then formally laid by Mrs. Evans, who used a handsome silver trowel, which bore the following inscription : "Presented to Mrs. Josiah Evans on the occasion of laying the foundation stone of the Haydock Cottage Hospital, August 7th, 1886.." She afterwards re- marked that they were all glad to meet for such a purpose as that, to manifest that they were people of peace, trying to save men's lives and not to destroy them. She commen- ted upon the valuable services of Dr. T. E. Hayward, sin re. gard to Ambulance instruction and said that might be con- sidered as the first step taken towards the erection of the hospital. She thanked them for the kind wish that she should have the honour of laying the foundation stone of that building, and she pronounced the stone to be duly and truly laid, with the fervent hope that in attempting to crown it no life should be lost nor limb injured, and that through their efficacious efforts many lives should be preserved. (Applause.) _

Mr. B. B. Glover then read a statement, giving a descrip- tion of the new building, from which it appeared that the bu4ding will contain on the ground floor an entrance hall, seven feet wide, and a waiting-room ten feet by eight feet, and two matron's rooms, each 12 feet by 12 feet. To the right of the entrance hall will be a ward for six beds, 30 feet by 21 feet, and 15 feet high, also a bathroom and w.c. Behind the waiting-room there will be an operating theatre, &c., and surgery 14 feet by 12 feet, kitchen and usual offi- ces. There will be cellars in the basement. On the first floor will be a convalescent ward, 23 feet by 12 feet, bed- room, bathroom, Jec.. At the extreme end of the site will be placed the mortuary. The plans have been prepared so that another ward can be added at the opposite side when required. The building will ne in the gothic style, of Parr bricks, faced with Doulton's pressed bricks, relieved with Ruabon terra-cotta for cornices, jambs, arches, bands, (Ste. The roof will be covered with Ruabon brown tiles and red ridges. The walls of the ward will he cemented and pain- ted. Ventilatiou will be provided for by a combin ttion of air inlets and vertical tubes for regulating ventilators at the mei. Special attention has been given to the sanitary arrangements. The site is an excellent one, adjoining the Elaydock Vicarage, and the building has been kept well up out of the ground. The work is being carried eut by Mr. Joseph Pennington, contractor, of Earlestown, from plans prepared by Mr. Beesley, architect, of Earles- town and Warrington. Mr. Glover during the course of a few temarks, said he looked upon Mrs Evans as the founder ,f the institution, as she had given £5OO towards it en the condition that the work was commenced in 12 months after he offer. ( Appl i use.) Mr. C. Pilkington, J.P., next read a financial statement in regard to the cottage hospital, near St. James's Church, dealing with the past three r.ars. The present balance in the bank was £lB2 Is Bd. The' cost of erecting the new

hospital had been estimated at £1,834 13s 2d,towards Which they had £1,512 81 31 promised, leaving £322 46 lid yet to be realised. He mentioned that in addition *iv Mrs Elan!, who had given £5OO, Mr. Evans bad also given £5O, and other members of the Evans' family had contrittoted large amounts. He (Mr. Pilkington) thought there were very' 17 few buildings started under such favourable circumstances, as to be only £3OO short of the total estimated cost, and he hoped they would strive to carry oat what they had ro begun. (Applause.)—The Rev. James Allatt offered op prayer and pronounced the benediction, and the procedillgt eoncluded.—A number of contributions, including £5 from Mrs Evans, were afterwards placed upon the stone.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NEWTON DIVISION OF THE COUNTY OF LANCASTER. Gurruttlan.—l have the honour to offer myself as a candidate for the representation of your division at the elee- lien rendered necessary by the elevation of Sir R. A. Crosse to the Peerage. At the last general election Mr. Gladstone was not suocessin in obtaining a majority in support of the measure he intro- duced to establish a better system of Government in Ireland by giving to the Irish people the right to legislate upon and manage their local affairs. His failure was due not to the opposition of the Conservative party, which is still in a minor- ity. but to the unfortunate differences which existed in the Liberal party, • These differences will not, I hope, continue to exist any longer. lam a supporter of Mr. Gladstone. and shall do all can to sleet him in pushing forward the great work he has taken in hand. I believe that his Irish policy in no way threatens or endangers the union between Great Britain and Ireland. This is a union which we believe must exist, and which we are determined shall exist; but is it wise to persist In maintaining the Union by coercion and a system of govern- ment which alienates the people of Ireland and leaves them dissatisfied, and seriously interferes with our ewe govern- ment In England? The Liberal party proposes to conirm and perpetuate the Union by a wise and prudent measure which will give to the Irish people the management of their own local affairs, reserving to the Imperial Parliament absolute con- trol over the general interests, and filly securing the integrity of the Empire. I believe the English people are not, and ought not to be, afraid to tenet the people of Ireland to manage their own affairs. Trust in the people has been the leading principle of Liberalism in all the great struggles which have been made in support of popular rights. I am satisfied that a broad and generous measure settling the Irish question will add to the prosperity of that country. giving to the Irish labourer home employment, so lessening the compekition now caused in the English labour market. I shall give close attention to all questions relating to the mining population, and shall give my most hearty and thorough support to measures for their benefit and protection. I think the question of the mining royalties now payable to landowners in many pats of the coun.ry should be inquired into and dealt with in those cases where it stops the working of mines and interferes with the employment of the people. The land laws of England stand in great need of reform: I am in:favour of the aholition of primogeniture. and the system of entailing land which crea, es great estates and interferes with the acquisition of small holdings by people of moderate means. Any changes should be in the direction of facilitsting and cheapening the trawsfer of land, so that every man may have an opportunity of acquiring an interest in the soil in the country in which he lives and labours. The positi.:e of English farmers is at present so unsatisfac- tory that I should gladly support any measures for giving full security for fixity of tenure and compensation for improve- ments. In this direction I think relief is to ,be found ia the depressed state of agriculture, and I should strongly oppose any schemes for taxing the food ef the people, which would be really in the landowners' f4vour. I am strongly in favour of religious Lbe, ty and equality, and shall offer the strongest opposition to any attempt to alter the present system of denominational education. If the law com- pels parents to educate their children, they Should have the right of securing for their children a religious education accord- ing to their own convic!ions. I am, your obedient servant, D. o'o. FRENCH.

!persons were bruised, but no serious injury resulted. At night serious riotswere with difficulty prevented . when the Queen's Island men marched in a body one thousand strong,•past the Catholic quarter, and it was only the overwhelming military force which prevented a collision. The situation is still very strained. Several inquests have been opened. The magistrates had several rioters before them on Tues- day, and inflicted exemplary punishment on them. Mr. Biggar, M.P., at a meeting of the-Catholic Com- mittee, accused the magistrates and Protestant clergy of having encouraged the rioters, and the magistrates especially for not acting justly on the Bench, and added that the Mayor of Belfast ought to be in the dock of the Criminal Court for having participated in the riots. There were no fresh outbreaks in Belfast on Wed- nesday, but the police and the military continued to exercise the greatest vigilance. During the day several persons who were killed during the riots were buried. Dr. Kane, the Orange Grand Master for the Ulster istrict, is reported to have stated in an interview with a representative of the press, in , , reference to. the Belfast riots, that the Catholics " began it," that they are " always the assailants," 1 but that, seeing the police ready to do their work, they cease fighting and go home as soon as the con- , stabulary interfere. , The news from Belfast is again peaceful, al- though Thursday was the anniyersary of "the re- lief of Derry." The historic event was celebrated by the Orangemen of Londonderryin the usual way. It is reported that a couple of bottles loaded with gunpowder and having burning. fuses attached to them were thrown at the Prentice Boys' Baud, but without doing any injury.
